## Before taking this medicine
Do not take tramadol if you are:
- are allergic to tramadol, to any of the other ingredients in your product, or to other opioids
- have significant breathing problems (respiratory depression)
- have acute or severe asthma and are somewhere you cannot be monitored, or where resuscitation equipment is not available
- have a known or suspected blockage of the stomach or intestines, including paralytic ileus
- have taken a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) in the past 14 days (such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, or tranylcypromine)
- are younger than 12 years of age
- are younger than 18 years of age and have recently had surgery to remove your tonsils or adenoids.
Seizures have occurred in some people taking tramadol. Your seizure risk may be higher if you have ever had:
- a head injury, epilepsy, or other seizure disorder
- drug or alcohol addiction or
- a metabolic disorder.
To make sure tramadol is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have a history of:
- Head injury or seizures
- Problems urinating
- Liver, kidney, or thyroid problems
- Pancrease or gallbladder problems, including pancreatitis or surgery on your pancreas
- A serious infection
- Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, opioid overdose, or mental health problems.
Also tell your doctor if you are dehydrated, are eating less or have changed your diet, are on a low-sodium (salt) diet, drink a lot of alcohol, or are planning to have surgery.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are:
- Living in a household where there are small children or someone who has abused street or prescription drugs
- Taking prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements. Taking tramadol with certain other medicines can cause serious side effects that could lead to death
- Notice your pain getting worse. If your pain gets worse after you take tramadol, do not take more tramadol without first talking to your doctor. Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain after taking tramadol.
Important Information Guiding Use in Pediatric Patients:
- Do not give tramadol to a child younger than 12 years of age or extended-release tramadol to anyone under 18 years.
- Do not give tramadol to a child younger than 18 years of age after surgery to remove the tonsils and/or adenoids.
- Avoid giving tramadol to children between 12 and 18 years of age who have risk factors for breathing problems. These include having recently had surgery, obstructive sleep apnea, obesity, severe lung disease, neuromuscular disease, and taking other medicines that can slow breathing.
Pregnancy:
Tramadol may harm an unborn baby and is not usually recommended during pregnancy. Use of tramadol for an extended period of time during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby that could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated. Neonatal seizures, neonatal withdrawal syndrome, fetal death, and stillbirth have all been reported. Tramadol is also not recommended during or immediately before labor. It should only be used in pregnancy if the benefits outweigh the risks. If you are already taking tramadol and become pregnant, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping suddenly can be harmful to you both.
Breastfeeding:
Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking tramadol, as it may harm your baby. Mothers who are ultra-rapid metabolizers of tramadol can have higher than expected levels of its active form in their breast milk, which can be dangerous for a breastfed infant. Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness. Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs.

## How should I take spironolactone?
Take spironolactone exactly as prescribed. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides.
- Take it the same way each day, either always with food or always without. Food increases how much spironolactone your body absorbs, roughly doubling it, so switching back and forth changes how much medicine you actually get.

- If you are being treated for high blood pressure, keep taking spironolactone even when you feel fine. High blood pressure usually has no symptoms.
- Tell any doctor or dentist treating you that you take spironolactone, and tell your surgeon before any operation.
- Spironolactone can interfere with one type of blood test used to measure digoxin, so mention it if you take digoxin.
- Do not share this medicine with anyone else.
- Store tablets at room temperature, 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C), and protect them from light. Store the oral liquid at room temperature and keep it in a tightly closed bottle.

## Spironolactone FAQs
Is spironolactone a diuretic?:
Yes. Spironolactone is a diuretic, or water pill, and it belongs to the group called potassium-sparing diuretics. It works by blocking aldosterone, a hormone that makes your kidneys hold onto salt and water. Unlike most water pills, which make you lose potassium, spironolactone makes your body keep potassium in. It is a weaker diuretic than medicines such as furosemide, which is one reason it is often given alongside another water pill rather than instead of one.
Is spironolactone used for acne?:
Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating acne, but doctors sometimes prescribe it off-label for hormonal acne in women. Off-label means a doctor is prescribing a medicine for something other than its approved uses, which is legal and common, but it means the FDA has not reviewed the medicine for that purpose.
The reason it is used this way relates to how spironolactone works. As well as blocking aldosterone, spironolactone attaches to the androgen receptor, the docking point for male hormones such as testosterone. Male hormones increase how much oil the skin produces, and oil production is one factor in acne.
Because acne is not an approved use, there is no FDA-approved dose for it. Any dose is chosen by the prescriber. Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy because it may affect how a male baby develops, which is an important consideration for anyone taking it for a skin condition rather than a heart or kidney condition.
If you are considering spironolactone for acne, this is a conversation to have with a doctor or dermatologist who can review your full medical history, since spironolactone still carries the same risk of raising your potassium level, whatever it is prescribed for.
Does spironolactone cause weight gain?:
Weight gain is not a recognized side effect of spironolactone, and it is not listed in the medicine's official prescribing information. Spironolactone is a diuretic, so it usually causes a small drop in weight in the first week or two as your body sheds extra fluid.
If you are gaining weight while taking it, it is worth telling your doctor rather than assuming the medicine is to blame. Rapid weight gain with swelling in your ankles or legs or shortness of breath can be a sign of fluid building up, which may mean the condition being treated needs a closer look. Slower weight gain is more often down to appetite, activity, or another medicine.
Does spironolactone cause hair loss?:
Hair thinning, known as alopecia, is listed as a possible side effect of spironolactone, though how often it happens is not known. It is reported far less often than breast tenderness or breast growth.
The picture is complicated because spironolactone is also prescribed off label for hair loss in women, on the basis that blocking male hormones may help with hormone-related thinning. Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating hair loss. If your hair is thinning while you take it, speak to your doctor, since there are several possible causes worth ruling out.
How long does it take for spironolactone to work?:
It depends what you are taking it for. Spironolactone reaches its highest level in your blood in about 2 to 3 hours, and its active breakdown product peaks at around 4 hours, so it starts having an effect on your kidneys the same day.
The results you notice take longer. For fluid build-up, spironolactone is given for at least five days before the dose is increased, because that is how long the full effect takes to show. For high blood pressure, the dose is adjusted at two-week intervals, so give it a couple of weeks before judging it. For heart failure, the benefit is a lower risk of being admitted to hospital and living longer, which is not something you feel week to week.
How long does spironolactone stay in your system?:
Spironolactone itself leaves your blood very quickly, with a half-life of about 1.4 hours, meaning half of it is gone in that time. Its active breakdown products last much longer, with half-lives of roughly 14 to 17 hours. Because of those, the effect of a dose carries on well after the spironolactone itself has gone, and it takes a few days for the medicine to clear fully after you stop. Clearance is slower if you have cirrhosis.
Is spironolactone a blood thinner?:
No. Spironolactone is not a blood thinner. It does not affect blood clotting and it is not used to prevent clots or strokes in the way that warfarin, apixaban, or aspirin are. It is a diuretic that lowers blood pressure and reduces fluid build-up.
Spironolactone does interact with some blood thinners indirectly. Heparin and low molecular weight heparin can raise potassium, so taking them with spironolactone increases the risk of a high potassium level.
Can I stop taking spironolactone suddenly?:
Spironolactone does not cause withdrawal symptoms and does not need to be tapered the way a steroid does. Even so, do not stop it without speaking to your doctor. Stopping it can allow fluid to build up again, your blood pressure to rise, or your heart failure to worsen, and if you are taking it for heart failure it is one of the medicines shown to help people live longer. If side effects are the reason you want to stop, a dose change or a different medicine may be an option.
Can you take spironolactone at night?:
There is no fixed time of day for spironolactone. What matters more is that you take it at the same time each day and always the same way with regard to food, since food changes how much you absorb. Many people prefer the morning because spironolactone makes you pass more urine, and a late dose can mean getting up in the night. If a nighttime dose suits you better, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.
Can you drink alcohol while taking spironolactone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and spironolactone, but drinking is best kept modest. Both can lower your blood pressure and make you light-headed, so together they raise the chance of feeling dizzy or faint, particularly when you stand up. Alcohol is also a problem in its own right if you are taking spironolactone for liver disease. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for your situation.
Can you take spironolactone while pregnant?:
Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy. It blocks the action of male hormones, and in animal studies male offspring exposed before birth developed abnormally. Human data are limited and have not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern is enough that the manufacturer advises avoiding it or discussing the potential risk to a male baby.
Do not stop spironolactone on your own if you find out you are pregnant. Tell your doctor straight away, because untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry serious risks in pregnancy and your treatment will need to be changed carefully.
Does spironolactone cause constipation?:
Constipation is not a listed side effect of spironolactone. The digestive side effects that have been reported are the opposite, including diarrhea and stomach cramping, along with nausea, vomiting, and indigestion. If you are constipated while taking spironolactone, another cause is more likely, and it is worth mentioning to your pharmacist, who can check the rest of your medicines.
Is 200 mg of spironolactone too much?:
It depends on the reason you are taking it. For fluid build-up, the approved dose range goes up to 200 mg a day, and for primary hyperaldosteronism it goes up to 400 mg a day, so 200 mg is within the licensed range for both.
For high blood pressure it would be above the usual range, since doses over 100 mg a day do not lower blood pressure any further. For heart failure the usual dose is 25 mg to 50 mg a day, so 200 mg would be well above what is normally used. Higher doses also carry a greater risk of high potassium and of breast growth in men. If your dose seems high for your condition, ask your prescriber rather than adjusting it yourself.
Why is spironolactone described as a high-risk medicine?:
The main reason is the risk of a high potassium level, which can cause a dangerous change in your heart rhythm and often gives no warning symptoms. The risk rises if your kidneys do not work well or if you take other medicines that raise potassium, and several very common medicines do, including ibuprofen and some blood pressure tablets.
This risk is manageable, which is why blood tests are built into treatment. Your potassium should be checked within a week of starting spironolactone or changing your dose, and regularly after that. Spironolactone also needs care in pregnancy and in people with liver disease.

## What is metformin?
Metformin is a first-line treatment used for type 2 diabetes in adults and children 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar levels. It is also used off-label to improve symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and other conditions. Metformin tablets should be used together with dietary changes and exercise for better results.
Metformin belongs to the drug class biguanides.
Metformin works by reducing glucose absorption from the intestines, lowering liver glucose production, and improving insulin sensitivity. Managing blood sugar levels with medications like metformin can prevent diabetes complications such as kidney damage, nerve issues, blindness, amputations, sexual dysfunction, and lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.

## Warnings
In rare cases, simvastatin can cause a condition that results in the breakdown of skeletal muscle tissue, potentially leading to kidney failure. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness especially if you also have fever, unusual tiredness, and dark colored urine.
Never take simvastatin in larger amounts, or for longer than recommended by your doctor. Follow your doctor's dosing instructions very carefully. Taking too much of this medication may cause serious or life-threatening side effects.
Before taking this medicine, tell your doctor if you have ever had liver or kidney disease, diabetes, a thyroid disorder, a muscle weakness condition (such as myasthenia gravis or ocular myasthenia), if you are of Chinese descent, or if you drink more than 2 alcoholic beverages daily.
Simvastatin can harm an unborn baby or cause birth defects. Do not use if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant.
Grapefruit and grapefruit juice may interact with simvastatin and lead to potentially dangerous effects. Do not consume grapefruit products while taking this medication.
Some medicines can cause unwanted or dangerous effects when used with simvastatin. Your doctor may need to change your treatment plan if you use certain antibiotics or antifungal medicines, heart medication, antiviral medications such as hepatitis C medications, HIV/AIDS medications, or Paxlovid for COVID-19.
Stop taking this medication and tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant.

## Metoprolol side effects
The most common side effects of metoprolol are tiredness, dizziness, low mood (depression), diarrhea, shortness of breath, a slow heartbeat (bradycardia), and itching or rash. Most side effects reported in studies were mild and did not last.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to metoprolol: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Common side effects of metoprolol:
In studies of people taking metoprolol for high blood pressure or angina:
- Tiredness and dizziness occurred in about 10% of people
- Low mood or depression was reported in about 5 out of 100 people
- Diarrhea occurred in about 5% of people
- Itching or rash occurred in about 5% of people
- Shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat occurred in about 3% of people
- Cold hands and feet, palpitations, swelling of the ankles, and low blood pressure were each reported in about 1% of people
- Nausea, dry mouth, stomach pain, constipation, gas, and heartburn were each reported in about 1% of people
Headache, nightmares, trouble sleeping, confusion, and short-term memory loss have also been reported.
In the heart failure study of extended-release metoprolol, dizziness or vertigo was reported by 1.8% of people taking metoprolol compared with 1.0% taking placebo, and a slow heartbeat by 1.5% compared with 0.4%.
Other reported side effects:
These have been reported since metoprolol came on the market. Their frequency is not known:
- Hair thinning or hair loss, which reversed after stopping
- Reduced sex drive and difficulty getting an erection
- Dry eyes, blurred vision, and ringing in the ears
- Sweating, sensitivity to sunlight, and worsening of psoriasis
- Change in taste, joint and muscle pain, and fainting
- Liver inflammation (hepatitis)
- A severe drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis), which can show up as fever, chills, or a sore throat
Serious side effects of metoprolol:
Some of these, such as shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat, are also listed as common side effects above. They need urgent attention when they are severe, new, or getting worse.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- A very slow heartbeat, pauses in your heartbeat, or a feeling that you might faint. Sinus pause, heart block, and cardiac arrest have all been reported.
- Signs that heart failure is getting worse, such as weight gain over a few days, more shortness of breath, or swelling of your feet or lower legs
- Wheezing or trouble breathing
- Chest pain that is worse or more frequent than usual, especially if you have recently stopped or missed doses
- Cold, pale, or blue fingers and toes, or pain in your legs when you walk
- Confusion, hallucinations, or memory problems
- Yellowing of your skin or eyes, which can be a sign of liver inflammation
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Sertraline FAQs
Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline has very little effect on norepinephrine and dopamine, and it has no meaningful effect on adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopamine, histamine, or benzodiazepine receptors, which is part of why it is described as selective.
How long does sertraline take to work?:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.
Should I take sertraline in the morning or at night?:
Either is fine. Sertraline is taken once a day, in the morning or the evening, and the label does not favor one over the other. What matters more is taking it at around the same time each day. Insomnia was reported by 20% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 13% on placebo, and sleepiness by 11% compared with 6%, so some people find one timing suits them better than the other. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does sertraline cause weight gain or weight loss?:
Reduced appetite is a common sertraline side effect, reported by 7% of adults in trials compared with 2% on placebo. Increased appetite was reported less often, in fewer than 2% of people. In children and teenagers taking sertraline for depression, there was a difference in weight change of roughly 1 kg compared with placebo over 10 weeks, representing slight weight loss on sertraline and slight gain on placebo. Around 7% of children lost more than 7% of their body weight, compared with none on placebo. In a longer 34 week extension study, weight gain was similar to what would be expected for their age. Height and weight should be monitored in younger patients. Tell your doctor about any weight change that concerns you.
Does sertraline make you tired or sleepy?:
It can. Sleepiness was reported by 11% of adults taking sertraline in trials, compared with 6% on placebo, and tiredness by 12% compared with 8%. Sertraline can also affect how clearly you think and how quickly you react, so do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.
Is sertraline a controlled substance?:
No. Sertraline is not a controlled substance. In a study comparing sertraline with alprazolam and d-amphetamine, sertraline did not produce the effects associated with a potential for misuse, such as euphoria or drug liking, that were seen with the other two medicines.
Can sertraline cause diarrhea or nausea?:
Yes, these are the two most common sertraline side effects. Nausea was reported by 26% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 12% on placebo, and diarrhea or loose stools by 20% compared with 10%. Nausea was also the most common reason people stopped treatment. Tell your doctor if these do not settle.
How do you stop taking sertraline safely?:
Lower the dose gradually rather than stopping all at once, and only under your doctor's guidance. Symptoms reported after stopping a serotonergic antidepressant, especially when it is stopped abruptly, include nausea, sweating, low or unstable mood, irritability, agitation, dizziness, unusual sensations such as electric shock feelings, tremor, anxiety, confusion, headache, lethargy, insomnia, hypomania, ringing in the ears, and seizures.
Can you drink alcohol while taking sertraline?:
Drinking alcohol is not recommended while you take sertraline. In healthy volunteers, sertraline did not increase the immediate effects of alcohol on thinking and coordination, but the advice for patients is still to avoid it. Separately, do not take sertraline oral solution with disulfiram, because the solution contains 12% alcohol.
Can you take sertraline while pregnant?:
That depends on your situation, and it is a decision to make with your doctor rather than on your own. Studies of first trimester use suggest no overall difference in the risk of major birth defects, but use late in pregnancy has been linked with newborn breathing problems and with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. At the same time, stopping an antidepressant during pregnancy raises the risk of depression coming back. The oral solution specifically is not recommended in pregnancy because it contains alcohol.
What are sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules for?:
Sertraline capsules come in 150 mg and 200 mg only, and they are not used to start treatment. They are for people who have already been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week and need a higher dose. The maximum is 200 mg a day, the same as for tablets. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not opened, crushed, or chewed. If you need to come off sertraline, the dose has to be lowered gradually using another sertraline product, because there is no capsule strength below 150 mg. Capsules are approved for depression in adults and OCD from age 6, not for panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, or PMDD.
Does sertraline interact with warfarin?:
Yes, in two ways. Sertraline can add to warfarin's effect on bleeding risk, and both medicines bind tightly to proteins in the blood, so taking them together can raise the free level of one or both. If you take warfarin with sertraline, your INR should be monitored carefully.

## Tramadol side effects
Common side effects:
The most common side effects of tramadol are:
- dizziness or vertigo
- nausea
- constipation
- headache
- drowsiness
- vomiting
- itching.
Dry mouth is also commonly reported with the extended-release forms of tramadol.
A person's genetics can affect their response to tramadol, including their risk of side effects (see How do genetics affect tramadol?).
Serious tramadol side effects and warnings:
Tramadol may cause serious side effects, some of which may be fatal.
Tramadol can slow or stop your breathing and may be habit-forming. MISUSE OF THIS MEDICINE CAN CAUSE ADDICTION, OVERDOSE, OR DEATH, especially in a child or other person using the medicine without a prescription. Keep this medicine where others cannot get to it. Do not take more tramadol than prescribed, as an overdose can be fatal. Selling or giving away this medicine is against the law.
- A person caring for you should give naloxone and seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you find it hard to wake up. Serious breathing problems may be more likely in older adults and people who are debilitated or have wasting syndrome or chronic breathing disorders.
- Call your doctor at once if you have: noisy breathing, sighing, shallow breathing, breathing that stops during sleep a slow heart rate or weak pulse a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out seizure (convulsions) or low cortisol levels (symptoms include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, dizziness, worsening tiredness or weakness) low sodium levels (hyponatremia). Symptoms include headache, confusion, weakness, unsteadiness, or feeling sick low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion, or a fast heartbeat.
Seek medical attention right away if you have symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Seizures have been reported in patients taking tramadol. Your risk of seizures is higher if you are taking higher doses than recommended. Seizure risk is also higher in those with epilepsy or a history of seizures, and in those taking certain antidepressants, other opioids, MAO inhibitors, or other medicines that lower the seizure threshold.
You should not take tramadol if you have significant breathing problems, acute or severe asthma in a setting where you cannot be monitored, a blockage in your stomach or intestines, or if you have taken an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days (isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, and others). Tell your doctor before starting tramadol if you have a head injury or increased pressure inside your skull, as tramadol should be used with particular care in these situations.
Prescribers are advised not to prescribe tramadol for people who are suicidal or prone to addiction, and to use it with caution in people taking tranquilizers or antidepressants, or drinking heavily. ## Cyclobenzaprine dosage
The usual cyclobenzaprine dose for muscle spasm is 5 mg three times a day, which may be increased to 10 mg three times a day if needed. The maximum dose is 30 mg per day. Cyclobenzaprine is taken for a maximum of 2 to 3 weeks. 1
Cyclobenzaprine dosage chart:
Immediate-release tablets: the usual starting dose is 5 mg three times a day, increased to 10 mg three times a day based on your response. In adults 65 and older and in people with mild liver problems, treatment should start at 5 mg and be increased slowly, if at all. The tablets are not recommended with moderate to severe liver impairment. 1
Amrix extended-release capsules: the recommended dose is 15 mg once daily for most adults; some people may need 30 mg once daily (one 30 mg capsule or two 15 mg capsules). Amrix is not recommended in adults 65 and older, or in anyone with liver impairment of any severity. 2
Tonmya sublingual tablets (fibromyalgia): The recommended starting dose of Tonmya is 2.8 mg (1 sublingual tablet) once daily at bedtime for the first 14 days, then increases to the target dose of 5.6 mg (2 sublingual tablets) once daily at bedtime from day 15 onward. The maximum is 5.6 mg once daily. In adults 65 and older and in people with mild liver impairment, the maximum is 2.8 mg once daily at bedtime, and Tonmya is not recommended with moderate or severe liver impairment. 3
Product | Usual adult dose | Maximum dose | How long
Immediate-release tablets, formerly sold as Flexeril (adults and children 15 and older) | 5 mg three times a day, increased to 10 mg three times a day if needed | 30 mg per day (10 mg three times a day) | Up to 2 to 3 weeks
Amrix extended-release capsules | 15 mg once daily | 30 mg once daily | Up to 2 to 3 weeks
Tonmya sublingual tablets (fibromyalgia) | 2.8 mg once daily at bedtime for 14 days, then 5.6 mg once daily at bedtime | 5.6 mg once daily | Ongoing, as directed
1,2,3
Can I take 2 cyclobenzaprine 10 mg at the same time?:
No. Do not take two cyclobenzaprine 10 mg tablets at once. The maximum recommended single dose of the immediate-release tablet is 10 mg, taken up to three times a day. Taking 20 mg at one time increases the risk of side effects such as severe drowsiness and fast heart rate, and in overdose cyclobenzaprine can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems, without providing better muscle spasm relief. If your dose is not controlling your symptoms, talk with your doctor rather than doubling up. 1
How often can you take cyclobenzaprine?:
Immediate-release tablets are taken three times a day. Amrix extended-release capsules and Tonmya sublingual tablets are taken once a day. Do not take extra doses between scheduled doses. 1,2,3
How long does cyclobenzaprine take to work, and how long does it last?:
In clinical trials of the immediate-release tablets, the muscle relaxant effect was measurable within the first several days, with significant improvement in muscle spasm and pain by day 3 or 4 of treatment. 1
With Amrix extended-release capsules, the drug is first detectable in the blood about 1.5 hours after a dose, with peak levels at 7 to 8 hours, and one daily dose provides day-long coverage. 2
How long does cyclobenzaprine stay in your system?:
Cyclobenzaprine stays in your system for about 3 to 7 days after your last dose. It has a half-life of around 18 hours for the immediate-release tablets, and a drug takes 4 to 5 half-lives to clear from the body. 1
The once-daily forms last longer: the half-life is about 32 hours for Amrix extended-release capsules and about 36 hours for Tonmya sublingual tablets, so these can take a week or more to fully clear. Cyclobenzaprine also stays in the body longer in older adults and in people with liver problems, in whom blood levels run higher. 1,2,3
Does cyclobenzaprine show up on a drug test?:
No, cyclobenzaprine does not usually show up on a drug test, as it is not a controlled substance and it is not one of the five substances (amphetamines, cannabinoids, cocaine, opiates, and phencyclidine) required on standard federal workplace drug tests. 3,5
However, cyclobenzaprine has a similar structure to tricyclic antidepressants, and it is a recognized cause of false positive results on tricyclic antidepressant immunoassays, including urine immunoassays. Tests for tricyclic antidepressants are not part of routine drugs-of-abuse screening. 5
If you take cyclobenzaprine and need a drug test, tell the testing provider what medicines you take. A screening result is only presumptive, and a confirmatory laboratory test such as gas chromatography-mass spectrometry can tell cyclobenzaprine apart from a tricyclic antidepressant. 5

## What is Tirzepatide?
Tirzepatide is a once-weekly injection available as two brands: Zepbound (for weight loss, weight management, and obstructive sleep apnea) and Mounjaro (for type 2 diabetes and to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in those with type 2 diabetes at high risk).
Zepbound (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity, or in overweight adults with at least one weight-related medical condition. Zepbound is also approved to treat moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity.
Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar (glucose) levels, used alongside diet and exercise. It is also approved to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events.
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist, meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar. It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes. It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

## Before taking this medicine
Do not take tramadol if you are:
- are allergic to tramadol, to any of the other ingredients in your product, or to other opioids
- have significant breathing problems (respiratory depression)
- have acute or severe asthma and are somewhere you cannot be monitored, or where resuscitation equipment is not available
- have a known or suspected blockage of the stomach or intestines, including paralytic ileus
- have taken a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) in the past 14 days (such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, or tranylcypromine)
- are younger than 12 years of age
- are younger than 18 years of age and have recently had surgery to remove your tonsils or adenoids.
Seizures have occurred in some people taking tramadol. Your seizure risk may be higher if you have ever had:
- a head injury, epilepsy, or other seizure disorder
- drug or alcohol addiction or
- a metabolic disorder.
To make sure tramadol is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have a history of:
- Head injury or seizures
- Problems urinating
- Liver, kidney, or thyroid problems
- Pancrease or gallbladder problems, including pancreatitis or surgery on your pancreas
- A serious infection
- Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, opioid overdose, or mental health problems.
Also tell your doctor if you are dehydrated, are eating less or have changed your diet, are on a low-sodium (salt) diet, drink a lot of alcohol, or are planning to have surgery.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are:
- Living in a household where there are small children or someone who has abused street or prescription drugs
- Taking prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements. Taking tramadol with certain other medicines can cause serious side effects that could lead to death
- Notice your pain getting worse. If your pain gets worse after you take tramadol, do not take more tramadol without first talking to your doctor. Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain after taking tramadol.
Important Information Guiding Use in Pediatric Patients:
- Do not give tramadol to a child younger than 12 years of age or extended-release tramadol to anyone under 18 years.
- Do not give tramadol to a child younger than 18 years of age after surgery to remove the tonsils and/or adenoids.
- Avoid giving tramadol to children between 12 and 18 years of age who have risk factors for breathing problems. These include having recently had surgery, obstructive sleep apnea, obesity, severe lung disease, neuromuscular disease, and taking other medicines that can slow breathing.
Pregnancy:
Tramadol may harm an unborn baby and is not usually recommended during pregnancy. Use of tramadol for an extended period of time during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby that could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated. Neonatal seizures, neonatal withdrawal syndrome, fetal death, and stillbirth have all been reported. Tramadol is also not recommended during or immediately before labor. It should only be used in pregnancy if the benefits outweigh the risks. If you are already taking tramadol and become pregnant, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping suddenly can be harmful to you both.
Breastfeeding:
Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking tramadol, as it may harm your baby. Mothers who are ultra-rapid metabolizers of tramadol can have higher than expected levels of its active form in their breast milk, which can be dangerous for a breastfed infant. Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness. Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs.

## What other drugs will affect metformin?
Many drugs can interact with metformin; this includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here. Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any medicine you start or stop using.
Medicines that have a carbonic anhydrase inhibiting effect like topiramate (often used for seizures or migraines), zonisamide (used for seizures), acetazolamide (used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, and other conditions), and dichlorphenamide (used for a muscle condition called periodic paralysis) can raise the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis when taken with metformin. These medicines commonly lower a substance in your blood called bicarbonate, which your body needs to keep its acid levels balanced. If you're taking metformin along with any of these medicines, your doctor may want to monitor you more closely.
Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.
Insulin or other diabetes medicines that raise insulin (like sulfonylureas): Combining these with metformin can lower your blood sugar too much. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you're taking more than one diabetes medicine.
Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis.
Contrast dye used in imaging tests (like CT scans): This type of dye can temporarily affect kidney function, which can let metformin build up in your body. Your doctor may have you stop taking metformin around the time of the test and restart it once your kidney function is confirmed to be back to normal.

## Cyclobenzaprine side effects
The most common cyclobenzaprine side effects are drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, fatigue, and headache. Most side effects are mild and settle as your body adjusts, but cyclobenzaprine can occasionally cause serious heart rhythm effects and serotonin syndrome. 1
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects may include: 1
- drowsiness and tiredness;
- dry mouth;
- dizziness;
- fatigue;
- headache;
- nausea, indigestion, or constipation;
- blurred vision;
- unpleasant taste;
- nervousness or confusion.
In placebo-controlled trials of the immediate-release tablets, side effects were dose-related, occurring more often with 10 mg than with 5 mg: 1
Side effect | Cyclobenzaprine 5 mg | Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg | Placebo
Drowsiness | 29% | 38% | 10%
Dry mouth | 21% | 32% | 7%
Fatigue | 6% | 6% | 3%
Headache | 5% | 5% | 8%
With Amrix, the most common side effects are dry mouth (up to 14% at 30 mg), dizziness, fatigue, constipation, nausea, indigestion, and drowsiness. 2
With Tonmya, because it dissolves under the tongue, the most common side effects involve the mouth: reduced feeling or numbness in the mouth (23%), mouth discomfort, abnormal taste, tingling, mouth pain, and canker sores, along with sleepiness, fatigue, and dry mouth. Mouth-related effects usually begin within minutes of a dose and most resolve within an hour. Moistening your mouth with sips of water before dosing reduces the risk of numbness. Tell your healthcare provider if mouth effects are severe. 3
Serious cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to cyclobenzaprine: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; or itching. 2,3
Stop taking cyclobenzaprine and call your doctor at once if you have: 1,2,3
- fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeats;
- chest pain or pressure, or pain spreading to your jaw or shoulder;
- sudden numbness or weakness, slurred speech, or balance problems; or
- symptoms of serotonin syndrome: agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness or twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Serious side effects, including confusion, hallucinations, and heart problems leading to falls, are more likely in older adults. 1
Does cyclobenzaprine make you sleepy?:
Yes, drowsiness is the most common side effect of the tablets, affecting up to 38% of people taking the 10 mg dose in clinical trials. This is one reason 5 mg is the usual starting dose, since it causes less drowsiness with comparable effectiveness. Analysis of trial data shows cyclobenzaprine relieves muscle spasm whether or not sedation occurs, so drowsiness is not required for it to work. 1
Does cyclobenzaprine cause constipation?:
Constipation is a known side effect, reported in 1% to 3% of people taking the immediate-release tablets and up to 3% of people taking Amrix 30 mg in clinical trials. It results from the drug's anticholinergic (drying) effects, the same mechanism behind dry mouth and blurred vision. 1,2
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Warnings
Cetirizine can cause side effects that may impair your thinking or reactions. Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be awake and alert. Avoid drinking alcohol. It can increase some of the side effects of cetirizine.
Tell your doctor if you regularly use other medicines that make you sleepy (such as other cold or allergy medicine, narcotic pain medicine, sleeping pills, muscle relaxers, and medicine for seizures, depression, or anxiety). They can add to sleepiness caused by cetirizine.
Call your doctor if your symptoms do not improve, if they get worse, or if you also have a fever.
If you are taking cetirizine for hives, get emergency medical help immediately if you have trouble swallowing, dizziness, swelling of the tongue or around the mouth, trouble speaking, drooling, or wheezing. Cetirizine is not a substitute for an epinephrine injector. Do not use cetirizine to prevent hives from known causes such as foods, insect stings, or medicines. Call your doctor if your hives do not improve after 3 days, if they last more than 6 weeks, or if they are an unusual color, look bruised or blistered, or do not itch.
Rarely, some people have reported severe itching when stopping cetirizine after daily, long-term use of at least a few months or several years. If you experience widespread, severe itching on stopping this medication, contact your healthcare provider.

## Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) dosage information
Your doctor will choose the smallest dose that controls your condition, and may adjust it over time. Follow your prescription label and do not change your dose yourself.
HCTZ dose for high blood pressure (adults):
Tablets: The starting dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once a day, which may be increased to 50 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Doses above 50 mg a day are often associated with a marked drop in blood potassium. Most people do not need more than 50 mg a day when hydrochlorothiazide is taken alongside other blood pressure medicines
Capsules: The starting dose is a hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg capsule once a day, whether taken on its own or with other blood pressure medicines. Total daily doses above 50 mg are not recommended. Capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
HCTZ dose for fluid retention (adults):
Tablets: The usual dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg to 100 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Many people with fluid retention respond to intermittent treatment, such as taking it every other day or on 3 to 5 days each week. Excessive response and undesirable electrolyte imbalance are less likely to occur with intermittent dosing.
HCTZ dose for children for high blood pressure and fluid retention:
The usual HCTZ dose in children, for both high blood pressure and fluid retention, is 1 mg to 2 mg per kilogram of body weight (0.5 mg to 1 mg per pound) a day, given as a single dose or split into two doses.
- Infants under 6 months: may be need doses of up to 3 mg per kilogram (1.5 mg per pound) a day, given as two divided doses up to the same maximum 37.5 mg daily limit
- Infants and children under 2 years: do not exceed 37.5 mg a day
- Children 2 to 12 years: do not exceed 100 mg a day
The dose is based on your child's weight and must be worked out by their doctor.
Taking the oral suspension:
If your child has been prescribed the liquid form (oral suspension), the following applies:
- Shake the bottle well before every dose.
- Measure each dose with the oral dosing syringe. Ask your pharmacist for a syringe and a bottle adapter if you do not have them.
- Never measure a dose with a household teaspoon or tablespoon, because these do not give an accurate amount.
- Store the made-up suspension at room temperature and do not freeze it.
- Throw away any unused suspension 30 days after it was made up. The pharmacist will write this date on the bottle.
The oral suspension can be taken with or without food.
What happens if I miss a dose?:
Take the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take two doses at one time.
What happens if I overdose?:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
Overdose symptoms may include nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, thirst, and muscle pain or weakness.

## What is spironolactone?
Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic (water pill) used for heart failure, high blood pressure, fluid build-up (edema) caused by liver or kidney disease, and a hormone condition called primary hyperaldosteronism. Spironolactone is sometimes prescribed off-label for women with acne or excessive facial hair growth (hirsutism).
Spironolactone works by blocking a hormone called aldosterone, which causes your body to pass more salt and water in your urine while keeping potassium in. This is why it is called potassium-sparing, and it is what makes spironolactone different from most other water pills, which flush potassium out.
Spironolactone also blocks androgens such as testosterone from binding to the androgen receptor, which explains several of its side effects, including breast tenderness and breast growth.
Spironolactone is FDA-approved to treat adults with:
- Heart failure (NYHA Class III-IV) with a reduced ejection fraction to help live longer, reduce swelling, and reduce the need for hospital stays. It is taken alongside other heart failure medicines rather than on its own.
- High blood pressure as an add-on treatment for people whose blood pressure is not controlled well enough by other medicines. Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of stroke and heart attack.
- Fluid build-up (edema) caused by cirrhosis of the liver when cutting back on fluid and salt has not been enough, and also for swelling caused by nephrotic syndrome (a kidney disorder) when treating the underlying disease and using other water pills have not worked well enough.
- Primary hyperaldosteronism, which is a condition where the adrenal glands make too much aldosterone. Spironolactone is used short-term to prepare for surgery, and long-term for people who are not suitable for surgery.
Spironolactone tablets come in 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg strengths. Spironolactone 25 mg is the strength most often used to start treatment. There is also a banana-flavored oral liquid for people who cannot swallow tablets. The liquid and the tablets are not interchangeable, so never switch between them without your doctor changing your dose.

## What is allopurinol?
Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors. It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body. High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur. Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid that builds up in the blood as tumors break down in people with certain types of cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy medications. It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

Take montelukast exactly as prescribed by your doctor and read all medication guides or instruction sheets about montelukast.

## What is hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) used for?
Hydrochlorothiazide is approved to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and fluid retention (edema) in certain patients.
High blood pressure:

- cirrhosis of the liver

- treatment with corticosteroid or estrogen medicines
The HCTZ oral suspension is approved for fluid retention associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and kidney disease including nephrotic syndrome, in both adults and children.
The capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.

## What other drugs will affect bupropion?
You may have a higher risk of seizures if you use certain other medicines while taking bupropion.
Many drugs can interact with bupropion. Tell your doctor about all medicines you use, and those you start or stop using during your treatment. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Some examples of drugs that interact with bupropion are:
- Digoxin: May decrease plasma digoxin levels. Monitor digoxin levels
- MAOIs: Increased risk of hypertensive reactions can occur when used concomitantly with this medication.
- Drugs that lower seizure threshold: Dose bupropion with caution.
- Medicines that are CYP2B6 inducers: Dose increase may be necessary if coadministered with CYP2B6 inducers (e.g., ritonavir, lopinavir, efavirenz, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, and phenytoin) based on clinical response, but should not exceed the maximum recommended dose.
- Medicines that are CYP2B6 inhibitors: Dose adjustment may be necessary if coadministered with CYP2B6 inhibitors (e.g., ticlopidine or clopidogrel).
- Medicines metabolized by CYP2D6: Bupropion inhibits CYP2D6 and can increase concentrations of antidepressants (e.g., venlafaxine, nortriptyline, imipramine, desipramine, paroxetine, fluoxetine, sertraline), antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol, risperidone, thioridazine), beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol), and Type 1C antiarrhythmics (e.g., propafenone, flecainide). A dose reduction of these medicines may be considered when used with bupropion.
- Dopaminergic drugs (levodopa and amantadine): CNS toxicity can occur when used concomitantly with this medicine.

## What is lisinopril?
Lisinopril is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children 6 years of age and older.
Lisinopril is also used in adults to treat congestive heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack.
Lisinopril belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. It works by decreasing certain chemicals that tighten the blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart can pump blood more efficiently.
High blood pressure is a common condition and when not treated, can cause damage to the brain, heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and other parts of the body. Damage to these organs may cause heart disease, a heart attack, heart failure, stroke, kidney failure, loss of vision, and other problems. In addition to taking medication, making lifestyle changes will also help to control your blood pressure. These changes include eating a diet that is low in fat and salt, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising at least 30 minutes most days, not smoking, and using alcohol in moderation.

## Before taking this medicine
Meloxicam can increase your risk of a fatal heart attack or stroke. Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG). Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding, which can be fatal.
Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding, which can be fatal. These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
You should not use meloxicam if you are allergic to it, or if you have ever had an asthma attack or severe allergic reaction after taking aspirin or an NSAID.
To make sure meloxicam is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- heart disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, or if you smoke;
- a heart attack, stroke, or blood clot;
- ulcers or stomach bleeding;
- asthma;
- kidney disease (or if you are on dialysis);
- liver disease; or
- fluid retention
- are pregnant or planning a pregnancy
- are breastfeeding or intending to breastfeed.
Meloxicam is not approved for use by anyone younger than 2 years old.
Pregnancy:
If you are pregnant, you should not take meloxicam unless your doctor tells you to. Taking an NSAID at about 20 weeks of pregnancy or later may harm your unborn baby. If you need to take this medicine for more than 2 days when you are between 20 and 30 weeks of pregnancy, your doctor may need to monitor the amount of fluid around your baby. You should not take meloxicam after about 30 weeks of pregnancy.
Planning a pregnancy:
Meloxicam may cause a delay in ovulation (the release of an egg from an ovary). You should not take this medicine if you are undergoing fertility treatment or are otherwise trying to get pregnant.
Breastfeeding:
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using this medicine.

## Tramadol side effects
Common side effects:
The most common side effects of tramadol are:
- dizziness or vertigo
- nausea
- constipation
- headache
- drowsiness
- vomiting
- itching.
Dry mouth is also commonly reported with the extended-release forms of tramadol.
A person's genetics can affect their response to tramadol, including their risk of side effects (see How do genetics affect tramadol?).
Serious tramadol side effects and warnings:
Tramadol may cause serious side effects, some of which may be fatal.
Tramadol can slow or stop your breathing and may be habit-forming. MISUSE OF THIS MEDICINE CAN CAUSE ADDICTION, OVERDOSE, OR DEATH, especially in a child or other person using the medicine without a prescription. Keep this medicine where others cannot get to it. Do not take more tramadol than prescribed, as an overdose can be fatal. Selling or giving away this medicine is against the law.
- A person caring for you should give naloxone and seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you find it hard to wake up. Serious breathing problems may be more likely in older adults and people who are debilitated or have wasting syndrome or chronic breathing disorders.
- Call your doctor at once if you have: noisy breathing, sighing, shallow breathing, breathing that stops during sleep a slow heart rate or weak pulse a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out seizure (convulsions) or low cortisol levels (symptoms include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, dizziness, worsening tiredness or weakness) low sodium levels (hyponatremia). Symptoms include headache, confusion, weakness, unsteadiness, or feeling sick low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion, or a fast heartbeat.
Seek medical attention right away if you have symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Seizures have been reported in patients taking tramadol. Your risk of seizures is higher if you are taking higher doses than recommended. Seizure risk is also higher in those with epilepsy or a history of seizures, and in those taking certain antidepressants, other opioids, MAO inhibitors, or other medicines that lower the seizure threshold.
You should not take tramadol if you have significant breathing problems, acute or severe asthma in a setting where you cannot be monitored, a blockage in your stomach or intestines, or if you have taken an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days (isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, and others). Tell your doctor before starting tramadol if you have a head injury or increased pressure inside your skull, as tramadol should be used with particular care in these situations.
Prescribers are advised not to prescribe tramadol for people who are suicidal or prone to addiction, and to use it with caution in people taking tranquilizers or antidepressants, or drinking heavily. If you are struggling with thoughts of harming yourself, or with your use of any medicine, tell your healthcare provider so they can help you find the right treatment and support.
Fatal side effects can occur if you use this medicine with alcohol, or with other drugs that cause drowsiness or slow your breathing. People taking extended-release forms of tramadol should not consume alcohol-containing beverages at the same time. Alcohol is also not advised with immediate-release forms of tramadol.
Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have occurred with tramadol, some of which caused death. People who are allergic to other opioids are at higher risk. Other hypersensitivity reactions include itching, hives, narrowing of the airways, swelling of the face and airways (angioedema), and serious skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome. Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to tramadol (symptoms include hives, difficulty breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning in your eyes, skin pain, a red or purple skin rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling).
Tramadol may make pain worse rather than better in some people, an effect called opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain after taking tramadol.
Tramadol extended-release capsules and tablets may complicate a healthcare provider’s clinical assessment of an acute abdominal condition. They are not recommended for people with severe liver or severe kidney impairment.
Taking tramadol during pregnancy may cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms in the newborn, known as neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS).
Some people are “ultra-rapid metabolizers” of tramadol because of a variation in an enzyme called CYP2D6. Their bodies convert tramadol into its active form faster than usual, which can produce dangerously high opioid levels even at a normal dose. Life-threatening breathing problems and deaths have occurred in children for this reason, including after surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Tramadol should not be given to a child younger than 12 years old, or to anyone younger than 18 years old who has recently had surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Extended-release tramadol should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years.
Tramadol may cause drowsiness or affect your ability to drive or perform hazardous tasks. Do not perform these tasks if tramadol causes confusion, mental impairment, or drowsiness.
Tramadol can cause withdrawal symptom s if stopped suddenly after being taken for a long period of time. Symptoms may include restlessness, drug craving, anxiety, and sweating. Do not stop taking tramadol suddenly without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping abruptly can cause serious withdrawal symptoms and uncontrolled pain (see How long does tramadol withdrawal last?).
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Insulin glargine is a long-acting insulin used to treat type 1 and type 2 diabetes in certain patients to improve and maintain blood glucose levels. Insulin glargine is a man-made form of human insulin that is used once daily to provide a base level of insulin that keeps working for 24 hours or longer.
Insulin glargine is available under the brand names Lantus, Basaglar, Toujeo, Semglee, and Rezvoglar. Langlara is an interchangeable biosimilar to Lantus that was FDA-approved on May 4, 2026.
Rezvoglar, Lantus, Langlara, Semglee, and Toujeo are FDA-approved to be used for use in adult and pediatric patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Basasglar is FDA-approved to be used by adults for type 2 diabetes and also for adults and pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes. In patients with type 1 diabetes, insulin glargine must be used together with a short-acting insulin.

## What is bupropion?
Bupropion is an antidepressant medication used to treat depression and seasonal affective disorder. It also supports smoking cessation and weight management. Bupropion is the active ingredient in Wellbutrin and Zyban, Auvelity contains bupropion and dextromethorphan, and Contrave contains bupropion and naltrexone. Bupropion improves mood regulation and nicotine cravings and, when combined with naltrexone, helps reduce food intake.
Bupropion is thought to work by changing levels of certain chemicals in the brain, including noradrenaline and dopamine.
Bupropion first became an FDA-approved medicine on 30 December 1985.

## Before taking this medicine
You should not use insulin glargine if you are allergic to insulin, or if you are having an episode of hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) or diabetic ketoacidosis (call your doctor for treatment).
Different brands of insulin glargine are specifically approved for different age groups and different diabetes types. The safety and effectiveness of insulin glargine in pediatric patients younger than 6 years of age with type 1 diabetes and pediatric patients with type 2 diabetes has not been established.
Tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- liver or kidney disease; or
- heart failure or other heart problems.
Tell your doctor if you also take pioglitazone or rosiglitazone (sometimes contained in combinations with glimepiride or metformin). Taking certain oral diabetes medicines while you are using insulin may increase your risk of serious heart problems.
Pregnancy:
Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant, as it is not known if insulin glargine will harm your unborn baby. Follow your doctor's instructions about using this medicine if you are pregnant or you become pregnant. Controlling diabetes is very important during pregnancy.
Breastfeeding:
Tell your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or are planning to breastfeed, as it is not known if insulin glargine may harm your breastfeeding baby.

## Who should not take hydroxyzine?
Do not take hydroxyzine if you:
- are allergic to hydroxyzine or to any ingredient in the medicine
- are allergic to cetirizine or levocetirizine
- have a prolonged QT interval, a heart rhythm finding seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG)
- are in early pregnancy
In animal studies, hydroxyzine caused birth defects in rats and mice at doses well above those used in people. There is not enough information in humans to know whether hydroxyzine is safe in early pregnancy, so it should not be used at that time.

Lisinopril can harm your kidneys, especially if you also use certain medicines for infections, cancer, or osteoporosis.
Tell your doctor about all your other medicines, especially:

## What is tramadol?
Tramadol is an opioid agonist that may be used to treat moderate to moderately severe chronic pain in adults, when other pain treatments such as non-opioid pain medicines do not treat your pain well enough, or you cannot tolerate them.
- Extended-release forms of tramadol may be used in adults who require around-the-clock treatment of their pain for an extended period.
- An opioid pain medicine such as tramadol can put you at risk for overdose and death. Even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed, you are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death.
Brands of tramadol include ConZip, Qdolo, Ryzolt, Ultram, Ultram ER, and Ultracet. Many have been discontinued, but generic tramadol is still available.
Taking tramadol in combination with other pain-relieving medicines such as acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin can provide better pain relief than just taking one pain-relieving medicine by itself (see Can you take tramadol in combination with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin?)
Tramadol first gained FDA approval on March 3, 1995. Originally, it was classified as a non-controlled substance, but it was reclassified in 2014 to Schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act with restrictions on its prescribing. Tramadol is an opioid (see Is tramadol an opioid?).
A person's genetics can affect the pain-relieving properties of tramadol (see How do genetics affect tramadol?).

## What other drugs will affect hydrochlorothiazide?
Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Medicines that need particular care:
- Lithium. Lithium and diuretics generally should not be taken together. Hydrochlorothiazide reduces how quickly the kidneys clear lithium, which carries a high risk of lithium toxicity.
- Cholestyramine and colestipol. These cholesterol-lowering resins bind hydrochlorothiazide in the gut and can reduce how much you absorb by up to 85 percent for cholestyramine and 43 percent for colestipol. The doses need to be separated. For the oral suspension, the label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide at least 4 hours before, or 4 to 6 hours after, the resin.
- NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), diclofenac, meloxicam, indomethacin, celecoxib and aspirin. These can reduce the fluid-clearing and blood-pressure-lowering effects of hydrochlorothiazide, and your doctor will check whether the medicine is still working as intended.
- Insulin and oral diabetes medicines. Your diabetes medicine dose may need adjusting.
- Corticosteroids and ACTH. Taken with hydrochlorothiazide, these increase the loss of salts from the body, particularly potassium.
- Digoxin and other digitalis medicines. Low potassium caused by hydrochlorothiazide can make the heart more sensitive to the toxic effects of digitalis, including irregular heart rhythms.
- Other blood pressure medicines. The effects add together, which may be intended, but can also lower blood pressure more than expected.
- Alcohol, barbiturates and opioid pain medicines. These can make the drop in blood pressure on standing worse, causing dizziness or fainting.
- Muscle relaxants used during surgery (nondepolarizing muscle relaxants such as tubocurarine). You may respond more strongly to them, so tell your surgeon and anesthetist that you take hydrochlorothiazide.
- Medicines that raise blood pressure (pressor amines such as norepinephrine). Your response to them may be reduced, although this does not usually prevent their use.
This list is not complete. Other medicines may affect hydrochlorothiazide, and hydrochlorothiazide may affect other medicines.

## What are the side effects of hydroxyzine?
The most common side effects of hydroxyzine are drowsiness, dry mouth, and headache. These are usually mild and do not last long.
A skin rash is different. If you develop a rash while taking hydroxyzine, stop taking it and call your doctor, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction.
Common side effects:
Common hydroxyzine side effects include dry mouth, headache, and drowsiness. The drowsiness is usually temporary and may go away after a few days of treatment or when the dose is lowered.
Serious side effects:
Stop taking hydroxyzine and call your doctor right away if you develop a skin rash, if a skin condition you are treating gets worse, or if you have any other sign of an allergic reaction.
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.
If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given. In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may happen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Dosing information
Usual Adult Dose for Erosive Esophagitis:
Treatment of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg orally once a day for up to 8 weeks; however an additional 8 weeks may be considered for patients who have not healed after the initial treatment. Safety and efficacy beyond 16 weeks of therapy have not been established. Maintenance of Healing of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg orally once a day. Controlled studies have been limited to 12 months of pantoprazole therapy.
Usual Adult Dose for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease:
Parenteral: 40 mg once a day for 7 to 10 days, administered via intravenous infusion over a period of 15 minutes. Intravenous therapy should be discontinued as soon as the patient is able to resume oral therapy. Oral: 40 mg orally once a day, for short-term administration (up to 8 weeks); however an additional 8 weeks may be considered for patients who have not healed after the initial treatment. Safety and efficacy beyond 16 weeks of therapy have not been established.
Usual Adult Dose for Duodenal Ulcer:
Study (n=54) 40 mg orally once a day, dose was increased every 12 weeks by 40 mg increments to a maximum of 120 mg per day, for 28 weeks. Data have revealed that monotherapy with daily doses of 40 mg have been associated with complete duodenal ulcer healing in up to 87% and 94% of patients after 4 weeks and 8 weeks respectively.
Usual Adult Dose for Gastric Ulcer:
40 mg orally once a day. Data have revealed that monotherapy with daily doses of 40 mg have been associated with complete gastric ulcer healing in up to 87% and 97% of patients after 4 weeks and 8 weeks respectively.
Usual Adult Dose for Helicobacter pylori Infection:
Study (n=242) - Triple therapy: 40 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, commonly in conjunction with clarithromycin and either amoxicillin or metronidazole to eradicate Helicobacter pylori, followed with 40 mg pantoprazole orally once daily until day 28. Triple therapy has resulted in eradication rates of greater than 95%. The QUADRATE Study (n=405) - Quadruple therapy: 40 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, concomitantly with bismuth subcitrate and tetracycline, both four times daily, and metronidazole 200 mg three times daily and 400 mg at bedtime. Helicobacter Pylori eradication was achieved in 82% of patients.
Usual Adult Dose for Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome:
Parenteral: 80 mg every 12 hours, administered by 15-minute infusion. Daily doses higher than 240 mg administered in equally divided doses by 15-minute infusion, or administered for more than 6 days have not been studied. Oral: 40 mg twice daily, to a maximum of 240 mg per day. Some patients have received treatment with pantoprazole for more than 2 years.
Usual Adult Dose for Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis:
Study (n=21) - Stress Ulcer bleeding prophylaxis in the Critical Care Setting: 80 mg twice daily, as a bolus infusion over a period of 15 minutes, to a maximum daily dose of 240 mg, divided into three equal doses. Study (n=20) - Peptic Ulcer rebleeding prophylaxis after hemostasis in the Critical Care Setting: 80 mg IV bolus, followed by continuous infusion of 8 mg/hr for 3 days, after which therapy may be continued with an oral PPI.
Usual Adult Dose for Peptic Ulcer:
Study (n=21) - Stress Ulcer bleeding prophylaxis in the Critical Care Setting: 80 mg twice daily, as a bolus infusion over a period of 15 minutes, to a maximum daily dose of 240 mg, divided into three equal doses. Study (n=20) - Peptic Ulcer rebleeding prophylaxis after hemostasis in the Critical Care Setting: 80 mg IV bolus, followed by continuous infusion of 8 mg/hr for 3 days, after which therapy may be continued with an oral PPI.
