Vomiting | 4% | 1%
Some side effects were more common with particular conditions. Sleepiness was more common in depression trials, insomnia and agitation in OCD trials, constipation and agitation in panic disorder trials, tiredness in PTSD trials, and insomnia, dizziness, tiredness, dry mouth, and a general feeling of being unwell in social anxiety disorder trials. In PMDD trials, sleepiness, dry mouth, dizziness, tiredness, and stomach pain were more common.
In these trials, 12% of people taking sertraline stopped treatment because of a side effect, compared with 4% of people taking placebo. The most common reasons for stopping were nausea (3%), diarrhea (2%), agitation (2%), and insomnia (2%).
Sexual side effects of sertraline:
SSRIs including sertraline can cause sexual problems. In men, this can mean delayed ejaculation or being unable to ejaculate, lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. In women, it can mean lower sex drive and delayed orgasm or being unable to have an orgasm.
Sexual side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Ejaculation failure (men) | 8% | 1%
Decreased libido (men) | 7% | 2%
Erectile dysfunction (men) | 4% | 1%
Ejaculation disorder (men) | 3% | 0%
Male sexual dysfunction | 2% | 0%
Decreased libido (women) | 4% | 2%
Changes in sex drive and sexual function can also be part of depression and anxiety themselves, so the timing of when symptoms started matters. These numbers may underestimate how often sexual side effects happen, because people and their providers do not always raise the subject. Tell your provider about any change in sexual function, since there may be ways to manage it.
Serious sertraline side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to sertraline: rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of serotonin syndrome, which can be life threatening: agitation, hallucinations, confusion, coma or other changes in mental state, a racing heartbeat, high or low blood pressure, dizziness, heavy sweating, fever, muscle stiffness, twitching or overactive reflexes, loss of coordination, seizures, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea;
- unusual bleeding or bruising, including nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in vomit or stools, or black tarry stools;
- signs of a manic episode: greatly increased energy, severe trouble sleeping, racing thoughts, reckless behavior, unusually grand ideas, excessive happiness or irritability, or talking more or faster than usual;
- seizures or convulsions;
- eye pain, changes in vision, or swelling or redness in or around the eye, which can be signs of angle-closure glaucoma (a sudden rise in pressure inside the eye);
- signs of low sodium in the blood (hyponatremia): headache, trouble concentrating or thinking, memory problems, confusion, weakness, or feeling unsteady, which can lead to falls. Severe cases have caused hallucinations, fainting, seizures, coma, and death;
- fainting, chest discomfort, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation.

The overall pattern of side effects in 281 children and teenagers treated with sertraline was generally similar to that seen in adults. ## Metformin for Weight Loss: What the Research Shows
Does metformin work for weight loss?:
Yes. Metformin can lead to a modest weight loss, though results vary, and it's generally smaller amount of weight loss than what's seen with medications specifically approved for weight loss.
In the landmark Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), a randomized controlled trial in people at high risk for diabetes, participants taking metformin lost more weight than those on placebo. Metformin patients lost 2.7% of body weight after one year, compared to 0.43% for placebo, and 2.1% after two years compared to essentially no change (0.02%) for placebo. Looking at it another way, 29% of people on metformin lost at least 5% of their starting body weight after one year, versus just 13% on placebo, a gap that held up at the two-year mark (26% vs. 14%).
Metformin is not FDA-approved for weight loss.

## Fluoxetine FAQ
Is 40mg of fluoxetine a high dose?
40mg of fluoxetine is considered a moderate maintenance dose in adults for major depressive disorder (MDD) and OCD. The standard starting dose for most conditions is 20mg per day, except for panic disorder, which starts at 10mg. If symptoms have not improved after several weeks, the dose may be increased, up to 40mg for MDD and OCD, or 20mg for panic disorder. The recommended dose for bulimia is 60mg per day. Your doctor will determine the right dose for you based on your condition and response to treatment.
Does fluoxetine cause weight gain?:
Fluoxetine is less likely to cause weight gain than many other antidepressants. In the short term, it can actually cause mild weight loss due to reduced appetite, which is one of its common side effects. However, some people do experience weight changes over longer-term use. If you notice significant weight changes while taking this medicine, speak to your doctor, as dose adjustments or alternative treatments may be available.
How long does fluoxetine take to work?:
Most people need to take fluoxetine for 4 to 6 weeks before feeling the full effects. Some improvement in sleep, appetite, or energy levels may be noticeable within the first 1 to 2 weeks, but mood and motivation typically take longer to improve. For obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), it may take 5 weeks or longer to see the full benefit. It is important to keep taking this medicine as prescribed, even if you do not feel immediate improvement. Do not stop without speaking to your doctor first.
Is fluoxetine a controlled substance?:
No, fluoxetine is not a controlled substance. It is not classified under the DEA Controlled Substances Act, meaning it does not have recognized potential for dependence or abuse in the way that drugs like opioids or benzodiazepines do. It is, however, a prescription-only medicine, so it still requires a valid prescription from a licensed healthcare provider.
Is fluoxetine an SSRI?:
Yes, fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). SSRIs work by blocking the reabsorption (reuptake) of serotonin in the brain, increasing the amount of serotonin available between nerve cells. Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that helps regulate mood, emotions, and sleep. Prozac was one of the first SSRIs approved and remains one of the most widely prescribed antidepressants worldwide.
What are the side effects of fluoxetine in females?:
Females may experience all of the common fluoxetine side effects, but some side effects are particularly relevant to women:
- Sexual side effects are common, including decreased sex drive (libido) and difficulty reaching orgasm. These can affect quality of life and should be discussed with your doctor, as treatment options are available.
- Weight changes - it may cause mild weight loss initially, though longer-term weight changes can occur.
- Menstrual changes - some women report changes to their menstrual cycle, though this is not among the most commonly reported side effects.
- Pregnancy - taking this medicine in late pregnancy may increase the risk of certain complications in newborns. Women who are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding should discuss the risks and benefits with their doctor before continuing or starting this medicine.
Does fluoxetine (Prozac) help with anxiety?:
Fluoxetine is not FDA-approved specifically for generalized anxiety disorder, but it is FDA-approved to treat panic disorder, which is a type of anxiety disorder. It is also approved for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), which has a significant anxiety component.
Although not FDA-approved for generalized anxiety disorder, it is sometimes prescribed off-label by doctors for anxiety symptoms, as SSRIs are a well-established treatment class for anxiety conditions. Off-label means the drug is being used in a way not specifically approved by the FDA, but supported by clinical evidence.
If you experience anxiety alongside depression, fluoxetine may help both, as it is FDA-approved for major depressive disorder and depression and anxiety commonly occur together.
Talk to your doctor about whether fluoxetine is appropriate for your anxiety symptoms.
How long does fluoxetine stay in your system?:
Fluoxetine stays in your system longer than most other antidepressants. After stopping this medicine, it takes approximately 1 to 4 days for the drug itself to be reduced by half, but fluoxetine also converts in the body to an active metabolite called norfluoxetine, which has a much longer half-life of 4 to 16 days. This means this medicine and its active metabolite can remain detectable in your system for up to 5 weeks after your last dose.
This is clinically important for two reasons:
- Switching medications: If you are switching from fluoxetine to certain other antidepressants, particularly MAOIs, your doctor will require a washout period of at least 5 weeks to allow fluoxetine to fully clear your system and avoid dangerous drug interactions.
- Stopping fluoxetine: The long half-life means withdrawal symptoms are generally milder with this medicine than with shorter-acting antidepressants, as the drug tapers itself out of your system gradually.
Always talk to your doctor before stopping fluoxetine or switching to another medication.

## What is amlodipine?
Amlodipine besylate is a prescription medicine used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to prevent certain types of angina (chest pain). It belongs to a class of medications called calcium channel blockers.
Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.
Amlodipine besylate controls angina chest pain by increasing the supply of blood to the heart. If taken regularly, this medicine controls chest pain, but it does not stop chest pain once it starts. Your doctor may prescribe a different medication to take when you have chest pain.
Amlodipine is also used alone or in combination with other medicines to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) in adults and children at least 6 years old. Lowering blood pressure may lower your risk of a stroke or heart attack.

## Warnings
Levothyroxine should not be used to treat obesity or weight problems. Dangerous side effects or death can occur from the misuse of this medicine, especially if you are taking any other weight-loss medications or appetite suppressants.
Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Levothyroxine has a narrow therapeutic index, which means the difference between too little and too much is small. Taking too much or too little over time can affect your heart, bones, blood sugar, cholesterol, digestion, memory and concentration, fertility, and, in children, growth and development. Your doctor will start you on a suitable dose and adjust it gradually based on blood tests.
You may not be able to use levothyroxine if you have certain medical conditions. Tell your doctor if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder or any heart problems such as a recent heart attack.
If you have an adrenal gland problem, you will need to start treatment with a steroid (glucocorticoid) medicine before you start levothyroxine. Starting levothyroxine first can trigger a sudden, serious drop in adrenal hormones known as an adrenal crisis.
Older adults and people with heart disease are usually started on a lower dose, because too much thyroid hormone can cause an irregular heartbeat (most commonly atrial fibrillation), angina, or other heart problems. Tell your doctor if you develop chest pain, breathlessness, or a fast or irregular heartbeat.
Taking more levothyroxine than your body needs over a long period can weaken your bones and lead to a higher risk of fractures. This is more likely after menopause. Your doctor will aim to give you the lowest dose that controls your thyroid levels.
Oral levothyroxine should not be used to treat myxedema coma. Levothyroxine given into a vein is used instead.

## How does gabapentin work?
Gabapentin works by calming overactive electrical signals in the brain and nervous system. It does this by binding to the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels in nerve cells, which is thought to normalize chemical signals nerves send to each other and results in a calmer, less excitable nerve circuit.
That same effect helps in different ways depending on what gabapentin is treating:
- Epilepsy - dampens the runaway electrical firing that causes seizures.
- Postherpetic neuralgia (shingles nerve pain) - reduces the abnormal pain signals from nerves damaged by shingles.
- Restless legs syndrome (gabapentin enacarbil / Horizant) - the exact mechanism is less clear, but the same calming effect on overactive nerves is thought to ease the urge-to-move sensation.
Gabapentin is not an opioid, sedative, or anti-inflammatory painkiller. It works directly on the nerves, which is why it helps nerve-related pain and why it isn't useful for everyday pain like headaches or sprains. Most people need 1 to 2 weeks of regular dosing for the full effect to build up.

## How should I use furosemide?
Take or administer furosemide exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Furosemide oral tablets and liquid are taken by mouth. Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device, not a kitchen spoon.
Furosemide injection is given in a muscle, under the skin, or in a vein. A healthcare provider will give you this injection if you are unable to take the medicine by mouth.
Using subcutaneous furosemide at home:
You or your caregiver should be trained before your first dose, and you should read the Instructions for Use that comes with your prescription. Wash your hands first, and check that the liquid is clear and colorless to slightly yellow. Do not use it if you see particles or if it is cloudy or discolored.
Subcutaneous furosemide is given into the abdomen only, and you should use a different spot on the abdomen each time.
Furoscix ReadyFlow autoinjector
- Choose a site at least two inches from your belly button, avoiding skin that is broken or irritated and any scars or stretch marks. Clean it and let it dry.
- Pull the blue cap straight off, then press the device firmly against your skin and hold it there for about 10 seconds, until the yellow plunger rod stops moving and fills the viewing window.
- If you lift the device away before the window is completely yellow, you may not get the full dose. Call your healthcare provider if this happens, and do not use a second device unless you are told to.
Furoscix On-Body Infusor and Lasix ONYU Infusor
- The infusion takes about 5 hours, so plan to stay somewhere you can relax and reach a bathroom.
- Apply the device to a flat, clean, hairless area of the abdomen below the rib cage and above the belt line, and press it firmly into place. Do not remove and reapply it.
- Limit your activity while wearing it and avoid bending as much as you can. Do not exercise or do anything that might knock it off.
- Do not get the infusor wet. Do not bathe, shower, or swim while wearing it, and do not apply lotions or creams to the area where it is placed.
- Traveling by car or airplane while wearing the infusor is not recommended, and the Furoscix On-Body Infusor cannot be used in an MRI setting.
- Do not use the infusor within 12 inches of mobile phones, tablets, computers, or wireless accessories such as a remote control or Bluetooth device.
- Your healthcare provider will show you what the indicator light and alarms mean. You must use the infusor in a setting where you can detect and respond to these alarms to ensure you receive the full dose. If the device falls off, or the light blinks red, call your healthcare provider and do not reuse it.
Dispose of used autoinjectors, infusors, and cartridges in a sharps container. Do not put them in household trash and do not recycle them.
General furosemide dosing information:
Do not use more than your recommended dose. High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
This medicine will make you urinate more often, and you may get dehydrated easily. Follow your doctor's instructions about using potassium supplements or getting enough salt and potassium in your diet.
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often, and you may need other medical tests.
If you have high blood pressure, keep using furosemide even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
If you need surgery, tell the surgeon ahead of time that you are using furosemide.

## Cyclobenzaprine side effects
The most common cyclobenzaprine side effects are drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, fatigue, and headache. Most side effects are mild and settle as your body adjusts, but cyclobenzaprine can occasionally cause serious heart rhythm effects and serotonin syndrome. 1
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects may include: 1
- drowsiness and tiredness;
- dry mouth;
- dizziness;
- fatigue;
- headache;
- nausea, indigestion, or constipation;
- blurred vision;
- unpleasant taste;
- nervousness or confusion.
In placebo-controlled trials of the immediate-release tablets, side effects were dose-related, occurring more often with 10 mg than with 5 mg: 1
Side effect | Cyclobenzaprine 5 mg | Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg | Placebo
Drowsiness | 29% | 38% | 10%
Dry mouth | 21% | 32% | 7%
Fatigue | 6% | 6% | 3%
Headache | 5% | 5% | 8%
With Amrix, the most common side effects are dry mouth (up to 14% at 30 mg), dizziness, fatigue, constipation, nausea, indigestion, and drowsiness. 2
With Tonmya, because it dissolves under the tongue, the most common side effects involve the mouth: reduced feeling or numbness in the mouth (23%), mouth discomfort, abnormal taste, tingling, mouth pain, and canker sores, along with sleepiness, fatigue, and dry mouth. Mouth-related effects usually begin within minutes of a dose and most resolve within an hour. Moistening your mouth with sips of water before dosing reduces the risk of numbness. Tell your healthcare provider if mouth effects are severe. 3
Serious cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to cyclobenzaprine: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; or itching. 2,3
Stop taking cyclobenzaprine and call your doctor at once if you have: 1,2,3
- fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeats;
- chest pain or pressure, or pain spreading to your jaw or shoulder;
- sudden numbness or weakness, slurred speech, or balance problems; or
- symptoms of serotonin syndrome: agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness or twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Serious side effects, including confusion, hallucinations, and heart problems leading to falls, are more likely in older adults. 1
Does cyclobenzaprine make you sleepy?:
Yes, drowsiness is the most common side effect of the tablets, affecting up to 38% of people taking the 10 mg dose in clinical trials. This is one reason 5 mg is the usual starting dose, since it causes less drowsiness with comparable effectiveness. Analysis of trial data shows cyclobenzaprine relieves muscle spasm whether or not sedation occurs, so drowsiness is not required for it to work. 1
Does cyclobenzaprine cause constipation?:
Constipation is a known side effect, reported in 1% to 3% of people taking the immediate-release tablets and up to 3% of people taking Amrix 30 mg in clinical trials. It results from the drug's anticholinergic (drying) effects, the same mechanism behind dry mouth and blurred vision. 1,2

## What other drugs will affect metformin?
Many drugs can interact with metformin; this includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here. Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any medicine you start or stop using.
Medicines that have a carbonic anhydrase inhibiting effect like topiramate (often used for seizures or migraines), zonisamide (used for seizures), acetazolamide (used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, and other conditions), and dichlorphenamide (used for a muscle condition called periodic paralysis) can raise the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis when taken with metformin. These medicines commonly lower a substance in your blood called bicarbonate, which your body needs to keep its acid levels balanced. If you're taking metformin along with any of these medicines, your doctor may want to monitor you more closely.
Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.
Insulin or other diabetes medicines that raise insulin (like sulfonylureas): Combining these with metformin can lower your blood sugar too much. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you're taking more than one diabetes medicine.
Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis.
Contrast dye used in imaging tests (like CT scans): This type of dye can temporarily affect kidney function, which can let metformin build up in your body. Your doctor may have you stop taking metformin around the time of the test and restart it once your kidney function is confirmed to be back to normal.

The most noticeable effect of hydrochlorothiazide is passing urine more often, particularly in the first few weeks. This is how the medicine works rather than a side effect, and it usually settles as your body adjusts.

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat.

- severe pain in your upper stomach that spreads to your back, with nausea and vomiting, which can be a sign of inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)
- yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice)
- fever, chills, sore throat, mouth sores or other signs of infection
- unusual bruising or bleeding, or pale skin and unusual tiredness, which can be signs of a blood problem

- dizziness, a spinning sensation (vertigo), headache, restlessness, or tingling and numbness (paresthesia)
- weakness
- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, stomach cramping, stomach irritation, or loss of appetite

The most common tirzepatide side effects are:
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting
- Constipation
- Nausea (mild to moderate)
- Decreased appetite
- Abdominal pain.
Serious side effects:
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:
- Severe stomach pain (pancreatitis): Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, or pain that spreads to your back.
- Kidney problems: Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration, which may lead to kidney problems. Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk and tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
- Gallbladder problems: Symptoms include severe upper stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or clay-colored stools.
- Serious allergic reactions: Seek emergency medical attention if you experience hives, difficulty breathing, feeling light-headed, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (anaphylaxis or angioedema).
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): Symptoms may include headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery.
- Vision changes: Tell your doctor about any blurred vision or other vision changes, particularly if you have type 2 diabetes.
- Thyroid tumor: Symptoms may include a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, or shortness of breath.
- Mental health changes: Tell your healthcare provider right away about any new or worsening depression, mood changes, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
- Aspiration during surgery: Tirzepatide slows stomach emptying, which may increase the risk of food or liquid entering the lungs during procedures using anesthesia or sedation. Tell all your healthcare providers you are taking tirzepatide before any planned surgery or procedure.
This is not a complete list of side effects. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects, or report them to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What happens if I overdose?
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.
Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death. If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep it with you at all times. A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up. Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.
Anyone can buy naloxone from a pharmacy or local health department. Make sure any person caring for you knows where you keep naloxone and how to use it.
The first signs of an acetaminophen overdose include loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, sweating, and confusion or weakness. Later symptoms may include pain in your upper stomach, dark urine, and yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes.

## What is the usual sertraline dosage?
The usual starting dose of sertraline is 25 mg or 50 mg once a day, depending on the condition being treated, and the usual treatment range is 50 mg to 200 mg a day. The maximum dose for most conditions is 200 mg a day.
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range or maximum
Depression (MDD), adults | 50 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
OCD, adults | 50 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
OCD, ages 6 to 12 | 25 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
OCD, ages 13 to 17 | 50 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
Panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder | 25 mg a day | 50 mg to 200 mg a day
PMDD, taken every day | 50 mg a day | Up to 150 mg a day
PMDD, taken in the luteal phase only | 50 mg a day | Up to 100 mg a day
If the starting dose is not enough, the dose can be raised in steps of 25 mg to 50 mg a day. Because sertraline stays in the body for about 24 hours, doses are usually changed no more often than once a week.
Dosing for PMDD. Sertraline can be taken every day of the menstrual cycle, or only during the luteal phase, meaning you start 14 days before your period is due and continue until it starts, then repeat with each cycle. On daily dosing, the dose can go up by 50 mg per cycle to a maximum of 150 mg a day. On luteal phase dosing, the maximum is 100 mg a day, taken as 50 mg for the first 3 days of the dosing cycle and 100 mg for the rest of it.
Sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules. These are not used to start treatment or to titrate a dose, because there are no lower capsule strengths. They can be started in someone who has been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week. The recommended capsule dose is 150 mg or 200 mg once a day, and the maximum is 200 mg a day. Because the dose cannot be lowered in steps using capsules alone, coming off treatment requires switching back to another sertraline product.
Liver problems. With sertraline tablets and oral solution, mild liver impairment (Child-Pugh score 5 or 6) means both the starting dose and the usual range are halved, and use is not recommended in moderate or severe liver impairment (Child-Pugh score 7 to 15). Sertraline capsules are not recommended in mild, moderate, or severe liver impairment, because the dose cannot be adjusted with the strengths available.
Kidney problems. No dose change is needed for mild, moderate, or severe kidney impairment, including in people on dialysis.

## What is cyclobenzaprine?
Cyclobenzaprine is a prescription muscle relaxant used short-term to relieve muscle spasms caused by sprains, strains, and injuries, including low back and neck pain. It is used together with rest and physical therapy to help relieve the pain, tenderness, and limited movement caused by muscle spasm. 1,2
Cyclobenzaprine is also used to treat fibromyalgia in adults, where it can help reduce pain. For fibromyalgia, it is taken as a sublingual (under the tongue) tablet at bedtime under the brand name Tonmya. In clinical trials, Tonmya significantly reduced fibromyalgia pain compared with placebo over 14 weeks, and close to half of treated patients achieved at least a 30% improvement in pain. 3
The Flexeril brand has been discontinued, but cyclobenzaprine is available as generic tablets and as the brand-name products Amrix (extended-release capsules) and Fexmid. 2,4

## Warnings
Boxed warning for lactic acidosis:
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).
Stop taking metformin and call your healthcare professional immediately if you have any symptoms of lactic acidosis, including if you feel:
- very weak and tired
- have unusual (not normal) muscle pain
- have trouble breathing
- have unusual sleepiness or sleep longer than usual
- have unexplained stomach or intestinal problems with nausea and vomiting, or diarrhea
- cold, especially in your arms and legs
- dizzy or lightheaded
- have a slow or irregular heartbeat
Other warnings:
Vitamin B12 deficiency: Metformin can lower your vitamin B12 levels over time. Your doctor may check your blood counts every year and your B12 levels every 2 to 3 years to catch any problems early.
Low blood sugar when taken with insulin or other diabetes medicines: Taking metformin along with insulin or certain other diabetes drugs (ones that boost insulin release) raises the risk of low blood sugar. If you're on one of these combinations, your doctor may lower the dose of the other medicine.
Macrovascular Outcomes: There have been no clinical studies that clearly show metformin reduces the risk of macrovascular disease, such as diseases or conditions that affect the coronary arteries, the aorta, and large arteries in the brain and limbs.

## Empagliflozin side effects
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction: hives, difficult breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Seek medical attention right away if you have signs of a serious genital infection (penis or vagina): burning, itching, odor, discharge, pain, tenderness, redness or swelling of the genital or rectal area, fever, not feeling well. These symptoms may get worse quickly.

- low blood sugar -- headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery;
- dehydration --dizziness, confusion, feeling very thirsty, less urination;
- ketoacidosis (too much acid in the blood) --nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, confusion, unusual drowsiness, or trouble breathing; or
- signs of a bladder infection --pain or burning when you urinate, blood in your urine, pain in pelvis or back.
Common side effects of empagliflozin may include:
- a bladder infection; or
- yeast infection in women (vaginal itching or discharge).

## How should I use Flonase Nasal Spray?
Use Flonase exactly as directed on the label, or as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Do not share this medicine with another person, even if they have the same symptoms you have. Sharing a bottle can spread germs.
Your dose will depend on the fluticasone brand or strength you use, and your dose may change once your symptoms improve. Follow all dosing instructions very carefully.
- A child using the nasal spray should be supervised by an adult.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Shake the bottle before each use. Flonase Allergy Relief should be shaken gently, and Flonase Sensimist should be shaken vigorously.
Use this product only once a day and do not use more than directed. Avoid getting the spray in your eyes or mouth.
If you switched to fluticasone from another steroid medicine, you should not stop using it suddenly. Follow your doctor's instructions about tapering your dose.
Storage differs between products. Store Flonase Allergy Relief and Children's Flonase Allergy Relief between 4°C and 30°C (39°F and 86°F). Store Flonase Sensimist between 15°C and 30°C (59°F and 86°F), and do not refrigerate or freeze it.
Throw the bottle away once you have used the number of sprays stated on the carton, even if there is still liquid in the bottle. The correct amount of medicine in each spray cannot be assured after the labeled number of sprays has been used. Bottle sizes vary between products and pack sizes, ranging from 30 to 144 metered sprays.
Dosing information:
Usual Adult Dose for Rhinitis (adults and children 12 years of age and older):
Flonase Allergy Relief Nasal Spray (fluticasone propionate 50 mcg per spray):
- Week 1: use 2 sprays in each nostril once daily
- Week 2 through 6 months: use 1 or 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, as needed to treat your symptoms
- After 6 months of daily use: ask your doctor if you can keep using this medicine
Flonase Sensimist Nasal Spray (fluticasone furoate 27.5 mcg per spray):
- Week 1: use 2 sprays in each nostril once daily
- Week 2 through 6 months: use 1 or 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, as needed to treat your symptoms
- After 6 months of daily use: ask your doctor if you can keep using this medicine
Usual Pediatric Dose for Rhinitis:
- 4 to 11 years: Flonase Allergy Relief or Children's Flonase Allergy Relief (fluticasone propionate 50 mcg per spray): 1 spray in each nostril once daily.
- 2 to 11 years: Flonase Sensimist or Children's Flonase Sensimist (fluticasone furoate 27.5 mcg per spray): 1 spray in each nostril once daily.
- Under 4 years: do not use fluticasone propionate nasal spray.
- Under 2 years: do not use fluticasone furoate nasal spray.
An adult should supervise a child using the spray. Children should use it for the shortest amount of time necessary to achieve symptom relief. Talk to your child's doctor if your child needs to use the spray for longer than two months a year.
What happens if I miss a dose?:
Use the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not use two doses at one time.
What happens if I overdose?:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.

## How does cyclobenzaprine work?
Cyclobenzaprine works by reducing the nerve signals in the brain that drive muscle tone and spasm, which allows tight, overactive muscles to relax. It acts within the central nervous system, primarily at the level of the brain stem, and does not act on the muscles themselves or at the junction between nerves and muscle. 1,2 Because cyclobenzaprine works through the nervous system in this way, it will not relieve muscle spasm caused by central nervous system disease, such as cerebral palsy or spinal cord disease. 1,2
The way cyclobenzaprine works in fibromyalgia is not known. Laboratory studies show it blocks several receptor types, including serotonin (5-HT2A), histamine, and muscarinic receptors. 3
Cyclobenzaprine is chemically related to tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline, which explains several of its side effects (such as drowsiness and dry mouth) and some of its most important drug interactions. 1,2

## What other drugs will affect hydrochlorothiazide?
Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Medicines that need particular care:
- Lithium. Lithium and diuretics generally should not be taken together. Hydrochlorothiazide reduces how quickly the kidneys clear lithium, which carries a high risk of lithium toxicity.
- Cholestyramine and colestipol. These cholesterol-lowering resins bind hydrochlorothiazide in the gut and can reduce how much you absorb by up to 85 percent for cholestyramine and 43 percent for colestipol. The doses need to be separated. For the oral suspension, the label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide at least 4 hours before, or 4 to 6 hours after, the resin.
- NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), diclofenac, meloxicam, indomethacin, celecoxib and aspirin. These can reduce the fluid-clearing and blood-pressure-lowering effects of hydrochlorothiazide, and your doctor will check whether the medicine is still working as intended.
- Insulin and oral diabetes medicines. Your diabetes medicine dose may need adjusting.
- Corticosteroids and ACTH. Taken with hydrochlorothiazide, these increase the loss of salts from the body, particularly potassium.
- Digoxin and other digitalis medicines. Low potassium caused by hydrochlorothiazide can make the heart more sensitive to the toxic effects of digitalis, including irregular heart rhythms.
- Other blood pressure medicines. The effects add together, which may be intended, but can also lower blood pressure more than expected.
- Alcohol, barbiturates and opioid pain medicines. These can make the drop in blood pressure on standing worse, causing dizziness or fainting.
- Muscle relaxants used during surgery (nondepolarizing muscle relaxants such as tubocurarine). You may respond more strongly to them, so tell your surgeon and anesthetist that you take hydrochlorothiazide.
- Medicines that raise blood pressure (pressor amines such as norepinephrine). Your response to them may be reduced, although this does not usually prevent their use.
This list is not complete. Other medicines may affect hydrochlorothiazide, and hydrochlorothiazide may affect other medicines.

## Warnings
You should not use ondansetron if you are also using apomorphine (Apokyn).
You should not use ondansetron if you are allergic to it or to similar medicines such as dolasetron (Anzemet), granisetron (Kytril), or palonosetron (Aloxi).
Before taking ondansetron, tell your doctor if you have liver disease, or a personal or family history of Long QT syndrome.
Ondansetron orally disintegrating tablets may contain phenylalanine. Tell your doctor if you have phenylketonuria (PKU).
Serious side effects of ondansetron include blurred vision or temporary vision loss (lasting from only a few minutes to several hours), slow heart rate, trouble breathing, anxiety, agitation, shivering, feeling like you might pass out, and urinating less than usual or not at all. Stop taking this medicine and call your doctor at once if you have any of these side effects. Ondansetron may impair your thinking or reactions. Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be alert.

## How does hydroxyzine work?
Hydroxyzine is thought to work by quieting activity in certain deeper regions of the brain, below the outer layer known as the cortex. It is not a cortical depressant, meaning it does not work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain the way some other sedatives do.
Hydroxyzine also blocks histamine, a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction. This is what relieves itching.
Laboratory and clinical studies have also shown that hydroxyzine relaxes skeletal muscle, widens the airways (bronchodilation), and reduces pain. These are effects that have been observed rather than uses the medicine is approved for.
Hydroxyzine has also been shown to reduce nausea and vomiting. This is an approved use for the injection, but not for the forms taken by mouth.

## How should I take escitalopram?
Take escitalopram exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Take escitalopram at the same time each day, with or without food.
Measure liquid medicine carefully. Use the dosing syringe provided, or use a medicine dose-measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
It may take up to 4 weeks before your symptoms improve. Keep using the medication as directed and tell your doctor if your symptoms do not improve.
Tell your doctor if you have any changes in sexual function, such as loss of interest in sex, trouble having an orgasm, or (in men) problems with erections or ejaculation. Some sexual problems can be treated.
Your doctor will need to check your progress on a regular basis. A child taking escitalopram should be checked for height and weight gain.
Do not stop using escitalopram suddenly, or you could have unpleasant withdrawal symptoms. Follow your doctor's instructions about tapering your dose.
Store escitalopram at room temperature away from moisture and heat.

## Before taking this medicine
You should not use methylphenidate if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
- glaucoma:
- pheochromocytoma (tumor of the adrenal gland);
- severe high blood pressure or a heart problem;
- overactive thyroid;
- a personal or family history of tics (muscle twitches) or Tourette's syndrome; or
- severe anxiety, tension, or agitation (stimulant medicine can make these symptoms worse).
Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in certain people. Tell your doctor if you have:
- heart problems or a congenital heart defect;
- high blood pressure; or
- a family history of heart disease or sudden death.
Do not use methylphenidate if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days. A dangerous drug interaction could occur. MAO inhibitors include isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, and tranylcypromine.
Tell your doctor if you also use opioid medicine, herbal products, or medicine for depression, mental illness, Parkinson's disease, migraine headaches, serious infections, or prevention of nausea and vomiting. An interaction with methylphenidate could cause a serious condition called serotonin syndrome.
Tell your doctor if you or anyone in your family has ever had:
- depression, mental illness, bipolar disorder, psychosis, or suicidal thoughts or actions;
- blood circulation problems in the hands or feet;
- alcoholism or drug addiction; or
- if you take Adhansia - an allergy to aspirin or yellow food dye.
- phenylketonuria (PKU), as some chewable tablets contain phenylalanine.
To make sure methylphenidate is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have::
- problems with the esophagus, stomach, or intestines; or
- seizures, epilepsy, or an abnormal brain wave test (EEG).
Becoming dependent on methylphenidate during pregnancy can cause premature birth or low birth weight. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. If you are pregnant, your name may be listed on a pregnancy registry to track the effects of methylphenidate on the baby.
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using this medicine. If you are breastfeeding, tell your doctor if you notice symptoms in the baby such as agitation, sleep problems, feeding problems, or reduced weight gain.
methylphenidate is not approved for use by anyone younger than 6 years old.

## What is the usual dosage of hydroxyzine?
The dose depends on what you are being treated for. The same doses apply to hydroxyzine hydrochloride tablets, hydroxyzine hydrochloride oral solution, and hydroxyzine pamoate capsules.
Dosage for anxiety and tension:
- Adults: 50 to 100 mg four times a day
- Children under 6 years: 50 mg a day, split into smaller doses
- Children 6 years and over: 50 to 100 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Dosage for itching:
- Adults: 25 mg three or four times a day
- Children under 6 years: 50 mg a day, split into smaller doses
- Children 6 years and over: 50 to 100 mg a day, split into smaller doses
Dosage for sedation before and after surgery:
- Adults: 50 to 100 mg
- Children: 0.6 mg for each kilogram of body weight
If treatment is started with an injection into a muscle, later doses can be given by mouth.
Dosage in older adults:
Doctors usually start older adults on a low dose. Sedating medicines can cause confusion and too much sedation in older people, so your doctor will watch you closely. Kidney, liver, and heart function often decline with age, and how much hydroxyzine leaves the body through the kidneys has not been established.

## Warnings
Pantoprazole is not for the immediate relief of heartburn symptoms.
Heartburn is often confused with the first symptoms of a heart attack. Seek emergency medical attention if you have chest pain or heavy feeling, pain spreading to the arm or shoulder, nausea, sweating, and a general ill feeling.
Long-term treatment with pantoprazole may also make it harder for your body to absorb vitamin B-12, resulting in a deficiency of this vitamin. Talk with your doctor if you need long-term pantoprazole treatment and you have concerns about vitamin B-12 deficiency.
Pantoprazole can cause kidney problems. Tell your doctor if you are urinating less than usual, or if you have blood in your urine.
Diarrhea may be a sign of a new infection. Call your doctor if you have diarrhea that is watery or has blood in it.
Pantoprazole may cause new or worsening symptoms of lupus. Tell your doctor if you have joint pain and a skin rash on your cheeks or arms that worsens in sunlight.
You may be more likely to have a broken bone while taking this medicine long term or more than once per day.

## Spironolactone FAQs
Is spironolactone a diuretic?:
Yes. Spironolactone is a diuretic, or water pill, and it belongs to the group called potassium-sparing diuretics. It works by blocking aldosterone, a hormone that makes your kidneys hold onto salt and water. Unlike most water pills, which make you lose potassium, spironolactone makes your body keep potassium in. It is a weaker diuretic than medicines such as furosemide, which is one reason it is often given alongside another water pill rather than instead of one.
Is spironolactone used for acne?:
Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating acne, but doctors sometimes prescribe it off-label for hormonal acne in women. Off-label means a doctor is prescribing a medicine for something other than its approved uses, which is legal and common, but it means the FDA has not reviewed the medicine for that purpose.
The reason it is used this way relates to how spironolactone works. As well as blocking aldosterone, spironolactone attaches to the androgen receptor, the docking point for male hormones such as testosterone. Male hormones increase how much oil the skin produces, and oil production is one factor in acne.
Because acne is not an approved use, there is no FDA-approved dose for it. Any dose is chosen by the prescriber. Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy because it may affect how a male baby develops, which is an important consideration for anyone taking it for a skin condition rather than a heart or kidney condition.
If you are considering spironolactone for acne, this is a conversation to have with a doctor or dermatologist who can review your full medical history, since spironolactone still carries the same risk of raising your potassium level, whatever it is prescribed for.
Does spironolactone cause weight gain?:
Weight gain is not a recognized side effect of spironolactone, and it is not listed in the medicine's official prescribing information. Spironolactone is a diuretic, so it usually causes a small drop in weight in the first week or two as your body sheds extra fluid.
If you are gaining weight while taking it, it is worth telling your doctor rather than assuming the medicine is to blame. Rapid weight gain with swelling in your ankles or legs or shortness of breath can be a sign of fluid building up, which may mean the condition being treated needs a closer look. Slower weight gain is more often down to appetite, activity, or another medicine.
Does spironolactone cause hair loss?:
Hair thinning, known as alopecia, is listed as a possible side effect of spironolactone, though how often it happens is not known. It is reported far less often than breast tenderness or breast growth.
The picture is complicated because spironolactone is also prescribed off label for hair loss in women, on the basis that blocking male hormones may help with hormone-related thinning. Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating hair loss. If your hair is thinning while you take it, speak to your doctor, since there are several possible causes worth ruling out.
How long does it take for spironolactone to work?:
It depends what you are taking it for. Spironolactone reaches its highest level in your blood in about 2 to 3 hours, and its active breakdown product peaks at around 4 hours, so it starts having an effect on your kidneys the same day.
The results you notice take longer. For fluid build-up, spironolactone is given for at least five days before the dose is increased, because that is how long the full effect takes to show. For high blood pressure, the dose is adjusted at two-week intervals, so give it a couple of weeks before judging it. For heart failure, the benefit is a lower risk of being admitted to hospital and living longer, which is not something you feel week to week.
How long does spironolactone stay in your system?:
Spironolactone itself leaves your blood very quickly, with a half-life of about 1.4 hours, meaning half of it is gone in that time. Its active breakdown products last much longer, with half-lives of roughly 14 to 17 hours. Because of those, the effect of a dose carries on well after the spironolactone itself has gone, and it takes a few days for the medicine to clear fully after you stop. Clearance is slower if you have cirrhosis.
Is spironolactone a blood thinner?:
No. Spironolactone is not a blood thinner. It does not affect blood clotting and it is not used to prevent clots or strokes in the way that warfarin, apixaban, or aspirin are. It is a diuretic that lowers blood pressure and reduces fluid build-up.
Spironolactone does interact with some blood thinners indirectly. Heparin and low molecular weight heparin can raise potassium, so taking them with spironolactone increases the risk of a high potassium level.
Can I stop taking spironolactone suddenly?:
Spironolactone does not cause withdrawal symptoms and does not need to be tapered the way a steroid does. Even so, do not stop it without speaking to your doctor. Stopping it can allow fluid to build up again, your blood pressure to rise, or your heart failure to worsen, and if you are taking it for heart failure it is one of the medicines shown to help people live longer. If side effects are the reason you want to stop, a dose change or a different medicine may be an option.
Can you take spironolactone at night?:
There is no fixed time of day for spironolactone. What matters more is that you take it at the same time each day and always the same way with regard to food, since food changes how much you absorb. Many people prefer the morning because spironolactone makes you pass more urine, and a late dose can mean getting up in the night. If a nighttime dose suits you better, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.
Can you drink alcohol while taking spironolactone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and spironolactone, but drinking is best kept modest. Both can lower your blood pressure and make you light-headed, so together they raise the chance of feeling dizzy or faint, particularly when you stand up. Alcohol is also a problem in its own right if you are taking spironolactone for liver disease. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for your situation.
Can you take spironolactone while pregnant?:
Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy. It blocks the action of male hormones, and in animal studies male offspring exposed before birth developed abnormally. Human data are limited and have not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern is enough that the manufacturer advises avoiding it or discussing the potential risk to a male baby.
Do not stop spironolactone on your own if you find out you are pregnant. Tell your doctor straight away, because untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry serious risks in pregnancy and your treatment will need to be changed carefully.
Does spironolactone cause constipation?:
Constipation is not a listed side effect of spironolactone. The digestive side effects that have been reported are the opposite, including diarrhea and stomach cramping, along with nausea, vomiting, and indigestion. If you are constipated while taking spironolactone, another cause is more likely, and it is worth mentioning to your pharmacist, who can check the rest of your medicines.
Is 200 mg of spironolactone too much?:
It depends on the reason you are taking it. For fluid build-up, the approved dose range goes up to 200 mg a day, and for primary hyperaldosteronism it goes up to 400 mg a day, so 200 mg is within the licensed range for both.
For high blood pressure it would be above the usual range, since doses over 100 mg a day do not lower blood pressure any further. For heart failure the usual dose is 25 mg to 50 mg a day, so 200 mg would be well above what is normally used. Higher doses also carry a greater risk of high potassium and of breast growth in men. If your dose seems high for your condition, ask your prescriber rather than adjusting it yourself.
Why is spironolactone described as a high-risk medicine?:
The main reason is the risk of a high potassium level, which can cause a dangerous change in your heart rhythm and often gives no warning symptoms. The risk rises if your kidneys do not work well or if you take other medicines that raise potassium, and several very common medicines do, including ibuprofen and some blood pressure tablets.
This risk is manageable, which is why blood tests are built into treatment. Your potassium should be checked within a week of starting spironolactone or changing your dose, and regularly after that. Spironolactone also needs care in pregnancy and in people with liver disease.

## What is furosemide?
Furosemide is a loop diuretic used to treat fluid retention (edema) in people with congestive heart failure, liver disease, or a chronic kidney disorder such as nephrotic syndrome. Furosemide is also used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension).
Furosemide works by increasing the amount of urine the body makes, which helps reduce swelling and symptoms of fluid retention and helps lower high blood pressure. Furosemide tablets are sometimes called water pills as they increase how much you urinate.
Furosemide is also known as frusemide in some countries. It has been available in the United States since the 1960s and comes as tablets (Lasix), an oral liquid, an intravenous solution, and subcutaneous injections and infusions that can be given at home (Furoscix, Lasix ONYU).

## How should I use furosemide?
Take or administer furosemide exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Furosemide oral tablets and liquid are taken by mouth. Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device, not a kitchen spoon.
Furosemide injection is given in a muscle, under the skin, or in a vein. A healthcare provider will give you this injection if you are unable to take the medicine by mouth.
Using subcutaneous furosemide at home:
You or your caregiver should be trained before your first dose, and you should read the Instructions for Use that comes with your prescription. Wash your hands first, and check that the liquid is clear and colorless to slightly yellow. Do not use it if you see particles or if it is cloudy or discolored.
Subcutaneous furosemide is given into the abdomen only, and you should use a different spot on the abdomen each time.
Furoscix ReadyFlow autoinjector
- Choose a site at least two inches from your belly button, avoiding skin that is broken or irritated and any scars or stretch marks. Clean it and let it dry.
- Pull the blue cap straight off, then press the device firmly against your skin and hold it there for about 10 seconds, until the yellow plunger rod stops moving and fills the viewing window.
- If you lift the device away before the window is completely yellow, you may not get the full dose. Call your healthcare provider if this happens, and do not use a second device unless you are told to.
Furoscix On-Body Infusor and Lasix ONYU Infusor
- The infusion takes about 5 hours, so plan to stay somewhere you can relax and reach a bathroom.
- Apply the device to a flat, clean, hairless area of the abdomen below the rib cage and above the belt line, and press it firmly into place. Do not remove and reapply it.
- Limit your activity while wearing it and avoid bending as much as you can. Do not exercise or do anything that might knock it off.
- Do not get the infusor wet. Do not bathe, shower, or swim while wearing it, and do not apply lotions or creams to the area where it is placed.
- Traveling by car or airplane while wearing the infusor is not recommended, and the Furoscix On-Body Infusor cannot be used in an MRI setting.
- Do not use the infusor within 12 inches of mobile phones, tablets, computers, or wireless accessories such as a remote control or Bluetooth device.
- Your healthcare provider will show you what the indicator light and alarms mean. You must use the infusor in a setting where you can detect and respond to these alarms to ensure you receive the full dose. If the device falls off, or the light blinks red, call your healthcare provider and do not reuse it.
Dispose of used autoinjectors, infusors, and cartridges in a sharps container. Do not put them in household trash and do not recycle them.
General furosemide dosing information:
Do not use more than your recommended dose. High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
This medicine will make you urinate more often, and you may get dehydrated easily. Follow your doctor's instructions about using potassium supplements or getting enough salt and potassium in your diet.
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often, and you may need other medical tests.
If you have high blood pressure, keep using furosemide even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
If you need surgery, tell the surgeon ahead of time that you are using furosemide.

Pantoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that decreases the amount of acid produced in the stomach.
Pantoprazole is used to treat erosive esophagitis (damage to the esophagus from stomach acid caused by gastroesophageal reflux disease, or GERD) in adults and children who are at least 5 years old. Pantoprazole is usually given for up to 8 weeks at a time while your esophagus heals.
Pantoprazole is also used to treat Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and other conditions involving excess stomach acid.

## What is amlodipine?
Amlodipine besylate is a prescription medicine used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to prevent certain types of angina (chest pain). It belongs to a class of medications called calcium channel blockers.
Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.
Amlodipine besylate controls angina chest pain by increasing the supply of blood to the heart. If taken regularly, this medicine controls chest pain, but it does not stop chest pain once it starts. Your doctor may prescribe a different medication to take when you have chest pain.
Amlodipine is also used alone or in combination with other medicines to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) in adults and children at least 6 years old. Lowering blood pressure may lower your risk of a stroke or heart attack.
Amlodipine besylate is available as:
- Amlodipine 5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 10 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 2.5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL solution (Norliqva)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL oral suspension (Katerzia)
- Amlodipine single-dose powder for oral solution (Sdamlo).

## Tirzepatide side effects
Common Side Effects:
The most common tirzepatide side effects are:
- Diarrhea
- Vomiting
- Constipation
- Nausea (mild to moderate)
- Decreased appetite
- Abdominal pain.
Serious side effects:
Tirzepatide can cause serious side effects. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following:
- Severe stomach pain (pancreatitis): Stop taking tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider immediately if you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, or pain that spreads to your back.
- Kidney problems: Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting can cause dehydration, which may lead to kidney problems. Drink plenty of fluids to reduce this risk and tell your doctor if you are unable to keep fluids down.
- Gallbladder problems: Symptoms include severe upper stomach pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), or clay-colored stools.
- Serious allergic reactions: Seek emergency medical attention if you experience hives, difficulty breathing, feeling light-headed, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (anaphylaxis or angioedema).
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia): Symptoms may include headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery.
- Vision changes: Tell your doctor about any blurred vision or other vision changes, particularly if you have type 2 diabetes.
- Thyroid tumor: Symptoms may include a lump or swelling in your neck, trouble swallowing, hoarseness, or shortness of breath.
- Mental health changes: Tell your healthcare provider right away about any new or worsening depression, mood changes, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm.
- Aspiration during surgery: Tirzepatide slows stomach emptying, which may increase the risk of food or liquid entering the lungs during procedures using anesthesia or sedation. Tell all your healthcare providers you are taking tirzepatide before any planned surgery or procedure.
This is not a complete list of side effects. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects, or report them to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Furosemide side effects
Common side effects:
Common furosemide side effects may include:
- diarrhea, constipation, loss of appetite
- numbness or tingling
- headache, dizziness
- blurred vision
- redness, bruising, swelling, or pain where a subcutaneous dose is given.
Serious furosemide side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to furosemide (hives, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).
Furosemide may cause other serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out
- ringing in your ears, hearing loss
- muscle spasms or contractions
- pale skin, easy bruising, unusual bleeding
- high blood sugar, with increased thirst, increased urination, dry mouth, or fruity breath odor
- kidney problems, with swelling, urinating less, feeling tired or short of breath
- signs of liver or pancreas problems, such as loss of appetite, upper stomach pain that may spread to your back, nausea or vomiting, dark urine, or jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes)
- signs of an electrolyte imbalance, such as increased thirst or urination, constipation, muscle weakness, leg cramps, numbness or tingling, feeling jittery, or fluttering in your chest.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is losartan?
Losartan is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children at least 6 years old.
Losartan is also used to decrease the risk of stroke in people who have high blood pressure and a heart condition called left ventricular hypertrophy (enlargement of the walls of the left side of the heart).
Losartan may not decrease the risk of stroke in African Americans who have these conditions.
Losartan is also used to treat kidney disease in people who have type 2 diabetes (condition in which the body does not use insulin normally and therefore cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood) and high blood pressure.
Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin II receptor antagonists. It works by blocking the action of certain natural substances that tighten the blood vessels, allowing the blood to flow more smoothly and the heart to pump more efficiently.

## What is the usual prednisone dosage?
The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
- There is no single standard dose. Your doctor will decide on a starting dose, then lower it in small steps to the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
- Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight, and must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days. A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days. Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes. Some people take it for a few days or weeks for a problem that will settle, such as an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction. Others take it every day for months or years for an ongoing condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or ulcerative colitis.
If you take prednisone long term, your doctor will settle you on a maintenance dose. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. It may need to go up for a time if your condition flares, or if you have surgery, a fever, an infection, or another serious illness, and it may come down again afterwards. Do not adjust it yourself.
How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Call your doctor if you feel unwell while your dose is being lowered or after you finish.

Common sertraline side effects:
The most common sertraline side effects are nausea, diarrhea or loose stools, trouble sleeping, dry mouth, tiredness, dizziness, sleepiness, tremor, indigestion, agitation, reduced appetite, increased sweating, and sexual problems.

Some side effects were more common with particular conditions. Sleepiness was more common in depression trials, insomnia and agitation in OCD trials, constipation and agitation in panic disorder trials, tiredness in PTSD trials, and insomnia, dizziness, tiredness, dry mouth, and a general feeling of being unwell in social anxiety disorder trials. In PMDD trials, sleepiness, dry mouth, dizziness, tiredness, and stomach pain were more common.
In these trials, 12% of people taking sertraline stopped treatment because of a side effect, compared with 4% of people taking placebo. The most common reasons for stopping were nausea (3%), diarrhea (2%), agitation (2%), and insomnia (2%).
Sexual side effects of sertraline:
SSRIs including sertraline can cause sexual problems. In men, this can mean delayed ejaculation or being unable to ejaculate, lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. In women, it can mean lower sex drive and delayed orgasm or being unable to have an orgasm.

Ejaculation disorder (men) | 3% | 0%
Male sexual dysfunction | 2% | 0%
Decreased libido (women) | 4% | 2%
Changes in sex drive and sexual function can also be part of depression and anxiety themselves, so the timing of when symptoms started matters. These numbers may underestimate how often sexual side effects happen, because people and their providers do not always raise the subject. Tell your provider about any change in sexual function, since there may be ways to manage it.
Serious sertraline side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to sertraline: rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of serotonin syndrome, which can be life threatening: agitation, hallucinations, confusion, coma or other changes in mental state, a racing heartbeat, high or low blood pressure, dizziness, heavy sweating, fever, muscle stiffness, twitching or overactive reflexes, loss of coordination, seizures, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea;
- unusual bleeding or bruising, including nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in vomit or stools, or black tarry stools;
- signs of a manic episode: greatly increased energy, severe trouble sleeping, racing thoughts, reckless behavior, unusually grand ideas, excessive happiness or irritability, or talking more or faster than usual;
- seizures or convulsions;
- eye pain, changes in vision, or swelling or redness in or around the eye, which can be signs of angle-closure glaucoma (a sudden rise in pressure inside the eye);
- signs of low sodium in the blood (hyponatremia): headache, trouble concentrating or thinking, memory problems, confusion, weakness, or feeling unsteady, which can lead to falls. Severe cases have caused hallucinations, fainting, seizures, coma, and death;
- fainting, chest discomfort, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation.

The overall pattern of side effects in 281 children and teenagers treated with sertraline was generally similar to that seen in adults. Side effects reported in at least 2% of children and teenagers, and at least twice as often as with placebo, that were not common in adults were fever, hyperkinesia (abnormally increased movement), urinary incontinence, aggression, nosebleeds, purpura (purple spots under the skin), joint pain, weight loss, muscle twitching, and anxiety.

## Cyclobenzaprine side effects
The most common cyclobenzaprine side effects are drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, fatigue, and headache. Most side effects are mild and settle as your body adjusts, but cyclobenzaprine can occasionally cause serious heart rhythm effects and serotonin syndrome. 1
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects may include: 1
- drowsiness and tiredness;
- dry mouth;
- dizziness;
- fatigue;
- headache;
- nausea, indigestion, or constipation;
- blurred vision;
- unpleasant taste;
- nervousness or confusion.
In placebo-controlled trials of the immediate-release tablets, side effects were dose-related, occurring more often with 10 mg than with 5 mg: 1
Side effect | Cyclobenzaprine 5 mg | Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg | Placebo
Drowsiness | 29% | 38% | 10%
Dry mouth | 21% | 32% | 7%
Fatigue | 6% | 6% | 3%
Headache | 5% | 5% | 8%
With Amrix, the most common side effects are dry mouth (up to 14% at 30 mg), dizziness, fatigue, constipation, nausea, indigestion, and drowsiness. 2
With Tonmya, because it dissolves under the tongue, the most common side effects involve the mouth: reduced feeling or numbness in the mouth (23%), mouth discomfort, abnormal taste, tingling, mouth pain, and canker sores, along with sleepiness, fatigue, and dry mouth. Mouth-related effects usually begin within minutes of a dose and most resolve within an hour. Moistening your mouth with sips of water before dosing reduces the risk of numbness. Tell your healthcare provider if mouth effects are severe. 3
Serious cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to cyclobenzaprine: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; or itching. 2,3
Stop taking cyclobenzaprine and call your doctor at once if you have: 1,2,3
- fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeats;
- chest pain or pressure, or pain spreading to your jaw or shoulder;
- sudden numbness or weakness, slurred speech, or balance problems; or
- symptoms of serotonin syndrome: agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness or twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Serious side effects, including confusion, hallucinations, and heart problems leading to falls, are more likely in older adults. 1
Does cyclobenzaprine make you sleepy?:
Yes, drowsiness is the most common side effect of the tablets, affecting up to 38% of people taking the 10 mg dose in clinical trials. This is one reason 5 mg is the usual starting dose, since it causes less drowsiness with comparable effectiveness. Analysis of trial data shows cyclobenzaprine relieves muscle spasm whether or not sedation occurs, so drowsiness is not required for it to work. 1
Does cyclobenzaprine cause constipation?:
Constipation is a known side effect, reported in 1% to 3% of people taking the immediate-release tablets and up to 3% of people taking Amrix 30 mg in clinical trials. It results from the drug's anticholinergic (drying) effects, the same mechanism behind dry mouth and blurred vision. 1,2

## Before taking this medicine
You should not use spironolactone if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
- a high level of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia);
- Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder); or
- if you are taking eplerenone.
To make sure spironolactone is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have or have ever had:
- kidney disease, or reduced kidney function;
- liver disease, especially cirrhosis or fluid in the abdomen (ascites);
- an electrolyte imbalance, such as a low sodium, magnesium, or calcium level;
- dehydration, or any illness causing vomiting or diarrhea;
- diabetes, since spironolactone can raise blood sugar;
- gout or a high uric acid level; or
- prostate cancer treated with abiraterone.
Pregnancy:
Spironolactone blocks the effect of male hormones, and male hormones are needed for a male baby to develop normally. In animal studies, male offspring exposed in the womb showed feminized development. The limited information available in humans has not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern remains. Your doctor will usually avoid spironolactone in pregnancy, or talk through the possible risk to a male baby with you. Untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry real risks in pregnancy, so this is a decision to make with your doctor rather than by stopping on your own.
Breastfeeding:
Spironolactone itself does not pass into breast milk. Its active breakdown product, canrenone, has been found in breast milk in very small amounts that are not expected to affect a breastfed baby. No side effects were reported in the one infant studied over a short period, and the long-term picture is not known. Talk to your doctor so you can weigh this up together.
Children:
Spironolactone has not been shown to be safe and effective in children. The oral liquid is specifically not recommended for treating high blood pressure in children, because of the hormonal effects of the medicine. Any use in a child must be decided and monitored by a specialist.
Older adults:
Spironolactone is cleared by the kidneys, and kidney function tends to fall with age. Older adults are therefore more likely to build up a high potassium level, so kidney function and potassium need monitoring.

Amlodipine besylate is a prescription medicine used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to prevent certain types of angina (chest pain). It belongs to a class of medications called calcium channel blockers.
Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.

Hydrochlorothiazide is approved to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and fluid retention (edema) in certain patients.
