## What is tamsulosin?
Tamsulosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH. These symptoms include a weak urine stream, trouble starting to urinate, dribbling, a feeling of not emptying the bladder completely, needing to urinate often or urgently, and getting up at night to urinate.
Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers. It works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck. Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there, which improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms.
Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened.
The tamsulosin brand name was Flomax, which has now been discontinued in the U.S., but generic tamsulosin is available.

## What is prednisone?
Prednisone is a prescription corticosteroid (steroid) used to reduce inflammation, suppress an overactive immune system, and treat endocrine and metabolic disorders. Prednisone is used for a wide range of conditions, including severe allergies, asthma and COPD flare-ups, rheumatoid arthritis and other forms of arthritis, lupus, psoriasis and other skin conditions, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, eye inflammation, some blood disorders, and low adrenal hormone levels.
Prednisone works by mimicking the effects of glucocorticoid hormones secreted naturally by our adrenal glands. Prednisone is a man-made (synthetic) version of these hormones. Prednisone is different from steroids taken to build muscle (anabolic steroids).
Prednisone belongs to the drug class called glucocorticoids, which are a type of corticosteroid.
Prednisone tablets come in 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, and 50 mg strengths. Prednisone 20 mg and prednisone 10 mg tablets are the strengths most often used for short courses in adults. Prednisone also comes as a delayed-release tablet (Rayos), as an oral liquid, and as a concentrated oral solution (Prednisone Intensol) that is measured with a special dropper.
Many of the original brands are discontinued; however, generic prednisone is available.

## Fluoxetine Side Effects
Like all medications, Prozac can cause side effects. Not everyone experiences them, and many improve after the first few weeks as your body adjusts to the medication. Tell your doctor if any side effects bother you or do not go away.
Common Fluoxetine Side Effects:
The most commonly reported side effects of fluoxetine (Prozac) include:
- Nausea
- Trouble sleeping (insomnia)
- Drowsiness or sleepiness
- Anxiety or feeling nervous or on edge
- Trembling or shaking (tremor)
- Excessive sweating
- Loss of appetite
- Diarrhea
- Dry mouth
- Indigestion or upset stomach
- Weakness or fatigue
- Sore throat
- Sinus congestion or infection
- Flu-like symptoms
- Skin rash
- Flushing or feeling of warmth
- Yawning
- Unusual or vivid dreams
- Decreased sex drive
- Difficulty getting or keeping an erection
- Delayed or abnormal ejaculation
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to this medicine (hives, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).
Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor, such as mood or behavior changes, anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, hyperactive (mentally or physically), more depressed, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself.
This medicine may cause serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- blurred vision, tunnel vision, eye pain or swelling, or seeing halos around lights;
- fast or pounding heartbeats, fluttering in your chest, shortness of breath, and sudden dizziness (like you might pass out);
- low levels of sodium in the body - headache, confusion, slurred speech, severe weakness, vomiting, loss of coordination, feeling unsteady; or
- severe nervous system reaction - very stiff (rigid) muscles, high fever, sweating, confusion, fast or uneven heartbeats, tremors, feeling like you might pass out.
Seek medical attention right away if you have symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as: agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Sertraline side effects
Common sertraline side effects:
The most common sertraline side effects are nausea, diarrhea or loose stools, trouble sleeping, dry mouth, tiredness, dizziness, sleepiness, tremor, indigestion, agitation, reduced appetite, increased sweating, and sexual problems.
The table below shows how often each side effect was reported in pooled placebo-controlled trials in 3,066 adults, compared with 2,293 people taking placebo.
Side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Nausea | 26% | 12%
Diarrhea or loose stools | 20% | 10%
Insomnia (trouble sleeping) | 20% | 13%
Dry mouth | 14% | 9%
Fatigue (tiredness) | 12% | 8%
Dizziness | 12% | 8%
Somnolence (sleepiness) | 11% | 6%
Tremor (shaking) | 9% | 2%
Dyspepsia (indigestion) | 8% | 4%
Agitation | 8% | 5%
Decreased appetite | 7% | 2%
Hyperhidrosis (heavy sweating) | 7% | 3%
Constipation | 6% | 4%
Decreased libido (lower sex drive) | 6% | 2%
Palpitations | 4% | 2%
Visual impairment | 4% | 2%
Vomiting | 4% | 1%
Some side effects were more common with particular conditions. Sleepiness was more common in depression trials, insomnia and agitation in OCD trials, constipation and agitation in panic disorder trials, tiredness in PTSD trials, and insomnia, dizziness, tiredness, dry mouth, and a general feeling of being unwell in social anxiety disorder trials. In PMDD trials, sleepiness, dry mouth, dizziness, tiredness, and stomach pain were more common.
In these trials, 12% of people taking sertraline stopped treatment because of a side effect, compared with 4% of people taking placebo. The most common reasons for stopping were nausea (3%), diarrhea (2%), agitation (2%), and insomnia (2%).
Sexual side effects of sertraline:
SSRIs including sertraline can cause sexual problems. In men, this can mean delayed ejaculation or being unable to ejaculate, lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. In women, it can mean lower sex drive and delayed orgasm or being unable to have an orgasm.
Sexual side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Ejaculation failure (men) | 8% | 1%
Decreased libido (men) | 7% | 2%
Erectile dysfunction (men) | 4% | 1%
Ejaculation disorder (men) | 3% | 0%
Male sexual dysfunction | 2% | 0%
Decreased libido (women) | 4% | 2%
Changes in sex drive and sexual function can also be part of depression and anxiety themselves, so the timing of when symptoms started matters. These numbers may underestimate how often sexual side effects happen, because people and their providers do not always raise the subject. Tell your provider about any change in sexual function, since there may be ways to manage it.
Serious sertraline side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to sertraline: rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of serotonin syndrome, which can be life threatening: agitation, hallucinations, confusion, coma or other changes in mental state, a racing heartbeat, high or low blood pressure, dizziness, heavy sweating, fever, muscle stiffness, twitching or overactive reflexes, loss of coordination, seizures, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea;
- unusual bleeding or bruising, including nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in vomit or stools, or black tarry stools;
- signs of a manic episode: greatly increased energy, severe trouble sleeping, racing thoughts, reckless behavior, unusually grand ideas, excessive happiness or irritability, or talking more or faster than usual;
- seizures or convulsions;
- eye pain, changes in vision, or swelling or redness in or around the eye, which can be signs of angle-closure glaucoma (a sudden rise in pressure inside the eye);
- signs of low sodium in the blood (hyponatremia): headache, trouble concentrating or thinking, memory problems, confusion, weakness, or feeling unsteady, which can lead to falls. Severe cases have caused hallucinations, fainting, seizures, coma, and death;
- fainting, chest discomfort, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation.
Sertraline side effects in children and teenagers:
The overall pattern of side effects in 281 children and teenagers treated with sertraline was generally similar to that seen in adults. Side effects reported in at least 2% of children and teenagers, and at least twice as often as with placebo, that were not common in adults were fever, hyperkinesia (abnormally increased movement), urinary incontinence, aggression, nosebleeds, purpura (purple spots under the skin), joint pain, weight loss, muscle twitching, and anxiety.
Reduced appetite and weight loss have been seen with SSRIs, so height and weight should be monitored during treatment.
Other reported side effects:
Less common side effects reported during studies include tachycardia (fast heartbeat), tinnitus (ringing in the ears), underactive thyroid, enlarged pupils, blurred vision, blood in the stools, swelling, unsteady walking, irritability, fever, raised liver enzymes, anaphylaxis, diabetes, high cholesterol, low blood sugar, increased appetite, joint pain, muscle spasms, poor coordination, coma, convulsions, reduced alertness, numbness, lethargy, restlessness, fainting, aggression, teeth grinding, confusion, euphoric mood, hallucination, blood in the urine, milk production from the breasts, priapism (a long-lasting erection), vaginal bleeding, wheezing, yawning, hair loss, cold sweats, skin inflammation, blistering, itching, rash, hives, bleeding, high blood pressure, and flushing.
Side effects reported after sertraline came onto the market include increased clotting times, AV block, slow heartbeat, atrial arrhythmias, QTc prolongation, ventricular tachycardia including Torsade de Pointes, breast enlargement in men, raised prolactin, irregular periods, SIADH, blindness, optic neuritis, cataract, severe liver problems including hepatitis, jaundice, and liver failure with some fatal outcomes, pancreatitis, several blood disorders, angioedema, low sodium, high blood sugar, rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), lockjaw, serotonin syndrome, movement disorders including akathisia and dystonia, psychosis, bedwetting, nightmares, sudden kidney failure, pulmonary hypertension, eosinophilic pneumonia, loss of smell, photosensitivity, severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, spasm of blood vessels in the brain, and vasculitis.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Metoprolol warnings
The most important warning with metoprolol is not to stop it suddenly. Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can bring on worse chest pain and, in some cases, a heart attack. If your treatment needs to stop, your prescriber will lower the dose gradually over 1 to 2 weeks and watch how you respond. This applies even if you only take metoprolol for blood pressure, because heart disease is common and is not always known about.
Talk to your care team before starting metoprolol if any of these apply to you.
- Asthma or other breathing problems. Beta blockers can tighten the airways. Metoprolol is used in people with these conditions only when other treatments are not suitable, at the lowest possible dose, with a reliever inhaler on hand.
- Heart failure. Heart failure can get worse while the dose is being increased. Tell your doctor about weight gain or increasing breathlessness.
- A slow heart rate or a conduction problem in the heart. This includes first-degree heart block, sinus node problems, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Your heart rate should be monitored.
- Diabetes or long gaps without food. Metoprolol can hide the early warning signs of low blood sugar, such as a fast heartbeat, and can make low blood sugar more severe or last longer. The risk is higher if you are fasting, not eating regularly, or vomiting.
- An overactive thyroid. Metoprolol can mask signs of an overactive thyroid. Stopping it suddenly can trigger a thyroid crisis.
- Circulation problems in your arms or legs. Beta blockers can make symptoms of poor circulation worse.
- A history of severe allergic reactions. If you have anaphylaxis while taking a beta blocker, the usual dose of injectable epinephrine may not work as well.
- Pheochromocytoma (a tumor of the adrenal gland). Metoprolol must only be started after an alpha blocker has been started, or blood pressure can rise sharply.
- Liver disease. Metoprolol is broken down by the liver, so levels can build up. Treatment is usually started at a lower dose.
Surgery. Tell your surgeon and dentist that you take metoprolol. Long-term beta blocker treatment is not usually stopped before surgery. Starting a high dose of extended-release metoprolol shortly before non-cardiac surgery is avoided, because in one large trial this was linked to more slow heartbeats, low blood pressure, strokes, and deaths.

## Before taking this medicine
Do not take tramadol if you are:
- are allergic to tramadol, to any of the other ingredients in your product, or to other opioids
- have significant breathing problems (respiratory depression)
- have acute or severe asthma and are somewhere you cannot be monitored, or where resuscitation equipment is not available
- have a known or suspected blockage of the stomach or intestines, including paralytic ileus
- have taken a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) in the past 14 days (such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, or tranylcypromine)
- are younger than 12 years of age
- are younger than 18 years of age and have recently had surgery to remove your tonsils or adenoids.
Seizures have occurred in some people taking tramadol. Your seizure risk may be higher if you have ever had:
- a head injury, epilepsy, or other seizure disorder
- drug or alcohol addiction or
- a metabolic disorder.
To make sure tramadol is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have a history of:
- Head injury or seizures
- Problems urinating
- Liver, kidney, or thyroid problems
- Pancrease or gallbladder problems, including pancreatitis or surgery on your pancreas
- A serious infection
- Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, opioid overdose, or mental health problems.
Also tell your doctor if you are dehydrated, are eating less or have changed your diet, are on a low-sodium (salt) diet, drink a lot of alcohol, or are planning to have surgery.
Tell your healthcare provider if you are:
- Living in a household where there are small children or someone who has abused street or prescription drugs
- Taking prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements. Taking tramadol with certain other medicines can cause serious side effects that could lead to death
- Notice your pain getting worse. If your pain gets worse after you take tramadol, do not take more tramadol without first talking to your doctor. Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain after taking tramadol.
Important Information Guiding Use in Pediatric Patients:
- Do not give tramadol to a child younger than 12 years of age or extended-release tramadol to anyone under 18 years.
- Do not give tramadol to a child younger than 18 years of age after surgery to remove the tonsils and/or adenoids.
- Avoid giving tramadol to children between 12 and 18 years of age who have risk factors for breathing problems. These include having recently had surgery, obstructive sleep apnea, obesity, severe lung disease, neuromuscular disease, and taking other medicines that can slow breathing.
Pregnancy:
Tramadol may harm an unborn baby and is not usually recommended during pregnancy. Use of tramadol for an extended period of time during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby that could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated. Neonatal seizures, neonatal withdrawal syndrome, fetal death, and stillbirth have all been reported. Tramadol is also not recommended during or immediately before labor. It should only be used in pregnancy if the benefits outweigh the risks. If you are already taking tramadol and become pregnant, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping suddenly can be harmful to you both.
Breastfeeding:
Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking tramadol, as it may harm your baby. Mothers who are ultra-rapid metabolizers of tramadol can have higher than expected levels of its active form in their breast milk, which can be dangerous for a breastfed infant. Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness. Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs.

## How should I use levothyroxine?
Take levothyroxine exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Some brands of levothyroxine have different dosage instructions and/or recommendations of how soon you need to take them before eating food. Always check the instructions on the label.
Oral levothyroxine:
Oral levothyroxine is taken by mouth and is available as tablets, capsules, and an oral solution.
- Keep using this medicine even if you feel well. It may take 4 to 6 weeks to get the full benefit of a dose.
- You will need frequent medical tests, and your next dose may be delayed based on the results.
- This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests. Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using this medicine.
- Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery or dental procedure.
- Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Tablets and capsules:
Take levothyroxine tablets and capsules on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast with a full glass of water. A full glass of water is important to avoid choking or gagging, because the tablet can start to break apart quickly. Take the medicine at the same time each day.
- Swallow the capsule whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it. Tell your doctor if your child cannot swallow a capsule whole.
- If you cannot swallow a tablet whole, crush the tablet and mix it with 1 or 2 teaspoons of water; give the mixture right away by spoon or dropper and make sure all of it is taken. Do not save it for later use. Do not mix it into soy-based infant formula or other foods that can stop levothyroxine being absorbed.
- Keep each tablet or capsule in the blister pack until you are ready to take one.
- Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Oral solution (liquid medicine):
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
- Dosages are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
- Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of levothyroxine. Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
- Tirosint-Sol oral solution comes in single-dose ampules and can be administered 15 minutes before eating breakfast. Squeeze the liquid directly into your mouth, onto a spoon, or into a glass of water to drink right away. Use all ampules within 3 months after opening the foil pouch.
- Ermeza and Thyquidity liquids should be taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast. Store them in their original bottle. Use Ermeza within 90 days and Thyquidity within 8 weeks of opening the bottle.
- Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Intravenous levothyroxine:
This is given as an injection into a vein by a healthcare provider and should only be used to treat myxedema coma.
Blood tests, biotin, and monitoring:
Your doctor will use blood tests to check that your dose is right, usually 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change, and then every 6 to 12 months once your dose is stable. Children are tested more often, including 2 and 4 weeks after starting treatment and 2 weeks after any dose change.
Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you take biotin, or a multivitamin, hair, skin, or nail supplement that contains biotin (sometimes listed as vitamin B7). Biotin can interfere with thyroid blood tests and give a falsely high or falsely low result, which could lead to the wrong dose change. Stop biotin and any biotin-containing supplements at least 2 days before a thyroid blood test.
If your symptoms and blood tests still suggest an underactive thyroid even though you are on a dose that should be enough, it may be because the medicine is not being absorbed properly, doses are being missed, or another medicine is interfering. Talk to your doctor before your dose is increased.

## Sertraline FAQs
Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline has very little effect on norepinephrine and dopamine, and it has no meaningful effect on adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopamine, histamine, or benzodiazepine receptors, which is part of why it is described as selective.
How long does sertraline take to work?:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.
Should I take sertraline in the morning or at night?:
Either is fine. Sertraline is taken once a day, in the morning or the evening, and the label does not favor one over the other. What matters more is taking it at around the same time each day. Insomnia was reported by 20% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 13% on placebo, and sleepiness by 11% compared with 6%, so some people find one timing suits them better than the other. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does sertraline cause weight gain or weight loss?:
Reduced appetite is a common sertraline side effect, reported by 7% of adults in trials compared with 2% on placebo. Increased appetite was reported less often, in fewer than 2% of people. In children and teenagers taking sertraline for depression, there was a difference in weight change of roughly 1 kg compared with placebo over 10 weeks, representing slight weight loss on sertraline and slight gain on placebo. Around 7% of children lost more than 7% of their body weight, compared with none on placebo. In a longer 34 week extension study, weight gain was similar to what would be expected for their age. Height and weight should be monitored in younger patients. Tell your doctor about any weight change that concerns you.
Does sertraline make you tired or sleepy?:
It can. Sleepiness was reported by 11% of adults taking sertraline in trials, compared with 6% on placebo, and tiredness by 12% compared with 8%. Sertraline can also affect how clearly you think and how quickly you react, so do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.
Is sertraline a controlled substance?:
No. Sertraline is not a controlled substance. In a study comparing sertraline with alprazolam and d-amphetamine, sertraline did not produce the effects associated with a potential for misuse, such as euphoria or drug liking, that were seen with the other two medicines.
Can sertraline cause diarrhea or nausea?:
Yes, these are the two most common sertraline side effects. Nausea was reported by 26% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 12% on placebo, and diarrhea or loose stools by 20% compared with 10%. Nausea was also the most common reason people stopped treatment. Tell your doctor if these do not settle.
How do you stop taking sertraline safely?:
Lower the dose gradually rather than stopping all at once, and only under your doctor's guidance. Symptoms reported after stopping a serotonergic antidepressant, especially when it is stopped abruptly, include nausea, sweating, low or unstable mood, irritability, agitation, dizziness, unusual sensations such as electric shock feelings, tremor, anxiety, confusion, headache, lethargy, insomnia, hypomania, ringing in the ears, and seizures.
Can you drink alcohol while taking sertraline?:
Drinking alcohol is not recommended while you take sertraline. In healthy volunteers, sertraline did not increase the immediate effects of alcohol on thinking and coordination, but the advice for patients is still to avoid it. Separately, do not take sertraline oral solution with disulfiram, because the solution contains 12% alcohol.
Can you take sertraline while pregnant?:
That depends on your situation, and it is a decision to make with your doctor rather than on your own. Studies of first trimester use suggest no overall difference in the risk of major birth defects, but use late in pregnancy has been linked with newborn breathing problems and with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. At the same time, stopping an antidepressant during pregnancy raises the risk of depression coming back. The oral solution specifically is not recommended in pregnancy because it contains alcohol.
What are sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules for?:
Sertraline capsules come in 150 mg and 200 mg only, and they are not used to start treatment. They are for people who have already been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week and need a higher dose. The maximum is 200 mg a day, the same as for tablets. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not opened, crushed, or chewed. If you need to come off sertraline, the dose has to be lowered gradually using another sertraline product, because there is no capsule strength below 150 mg. Capsules are approved for depression in adults and OCD from age 6, not for panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, or PMDD.
Does sertraline interact with warfarin?:
Yes, in two ways. Sertraline can add to warfarin's effect on bleeding risk, and both medicines bind tightly to proteins in the blood, so taking them together can raise the free level of one or both. If you take warfarin with sertraline, your INR should be monitored carefully.

Simvastatin belongs to a group of drugs called HMG CoA reductase inhibitors, or "statins."

## Warnings
Adderall has a Boxed Warning for abuse, misuse, and addiction.
Abuse, misuse, and addiction:
Adderall has a high chance of abuse and misuse and may lead to substance use problems, including addiction. Misuse and abuse of Adderall, other amphetamine-containing medicines, and methylphenidate-containing medicines can lead to overdose and death. The risk of overdose and death is increased with higher doses or when the medicine is used in ways that are not approved, such as snorting or injection.
Adderall may lead to physical dependence after prolonged use, even if taken as directed. Your healthcare provider should check you or your child for the risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction before starting treatment and will monitor you or your child during treatment. Tell your healthcare provider if you or your child has ever abused or been dependent on alcohol, prescription medicines, or street drugs.
Heart-related risks:
Stimulants have caused stroke, heart attack, and sudden death in people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or a heart defect. Your healthcare provider should check you or your child carefully for heart problems before starting Adderall and should check blood pressure and heart rate regularly during treatment.
Call your healthcare provider right away or go to the nearest hospital emergency room if you or your child have any signs of heart problems, such as chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting during treatment.
Mental (psychiatric) problems:
Adderall may cause new or worse behavior and thought problems, new or worse bipolar illness, or new psychotic symptoms (such as hearing voices, or seeing or believing things that are not real) or new manic symptoms. This is more likely if you have a history of depression, mental illness, or bipolar disorder. Tell your healthcare provider about any mental problems you or your child have, or about a family history of suicide, bipolar illness, or depression.
Call your healthcare provider right away if you or your child have any new or worsening mental symptoms during treatment, especially hearing voices, seeing or believing things that are not real, or new manic symptoms.
Circulation problems:
You may have blood circulation problems that can cause numbness, pain, or discoloration in your fingers or toes. Call your doctor right away if you have unexplained wounds appearing on your fingers or toes during treatment.
Other warnings:
Do not use Adderall if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine, or if you have received a methylene blue injection. A dangerous drug interaction could occur.
You may not be able to use Adderall if you have glaucoma, an overactive thyroid, severe anxiety or agitation, moderate to severe high blood pressure, heart disease or coronary artery disease, vascular disease, or a history of drug or alcohol addiction.

## Before taking this medicine
You should not use spironolactone if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
- a high level of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia);
- Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder); or
- if you are taking eplerenone.
To make sure spironolactone is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have or have ever had:
- kidney disease, or reduced kidney function;
- liver disease, especially cirrhosis or fluid in the abdomen (ascites);
- an electrolyte imbalance, such as a low sodium, magnesium, or calcium level;
- dehydration, or any illness causing vomiting or diarrhea;
- diabetes, since spironolactone can raise blood sugar;
- gout or a high uric acid level; or
- prostate cancer treated with abiraterone.
Pregnancy:
Spironolactone blocks the effect of male hormones, and male hormones are needed for a male baby to develop normally. In animal studies, male offspring exposed in the womb showed feminized development. The limited information available in humans has not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern remains. Your doctor will usually avoid spironolactone in pregnancy, or talk through the possible risk to a male baby with you. Untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry real risks in pregnancy, so this is a decision to make with your doctor rather than by stopping on your own.
Breastfeeding:
Spironolactone itself does not pass into breast milk. Its active breakdown product, canrenone, has been found in breast milk in very small amounts that are not expected to affect a breastfed baby. No side effects were reported in the one infant studied over a short period, and the long-term picture is not known. Talk to your doctor so you can weigh this up together.
Children:
Spironolactone has not been shown to be safe and effective in children. The oral liquid is specifically not recommended for treating high blood pressure in children, because of the hormonal effects of the medicine. Any use in a child must be decided and monitored by a specialist.
Older adults:
Spironolactone is cleared by the kidneys, and kidney function tends to fall with age. Older adults are therefore more likely to build up a high potassium level, so kidney function and potassium need monitoring.

## How should I use furosemide?
Take or administer furosemide exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Furosemide oral tablets and liquid are taken by mouth. Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device, not a kitchen spoon.
Furosemide injection is given in a muscle, under the skin, or in a vein. A healthcare provider will give you this injection if you are unable to take the medicine by mouth.
Using subcutaneous furosemide at home:
You or your caregiver should be trained before your first dose, and you should read the Instructions for Use that comes with your prescription. Wash your hands first, and check that the liquid is clear and colorless to slightly yellow. Do not use it if you see particles or if it is cloudy or discolored.
Subcutaneous furosemide is given into the abdomen only, and you should use a different spot on the abdomen each time.
Furoscix ReadyFlow autoinjector
- Choose a site at least two inches from your belly button, avoiding skin that is broken or irritated and any scars or stretch marks. Clean it and let it dry.
- Pull the blue cap straight off, then press the device firmly against your skin and hold it there for about 10 seconds, until the yellow plunger rod stops moving and fills the viewing window.
- If you lift the device away before the window is completely yellow, you may not get the full dose. Call your healthcare provider if this happens, and do not use a second device unless you are told to.
Furoscix On-Body Infusor and Lasix ONYU Infusor
- The infusion takes about 5 hours, so plan to stay somewhere you can relax and reach a bathroom.
- Apply the device to a flat, clean, hairless area of the abdomen below the rib cage and above the belt line, and press it firmly into place. Do not remove and reapply it.
- Limit your activity while wearing it and avoid bending as much as you can. Do not exercise or do anything that might knock it off.
- Do not get the infusor wet. Do not bathe, shower, or swim while wearing it, and do not apply lotions or creams to the area where it is placed.
- Traveling by car or airplane while wearing the infusor is not recommended, and the Furoscix On-Body Infusor cannot be used in an MRI setting.
- Do not use the infusor within 12 inches of mobile phones, tablets, computers, or wireless accessories such as a remote control or Bluetooth device.
- Your healthcare provider will show you what the indicator light and alarms mean. You must use the infusor in a setting where you can detect and respond to these alarms to ensure you receive the full dose. If the device falls off, or the light blinks red, call your healthcare provider and do not reuse it.
Dispose of used autoinjectors, infusors, and cartridges in a sharps container. Do not put them in household trash and do not recycle them.
General furosemide dosing information:
Do not use more than your recommended dose. High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
This medicine will make you urinate more often, and you may get dehydrated easily. Follow your doctor's instructions about using potassium supplements or getting enough salt and potassium in your diet.
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often, and you may need other medical tests.
If you have high blood pressure, keep using furosemide even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
If you need surgery, tell the surgeon ahead of time that you are using furosemide.

## How atorvastatin improves cholesterol and heart health
When cholesterol and fats build up along your artery walls, in a process called atherosclerosis, they narrow the blood vessels and reduce blood and oxygen flow to your heart, brain, and other parts of your body. By slowing cholesterol production, atorvastatin helps prevent this buildup to keep blood flowing more freely to vital organs.
Lowering your blood level of cholesterol and fats with atorvastatin may help prevent heart disease, angina (chest pain), strokes, and heart attacks.
Your healthcare provider will check your blood lipid levels regularly to assess how well your treatment is working. These measurements include:
- LDL-C: Low-density lipoprotein (“bad” cholesterol)
- HDL-C: High-density lipoprotein (“good” cholesterol)
- TG: Triglycerides (a type of blood fat)
- Total-C: Total cholesterol

## How should I take tramadol?
Do not change your dose. Take tramadol exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. Use the lowest dose possible for the shortest time needed. Tell your doctor if you feel an increased urge to take more of this medicine.
- For acute (short-term) pain, you may only need to take tramadol for a few days. You may have some tramadol left over that you did not use. See disposal information at the bottom of this section for directions on how to safely dispose of tramadol.
- Take your prescribed dose as indicated by your healthcare provider. Take your prescribed dose as indicated by your healthcare provider. After your dose has been settled, immediate-release tramadol is usually taken as 50 mg to 100 mg (one or two 50 mg tablets) every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain. Do not take more than your prescribed dose, and do not take more than 400 mg of tramadol in one day. For immediate-release tramadol, that is eight 50 mg tablets a day, taken in divided doses, or 80 mL of the 5 mg/mL oral solution. Extended-release tramadol has a lower daily limit of 300 mg, taken as one dose once a day. Always check the strength printed on your own bottle or packet. Do not take tramadol together with any other medicine that contains tramadol.
- If you miss a dose, take your next dose at your usual time.
- Swallow the capsule or tablet whole to avoid exposure to a potentially fatal overdose. Do not crush, chew, break, open, or dissolve.
- Never crush or break a tramadol tablet to inhale the powder or mix it into a liquid to inject the drug into your vein. This practice has resulted in death.
- May be taken with or without food.
If you take the oral solution:
Tramadol oral solution is measured in millilitres (mL), not milligrams (mg), and contains 5 mg of tramadol in every 1 mL. Confusing the two units can cause a fatal overdose. Always measure your dose with a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup marked in mL, which your pharmacy can supply, and never with a household teaspoon or tablespoon. If your prescription is written in milligrams, ask your pharmacist to confirm how many millilitres that is before you take your first dose.
Notes:
You may have withdrawal symptoms if you stop using tramadol suddenly. Ask your doctor before stopping the medicine.
Ask your healthcare provider about medicines like naloxone or nalmefene that can be used in an emergency to reverse an opioid overdose.
Do not keep leftover tramadol. Just one dose can cause death if someone uses it accidentally or improperly. Ask your pharmacist where to locate a drug take-back disposal program. If there is no take-back program, mix the leftover medicine with cat litter or coffee grounds in a sealed plastic bag and throw the bag in the trash.
Call your healthcare provider if the dose you are taking does not control your pain.
If you have been taking tramadol regularly, do not stop taking tramadol without talking to your healthcare provider.

Ozempic Injection Recommended Dosage:
- Start Ozempic with a 0.25 mg subcutaneous injection (injection under the skin) once weekly for 4 weeks. The 0.25 mg dosage is intended for treatment initiation and is not effective for glycemic control.
- After 4 weeks on the 0.25 mg dosage, increase the dosage to 0.5 mg once weekly.

- If additional glycemic control is needed after at least 4 weeks on the 1 mg dosage, the dosage may be increased to 2 mg once weekly. The maximum recommended dosage is 2 mg once weekly.
- Administer Ozempic once weekly, on the same day each week, at any time of the day, with or without meals.
- The day of weekly administration can be changed if necessary, as long as the time between two doses is at least 2 days (>48 hours).
- If a dose is missed, administer Ozempic as soon as possible within 5 days after the missed dose. If more than 5 days have passed, skip the missed dose and administer the next dose on the regularly scheduled day. In each case, patients can then resume their regular once-weekly dosing schedule.

- 0.25 mg or 0.5 mg dose pen (4 doses of 0.25 mg and 2 doses of 0.5 mg, or 4 doses of 0.5 mg)

## Apixaban side effects
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction: hives, difficult breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Also seek emergency medical attention if you have symptoms of a spinal blood clot: back pain, numbness, tingling, muscle weakness in your lower body, or loss of bladder or bowel control.
Apixaban can cause you to bleed more easily. Call your doctor at once if you have signs of bleeding such as:
- bruising or bleeding that will not stop, unusual bleeding (nosebleeds, bleeding gums, vaginal bleeding);
- unexpected pain, joint pain or swelling;
- headache, dizziness, weakness, feeling like you might pass out;
- urine that looks red, pink, or brown; or
- bloody or tarry stools, coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Common side effects of apixaban may include:
- bleeding, including heavy menstrual bleeding; or
- headache, vomiting.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Important Information About Tramadol
Get emergency help or call 911 right away if you take too many tramadol (overdose). When you first start taking tramadol, when your dose is changed, or if you take too much (overdose), serious or life-threatening breathing problems that can lead to death may occur. Ask your healthcare provider about medicines like naloxone or nalmefene that can be used in an emergency to reverse an opioid overdose.
Taking tramadol with other opioid medicines, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids (gabapentin or pregabalin), alcohol, or other central nervous system depressants (including street drugs) can cause severe drowsiness, decreased awareness, breathing problems, coma, and death.
Do not take tramadol with any other medicine that contains tramadol. Check the label of every pain medicine you take, as some combination products contain tramadol.
You should be given a Medication Guide each time you fill a tramadol prescription. Read it every time, even if you have taken tramadol before, because the information may have changed. Your healthcare provider or pharmacist should also go through the risks of tramadol and how to take it safely with you, and explain what to do in an emergency.
Never give anyone else your tramadol. They could die from taking it. Selling or giving away tramadol is against the law.
Store tramadol securely, out of sight and reach of children, and in a location not accessible by others, including visitors to the home.

## Warnings
Do not use this medication if you are allergic to amoxicillin or to any other penicillin antibiotic, such as ampicillin (Omnipen, Principen), dicloxacillin (Dycill, Dynapen), oxacillin (Bactocill), penicillin (Beepen-VK, Ledercillin VK, Pen-V, Pen-Vee K, Pfizerpen, V-Cillin K, Veetids), and others.
Before using amoxicillin, tell your doctor if you are allergic to cephalosporins such as Omnicef, Cefzil, Ceftin, Keflex, and others. Also, tell your doctor if you have asthma, liver or kidney disease, a bleeding or blood-clotting disorder, mononucleosis (also called "mono"), or any type of allergy.
Amoxicillin can make birth control pills less effective. Ask your doctor about using a non-hormone method of birth control (such as a condom, diaphragm, or spermicide) to prevent pregnancy while taking this medicine. Take this medication for the full prescribed length of time. Your symptoms may improve before the infection is completely cleared. Amoxicillin will not treat a viral infection such as the common cold or flu. Do not share this medication with another person, even if they have the same symptoms you have.
Antibiotic medicines can cause diarrhea. This may happen while you are taking amoxicillin, or within a few months after you stop taking it. This may be a sign of a new infection. If you have diarrhea that is watery or bloody, stop taking this medicine and call your doctor. Do not use anti-diarrhea medicine unless your doctor tells you to.

## How should I take lisinopril?
Take lisinopril exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose..
You may take lisinopril with or without food.
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often and you may need frequent blood tests.
Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery.
Call your doctor if you have ongoing vomiting or diarrhea, or if you are sweating more than usual. You can easily become dehydrated while taking lisinopril. This can lead to very low blood pressure, an electrolyte imbalance, or kidney failure.
If you have high blood pressure, keep using lisinopril even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
Store tightly closed at room temperature, away from moisture and heat. Do not freeze.

## What happens if I overdose?
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.
Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death. If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep it with you at all times. A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up. Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.
Anyone can buy naloxone from a pharmacy or local health department. Make sure any person caring for you knows where you keep naloxone and how to use it.
The first signs of an acetaminophen overdose include loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, sweating, and confusion or weakness. Later symptoms may include pain in your upper stomach, dark urine, and yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes.

## How should I use Flonase Nasal Spray?
Use Flonase exactly as directed on the label, or as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Do not share this medicine with another person, even if they have the same symptoms you have. Sharing a bottle can spread germs.
Your dose will depend on the fluticasone brand or strength you use, and your dose may change once your symptoms improve. Follow all dosing instructions very carefully.
- A child using the nasal spray should be supervised by an adult.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Shake the bottle before each use. Flonase Allergy Relief should be shaken gently, and Flonase Sensimist should be shaken vigorously.
Use this product only once a day and do not use more than directed. Avoid getting the spray in your eyes or mouth.
If you switched to fluticasone from another steroid medicine, you should not stop using it suddenly. Follow your doctor's instructions about tapering your dose.
Storage differs between products. Store Flonase Allergy Relief and Children's Flonase Allergy Relief between 4°C and 30°C (39°F and 86°F). Store Flonase Sensimist between 15°C and 30°C (59°F and 86°F), and do not refrigerate or freeze it.
Throw the bottle away once you have used the number of sprays stated on the carton, even if there is still liquid in the bottle. The correct amount of medicine in each spray cannot be assured after the labeled number of sprays has been used. Bottle sizes vary between products and pack sizes, ranging from 30 to 144 metered sprays.
Dosing information:
Usual Adult Dose for Rhinitis (adults and children 12 years of age and older):
Flonase Allergy Relief Nasal Spray (fluticasone propionate 50 mcg per spray):
- Week 1: use 2 sprays in each nostril once daily
- Week 2 through 6 months: use 1 or 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, as needed to treat your symptoms
- After 6 months of daily use: ask your doctor if you can keep using this medicine
Flonase Sensimist Nasal Spray (fluticasone furoate 27.5 mcg per spray):
- Week 1: use 2 sprays in each nostril once daily
- Week 2 through 6 months: use 1 or 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, as needed to treat your symptoms
- After 6 months of daily use: ask your doctor if you can keep using this medicine
Usual Pediatric Dose for Rhinitis:
- 4 to 11 years: Flonase Allergy Relief or Children's Flonase Allergy Relief (fluticasone propionate 50 mcg per spray): 1 spray in each nostril once daily.
- 2 to 11 years: Flonase Sensimist or Children's Flonase Sensimist (fluticasone furoate 27.5 mcg per spray): 1 spray in each nostril once daily.
- Under 4 years: do not use fluticasone propionate nasal spray.
- Under 2 years: do not use fluticasone furoate nasal spray.
An adult should supervise a child using the spray. Children should use it for the shortest amount of time necessary to achieve symptom relief. Talk to your child's doctor if your child needs to use the spray for longer than two months a year.
What happens if I miss a dose?:
Use the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not use two doses at one time.
What happens if I overdose?:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
An overdose of Flonase is not expected to produce life-threatening symptoms. Using more than the recommended dose, or using it for longer than directed, may increase the chance of corticosteroid-related side effects such as cataracts or glaucoma, adrenal gland problems, an increased risk of infection, sores inside the nose, or slower growth in children.

## What is allopurinol?
Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors. It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body. High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). ## Warnings and precautions
Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin).

An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together. Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.
Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery. Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken it in the past, even if you stopped months ago. Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to. If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again. You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose.

## Tramadol side effects
Common side effects:
The most common side effects of tramadol are:
- dizziness or vertigo
- nausea
- constipation
- headache
- drowsiness
- vomiting
- itching.
Dry mouth is also commonly reported with the extended-release forms of tramadol.
A person's genetics can affect their response to tramadol, including their risk of side effects (see How do genetics affect tramadol?).
Serious tramadol side effects and warnings:
Tramadol may cause serious side effects, some of which may be fatal.
Tramadol can slow or stop your breathing and may be habit-forming. MISUSE OF THIS MEDICINE CAN CAUSE ADDICTION, OVERDOSE, OR DEATH, especially in a child or other person using the medicine without a prescription. Keep this medicine where others cannot get to it. Do not take more tramadol than prescribed, as an overdose can be fatal. Selling or giving away this medicine is against the law.
- A person caring for you should give naloxone and seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you find it hard to wake up. Serious breathing problems may be more likely in older adults and people who are debilitated or have wasting syndrome or chronic breathing disorders.
- Call your doctor at once if you have: noisy breathing, sighing, shallow breathing, breathing that stops during sleep a slow heart rate or weak pulse a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out seizure (convulsions) or low cortisol levels (symptoms include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, dizziness, worsening tiredness or weakness) low sodium levels (hyponatremia). Symptoms include headache, confusion, weakness, unsteadiness, or feeling sick low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion, or a fast heartbeat.
Seek medical attention right away if you have symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Seizures have been reported in patients taking tramadol. Your risk of seizures is higher if you are taking higher doses than recommended. Seizure risk is also higher in those with epilepsy or a history of seizures, and in those taking certain antidepressants, other opioids, MAO inhibitors, or other medicines that lower the seizure threshold.
You should not take tramadol if you have significant breathing problems, acute or severe asthma in a setting where you cannot be monitored, a blockage in your stomach or intestines, or if you have taken an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days (isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, and others). Tell your doctor before starting tramadol if you have a head injury or increased pressure inside your skull, as tramadol should be used with particular care in these situations.
Prescribers are advised not to prescribe tramadol for people who are suicidal or prone to addiction, and to use it with caution in people taking tranquilizers or antidepressants, or drinking heavily. If you are struggling with thoughts of harming yourself, or with your use of any medicine, tell your healthcare provider so they can help you find the right treatment and support.
Fatal side effects can occur if you use this medicine with alcohol, or with other drugs that cause drowsiness or slow your breathing. People taking extended-release forms of tramadol should not consume alcohol-containing beverages at the same time. Alcohol is also not advised with immediate-release forms of tramadol.
Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have occurred with tramadol, some of which caused death. People who are allergic to other opioids are at higher risk. Other hypersensitivity reactions include itching, hives, narrowing of the airways, swelling of the face and airways (angioedema), and serious skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome. Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to tramadol (symptoms include hives, difficulty breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning in your eyes, skin pain, a red or purple skin rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling).
Tramadol may make pain worse rather than better in some people, an effect called opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain after taking tramadol.
Tramadol extended-release capsules and tablets may complicate a healthcare provider’s clinical assessment of an acute abdominal condition. They are not recommended for people with severe liver or severe kidney impairment.
Taking tramadol during pregnancy may cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms in the newborn, known as neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS).
Some people are “ultra-rapid metabolizers” of tramadol because of a variation in an enzyme called CYP2D6. Their bodies convert tramadol into its active form faster than usual, which can produce dangerously high opioid levels even at a normal dose. Life-threatening breathing problems and deaths have occurred in children for this reason, including after surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Tramadol should not be given to a child younger than 12 years old, or to anyone younger than 18 years old who has recently had surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Extended-release tramadol should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years.
Tramadol may cause drowsiness or affect your ability to drive or perform hazardous tasks. Do not perform these tasks if tramadol causes confusion, mental impairment, or drowsiness.
Tramadol can cause withdrawal symptom s if stopped suddenly after being taken for a long period of time. Symptoms may include restlessness, drug craving, anxiety, and sweating. Do not stop taking tramadol suddenly without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping abruptly can cause serious withdrawal symptoms and uncontrolled pain (see How long does tramadol withdrawal last?).
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What other drugs will affect hydrochlorothiazide?
Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Medicines that need particular care:
- Lithium. Lithium and diuretics generally should not be taken together. Hydrochlorothiazide reduces how quickly the kidneys clear lithium, which carries a high risk of lithium toxicity.
- Cholestyramine and colestipol. These cholesterol-lowering resins bind hydrochlorothiazide in the gut and can reduce how much you absorb by up to 85 percent for cholestyramine and 43 percent for colestipol. The doses need to be separated. For the oral suspension, the label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide at least 4 hours before, or 4 to 6 hours after, the resin.
- NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), diclofenac, meloxicam, indomethacin, celecoxib and aspirin. These can reduce the fluid-clearing and blood-pressure-lowering effects of hydrochlorothiazide, and your doctor will check whether the medicine is still working as intended.
- Insulin and oral diabetes medicines. Your diabetes medicine dose may need adjusting.
- Corticosteroids and ACTH. Taken with hydrochlorothiazide, these increase the loss of salts from the body, particularly potassium.
- Digoxin and other digitalis medicines. Low potassium caused by hydrochlorothiazide can make the heart more sensitive to the toxic effects of digitalis, including irregular heart rhythms.
- Other blood pressure medicines. The effects add together, which may be intended, but can also lower blood pressure more than expected.
- Alcohol, barbiturates and opioid pain medicines. These can make the drop in blood pressure on standing worse, causing dizziness or fainting.
- Muscle relaxants used during surgery (nondepolarizing muscle relaxants such as tubocurarine). You may respond more strongly to them, so tell your surgeon and anesthetist that you take hydrochlorothiazide.
- Medicines that raise blood pressure (pressor amines such as norepinephrine). Your response to them may be reduced, although this does not usually prevent their use.
This list is not complete. Other medicines may affect hydrochlorothiazide, and hydrochlorothiazide may affect other medicines.

## What is the difference between hydroxyzine hydrochloride and hydroxyzine pamoate?
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) and hydroxyzine pamoate are two salt forms of the same active medicine. Taken by mouth, FDA-approved labeling gives them the same approved uses, the same doses, the same warnings, and the same side effects.
The injection is the exception. It is a hydroxyzine HCl product; there is no pamoate injection, and it has its own approved uses, doses, and warnings.
The practical differences are:
- Form. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride comes as tablets and as an oral solution. Hydroxyzine pamoate comes as capsules.
- How they dissolve. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride is very soluble in water. Hydroxyzine pamoate is practically insoluble in water.
- How the strength is measured. Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules are labeled by the amount of hydroxyzine HCl they are equivalent to. A 25 mg pamoate capsule delivers the same amount of active medicine as a hydroxyzine hydrochloride 25 mg tablet.
The two salts also had different brand names. Vistaril was the brand name for hydroxyzine pamoate, and Atarax was the brand name for hydroxyzine hydrochloride. Both brands have been discontinued in the United States, and hydroxyzine is now available as a generic medicine.
Is hydroxyzine pamoate stronger or longer lasting than hydroxyzine hydrochloride?:
No. You may read that hydroxyzine pamoate works better for anxiety, lasts longer, or reaches the brain more effectively than hydroxyzine hydrochloride. FDA-approved labeling does not support this.
Labeling for both salt forms states that hydroxyzine's effects are usually noticed within 15 to 30 minutes of a dose taken by mouth. Both are approved for the same three uses. Both carry the same doses, which are 50 to 100 mg four times a day for anxiety in adults, and 25 mg three or four times a day for itching. No FDA labeling describes a difference in how strongly or how long either form works.
The reason the doses match is that hydroxyzine pamoate capsules are labeled by their hydroxyzine hydrochloride equivalent. A 25 mg pamoate capsule and a 25 mg hydrochloride tablet deliver the same amount of active medicine.
If you feel that one form suits you better than the other, tell your doctor. People can respond differently to the same medicine.

## Before taking this medicine
Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions and medications before starting fluoxetine (Prozac), as some may interact with it or affect whether it is safe for you.
Tell your doctor if you take any of the following medications or supplements:
- Triptans (for migraine)
- Antidepressants or mood stabilizers, including SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, MAOIs, lithium, buspirone, or antipsychotics
- Amphetamines
- Opioid pain medications, including tramadol, fentanyl, meperidine, or methadone
- Over-the-counter supplements such as St. John's Wort or tryptophan
- Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
Many of these combinations can increase the risk of serotonin syndrome, a potentially serious condition.
Tell your doctor if you have or have had any of the following:
- Liver, kidney, or heart problems
- Seizures or epilepsy
- Bipolar disorder or mania
- Low sodium levels in the blood
- A stroke or high blood pressure
- Bleeding problems
Pregnancy
Tell your healthcare provider if you are pregnant, become pregnant, or plan to become pregnant while taking fluoxetine tablets. Using fluoxetine later in pregnancy may increase the risk of complications in the newborn, including problems that need a longer hospital stay, breathing support, or tube feeding, and a serious lung condition called persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Untreated depression also carries risks in pregnancy, so discuss the benefits and risks of treatment with your healthcare provider rather than stopping on your own.
If you become pregnant while taking fluoxetine tablets, ask your healthcare provider about joining the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants, which tracks pregnancy outcomes in women who take these medicines. You can enroll by calling 1-866-961-2388 or visiting womensmentalhealth.org.
Breastfeeding:
Fluoxetine passes into breast milk. Tell your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed, and discuss the best way to feed your baby while you are taking fluoxetine tablets. If you do breastfeed, watch your baby for agitation, irritability, poor feeding, or poor weight gain, and seek medical advice if you notice any of these.

## How should I use insulin glargine?
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Use the medicine exactly as directed. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you don't understand how to use an injection.
Prepare an injection only when you are ready to give it. Do not use it if the medicine looks cloudy, has changed colors, or has particles in it.
Insulin glargine is injected under the skin, using a syringe or insulin pen, once per day at the same time of day.
Insulin can be injected into your upper legs (thighs), upper arms, or stomach area (abdomen). Do not inject into the same place two times in a row. Avoid injecting into skin that is damaged, tender, bruised, pitted, thickened, scaly, or has a scar or hard lump.
When treating type 1 diabetes, use your short-acting insulin before meals as directed by your doctor.
Insulin glargine must not be given with an insulin pump or mixed with other insulins. Do not inject insulin glargine into a vein or a muscle.
Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of this medicine. Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
If you use an injection pen, use only the injection pen that comes with insulin glargine. Attach a new needle before each use. Do not transfer the insulin from the pen into a syringe.
Never share an injection pen, even if you changed the needle. Sharing these devices can pass infections from person to person.
Blood sugar can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can make you feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, or shaky. To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink hard candy, crackers, raisins, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. Your doctor may prescribe glucagon injections in case of severe hypoglycemia.
Tell your doctor if you have frequent symptoms of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia), such as increased thirst or urination. Ask your doctor before changing your medication dosage.
Wear a medical alert tag or carry an ID card to let others know you have diabetes.

## How should I take tramadol?
Do not change your dose. Take tramadol exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. Use the lowest dose possible for the shortest time needed. Tell your doctor if you feel an increased urge to take more of this medicine.
- For acute (short-term) pain, you may only need to take tramadol for a few days. You may have some tramadol left over that you did not use. See disposal information at the bottom of this section for directions on how to safely dispose of tramadol.
- Take your prescribed dose as indicated by your healthcare provider. Take your prescribed dose as indicated by your healthcare provider. After your dose has been settled, immediate-release tramadol is usually taken as 50 mg to 100 mg (one or two 50 mg tablets) every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain. Do not take more than your prescribed dose, and do not take more than 400 mg of tramadol in one day. For immediate-release tramadol, that is eight 50 mg tablets a day, taken in divided doses, or 80 mL of the 5 mg/mL oral solution. Extended-release tramadol has a lower daily limit of 300 mg, taken as one dose once a day. Always check the strength printed on your own bottle or packet. Do not take tramadol together with any other medicine that contains tramadol.
- If you miss a dose, take your next dose at your usual time.
- Swallow the capsule or tablet whole to avoid exposure to a potentially fatal overdose. Do not crush, chew, break, open, or dissolve.
- Never crush or break a tramadol tablet to inhale the powder or mix it into a liquid to inject the drug into your vein. This practice has resulted in death.
- May be taken with or without food.
If you take the oral solution:
Tramadol oral solution is measured in millilitres (mL), not milligrams (mg), and contains 5 mg of tramadol in every 1 mL. Confusing the two units can cause a fatal overdose. Always measure your dose with a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup marked in mL, which your pharmacy can supply, and never with a household teaspoon or tablespoon. If your prescription is written in milligrams, ask your pharmacist to confirm how many millilitres that is before you take your first dose.
Notes:
You may have withdrawal symptoms if you stop using tramadol suddenly. Ask your doctor before stopping the medicine.
Ask your healthcare provider about medicines like naloxone or nalmefene that can be used in an emergency to reverse an opioid overdose.
Do not keep leftover tramadol. Just one dose can cause death if someone uses it accidentally or improperly. Ask your pharmacist where to locate a drug take-back disposal program. If there is no take-back program, mix the leftover medicine with cat litter or coffee grounds in a sealed plastic bag and throw the bag in the trash.
Call your healthcare provider if the dose you are taking does not control your pain.
If you have been taking tramadol regularly, do not stop taking tramadol without talking to your healthcare provider.

## How should I use furosemide?
Take or administer furosemide exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Furosemide oral tablets and liquid are taken by mouth. Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device, not a kitchen spoon.
Furosemide injection is given in a muscle, under the skin, or in a vein. A healthcare provider will give you this injection if you are unable to take the medicine by mouth.
Using subcutaneous furosemide at home:
You or your caregiver should be trained before your first dose, and you should read the Instructions for Use that comes with your prescription. Wash your hands first, and check that the liquid is clear and colorless to slightly yellow. Do not use it if you see particles or if it is cloudy or discolored.
Subcutaneous furosemide is given into the abdomen only, and you should use a different spot on the abdomen each time.
Furoscix ReadyFlow autoinjector
- Choose a site at least two inches from your belly button, avoiding skin that is broken or irritated and any scars or stretch marks. Clean it and let it dry.
- Pull the blue cap straight off, then press the device firmly against your skin and hold it there for about 10 seconds, until the yellow plunger rod stops moving and fills the viewing window.
- If you lift the device away before the window is completely yellow, you may not get the full dose. Call your healthcare provider if this happens, and do not use a second device unless you are told to.
Furoscix On-Body Infusor and Lasix ONYU Infusor
- The infusion takes about 5 hours, so plan to stay somewhere you can relax and reach a bathroom.
- Apply the device to a flat, clean, hairless area of the abdomen below the rib cage and above the belt line, and press it firmly into place. Do not remove and reapply it.
- Limit your activity while wearing it and avoid bending as much as you can. Do not exercise or do anything that might knock it off.
- Do not get the infusor wet. Do not bathe, shower, or swim while wearing it, and do not apply lotions or creams to the area where it is placed.
- Traveling by car or airplane while wearing the infusor is not recommended, and the Furoscix On-Body Infusor cannot be used in an MRI setting.
- Do not use the infusor within 12 inches of mobile phones, tablets, computers, or wireless accessories such as a remote control or Bluetooth device.
- Your healthcare provider will show you what the indicator light and alarms mean. You must use the infusor in a setting where you can detect and respond to these alarms to ensure you receive the full dose. If the device falls off, or the light blinks red, call your healthcare provider and do not reuse it.
Dispose of used autoinjectors, infusors, and cartridges in a sharps container. Do not put them in household trash and do not recycle them.
General furosemide dosing information:
Do not use more than your recommended dose. High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
This medicine will make you urinate more often, and you may get dehydrated easily. Follow your doctor's instructions about using potassium supplements or getting enough salt and potassium in your diet.
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often, and you may need other medical tests.
If you have high blood pressure, keep using furosemide even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
If you need surgery, tell the surgeon ahead of time that you are using furosemide.

Simvastatin belongs to a group of drugs called HMG CoA reductase inhibitors, or "statins."
Simvastatin is used to lower blood levels of "bad" cholesterol (low-density lipoprotein, or LDL), to increase levels of "good" cholesterol (high-density lipoprotein, or HDL), and to lower triglycerides (a type of fat in the blood).

## Warnings
Like all medications, Prozac carries some important warnings you should be aware of before and during treatment. Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following.
Boxed warning:
Fluoxetine carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious warning, regarding suicidal thoughts and behavior. Antidepressants, including fluoxetine, may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents, and young adult s, particularly in the first few months of treatment or when your dose is changed. This risk was not seen in adults over 24, and adults 65 and older actually showed a reduced risk.
Anyone starting this medicine should be closely monitored for worsening mood or new or worsening suicidal thoughts, and families and caregivers should stay in regular contact with the prescriber.
Other warnings:
- Serotonin syndrome: A potentially life-threatening condition that can occur when serotonin builds up to dangerous levels. This can occur when taken alone, but is more likely when taken with other serotonergic medications. Seek emergency care immediately if you experience agitation, hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, high fever, muscle rigidity, tremor, or seizures.
- Severe allergic reactions: Stop taking this medicine and seek emergency help if you develop trouble breathing, facial swelling, hives, or blistering rash.
- Abnormal bleeding: This medicine may increase the risk of bleeding or bruising, particularly if taken with blood thinners (such as warfarin), NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen), or aspirin.
- Eye problems (angle-closure glaucoma): This medicine can cause angle-closure glaucoma with symptoms of eye pain, vision changes, or swelling around the eye in some people. An eye exam before starting treatment may be recommended for some people to assess their risk.
- Seizures: Tell your doctor if you have a history of seizures before starting this medicine, or have conditions that potentially increase your risk of seizures
- Manic episodes Fluoxetine may trigger mania, including racing thoughts, reckless behavior, drastically reduced need for sleep, and unusual bursts of energy or irritability.
- Changes in appetite or weight: Weight and appetite changes can occur, with some patients having significant weight loss. Children and adolescents should have their height and weight monitored regularly during treatment.
- Low sodium (hyponatremia): Low blood sodium levels can occur, particularly in older adults. Symptoms include headache, weakness, confusion, and difficulty concentrating.
- Heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation): Fluoxetine can affect the heart's electrical activity, potentially causing a serious and life-threatening irregular heartbeat. Seek medical attention if you experience a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, or fainting.
- Sexual dysfunction: SSRIs, including fluoxetine, commonly affect sexual function. In men, this may include delayed or absent ejaculation or erectile problems. In women, it may include decreased libido or difficulty reaching orgasm. Talk to your doctor if this occurs, as treatment options are available.
- Drowsiness and impaired concentration: This medicine may affect your ability to think clearly, make decisions, or react quickly. Use caution when driving or operating machinery until you know how this medication affects you.
- Anxiety and Insomnia: May occur in some patients while taking this medicine.
- Blood sugar changes: People with diabetes may experience low blood sugar while taking this medicine, and high blood sugar when it is stopped. Your doctor may need to adjust your diabetes medications.
