## How should I take bupropion?
Take bupropion exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label. Do not take this medicine in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended. Too much of this medicine can increase your risk of a seizure.
Do not crush, chew, or break tablets. Swallow the tablet whole.
Take bupropion with food if the medication upsets your stomach.
If you have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, do not take tablets too close to bedtime.
Your doctor will probably start you on a low dose of this medicine and gradually increase your dose.
It may take 4 weeks or longer before you feel the full benefit of this medicine. Continue to take your tablets even if you feel well. Do not stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor. Your doctor may decrease your dose gradually.
You should not change your dose or stop using bupropion suddenly unless you have a seizure while taking this medicine. Stopping suddenly can cause unpleasant withdrawal symptoms.
Ask your doctor how to stop using bupropion safely.
Some people taking bupropion have severe high blood pressure, especially when using a nicotine replacement product (patch or gum). Your blood pressure may need to be checked before and during treatment with this medicine.
This medicine can cause you to have a false positive drug screening test (amphetamines). If you provide a urine sample for drug screening, tell the laboratory staff you are taking this medicine.
For smoking cessation.
If you take bupropion to help you stop smoking, you may continue to smoke for about 1 week after you start the medicine. Set a date to quit smoking during the second week of treatment. Talk to your doctor if you are having trouble quitting after you have used bupropion for at least 7 to 12 weeks.
Your doctor may prescribe a nicotine replacement product (such as patches or gum) to help you stop smoking. Start using the nicotine replacement product on the same day you stop (quit) smoking or using tobacco products.
You may have nicotine withdrawal symptoms when you stop smoking, including increased appetite, weight gain, trouble sleeping, trouble concentrating, slower heart rate, having the urge to smoke, and feeling anxious, restless, depressed, angry, frustrated, or irritated. These symptoms may occur with or without using medication such as bupropion.
Smoking cessation may also cause new or worsening mental health problems, such as depression.

## How atorvastatin improves cholesterol and heart health
When cholesterol and fats build up along your artery walls, in a process called atherosclerosis, they narrow the blood vessels and reduce blood and oxygen flow to your heart, brain, and other parts of your body. By slowing cholesterol production, atorvastatin helps prevent this buildup to keep blood flowing more freely to vital organs.
Lowering your blood level of cholesterol and fats with atorvastatin may help prevent heart disease, angina (chest pain), strokes, and heart attacks.
Your healthcare provider will check your blood lipid levels regularly to assess how well your treatment is working. These measurements include:
- LDL-C: Low-density lipoprotein (“bad” cholesterol)
- HDL-C: High-density lipoprotein (“good” cholesterol)
- TG: Triglycerides (a type of blood fat)
- Total-C: Total cholesterol

Like all medications, Prozac can cause side effects. Not everyone experiences them, and many improve after the first few weeks as your body adjusts to the medication. Tell your doctor if any side effects bother you or do not go away.
Common Fluoxetine Side Effects:
The most commonly reported side effects of fluoxetine (Prozac) include:
- Nausea
- Trouble sleeping (insomnia)
- Drowsiness or sleepiness
- Anxiety or feeling nervous or on edge
- Trembling or shaking (tremor)
- Excessive sweating
- Loss of appetite
- Diarrhea
- Dry mouth
- Indigestion or upset stomach
- Weakness or fatigue
- Sore throat
- Sinus congestion or infection
- Flu-like symptoms
- Skin rash
- Flushing or feeling of warmth
- Yawning
- Unusual or vivid dreams
- Decreased sex drive
- Difficulty getting or keeping an erection
- Delayed or abnormal ejaculation
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to this medicine (hives, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).
Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor, such as mood or behavior changes, anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, hyperactive (mentally or physically), more depressed, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself.
This medicine may cause serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- blurred vision, tunnel vision, eye pain or swelling, or seeing halos around lights;
- fast or pounding heartbeats, fluttering in your chest, shortness of breath, and sudden dizziness (like you might pass out);
- low levels of sodium in the body - headache, confusion, slurred speech, severe weakness, vomiting, loss of coordination, feeling unsteady; or
- severe nervous system reaction - very stiff (rigid) muscles, high fever, sweating, confusion, fast or uneven heartbeats, tremors, feeling like you might pass out.

Furosemide injection is given in a muscle, under the skin, or in a vein. A healthcare provider will give you this injection if you are unable to take the medicine by mouth.
Using subcutaneous furosemide at home:
You or your caregiver should be trained before your first dose, and you should read the Instructions for Use that comes with your prescription. Wash your hands first, and check that the liquid is clear and colorless to slightly yellow. Do not use it if you see particles or if it is cloudy or discolored.
Subcutaneous furosemide is given into the abdomen only, and you should use a different spot on the abdomen each time.
Furoscix ReadyFlow autoinjector
- Choose a site at least two inches from your belly button, avoiding skin that is broken or irritated and any scars or stretch marks. Clean it and let it dry.
- Pull the blue cap straight off, then press the device firmly against your skin and hold it there for about 10 seconds, until the yellow plunger rod stops moving and fills the viewing window.
- If you lift the device away before the window is completely yellow, you may not get the full dose. Call your healthcare provider if this happens, and do not use a second device unless you are told to.
Furoscix On-Body Infusor and Lasix ONYU Infusor
- The infusion takes about 5 hours, so plan to stay somewhere you can relax and reach a bathroom.
- Apply the device to a flat, clean, hairless area of the abdomen below the rib cage and above the belt line, and press it firmly into place. Do not remove and reapply it.
- Limit your activity while wearing it and avoid bending as much as you can. Do not exercise or do anything that might knock it off.
- Do not get the infusor wet. Do not bathe, shower, or swim while wearing it, and do not apply lotions or creams to the area where it is placed.
- Traveling by car or airplane while wearing the infusor is not recommended, and the Furoscix On-Body Infusor cannot be used in an MRI setting.
- Do not use the infusor within 12 inches of mobile phones, tablets, computers, or wireless accessories such as a remote control or Bluetooth device.
- Your healthcare provider will show you what the indicator light and alarms mean. You must use the infusor in a setting where you can detect and respond to these alarms to ensure you receive the full dose. If the device falls off, or the light blinks red, call your healthcare provider and do not reuse it.
Dispose of used autoinjectors, infusors, and cartridges in a sharps container. Do not put them in household trash and do not recycle them.
General furosemide dosing information:
Do not use more than your recommended dose. High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
This medicine will make you urinate more often, and you may get dehydrated easily. Follow your doctor's instructions about using potassium supplements or getting enough salt and potassium in your diet.
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often, and you may need other medical tests.
If you have high blood pressure, keep using furosemide even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
If you need surgery, tell the surgeon ahead of time that you are using furosemide.

## Warnings
Levothyroxine should not be used to treat obesity or weight problems. Dangerous side effects or death can occur from the misuse of this medicine, especially if you are taking any other weight-loss medications or appetite suppressants.
Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Levothyroxine has a narrow therapeutic index, which means the difference between too little and too much is small. Taking too much or too little over time can affect your heart, bones, blood sugar, cholesterol, digestion, memory and concentration, fertility, and, in children, growth and development. Your doctor will start you on a suitable dose and adjust it gradually based on blood tests.
You may not be able to use levothyroxine if you have certain medical conditions. Tell your doctor if you have an untreated or uncontrolled adrenal gland disorder or any heart problems such as a recent heart attack.
If you have an adrenal gland problem, you will need to start treatment with a steroid (glucocorticoid) medicine before you start levothyroxine. Starting levothyroxine first can trigger a sudden, serious drop in adrenal hormones known as an adrenal crisis.
Older adults and people with heart disease are usually started on a lower dose, because too much thyroid hormone can cause an irregular heartbeat (most commonly atrial fibrillation), angina, or other heart problems. Tell your doctor if you develop chest pain, breathlessness, or a fast or irregular heartbeat.
Taking more levothyroxine than your body needs over a long period can weaken your bones and lead to a higher risk of fractures. This is more likely after menopause. Your doctor will aim to give you the lowest dose that controls your thyroid levels.
Oral levothyroxine should not be used to treat myxedema coma. Levothyroxine given into a vein is used instead.

## Warnings and precautions
Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole. These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up, which may make you feel dizzy or faint. This is most likely when you first start taking it, when your dose changes, or when you start it again after a break. Get up slowly from sitting or lying down. Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases (probably fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients), tamsulosin can cause priapism, a painful erection that lasts a long time and is not related to sexual activity. Get medical help straight away if this happens, because without prompt treatment it can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction.
An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together. Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.
Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery. Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken it in the past, even if you stopped months ago. Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to. If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again. You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose.
Many other medicines can interact with tamsulosin. Tell your doctor about everything you take, including prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

Semaglutide FDA-approved uses for each brand are Ozempic (type 2 diabetes, reducing cardiovascular event risks, reducing risk of kidney function decline), Wegovy (weight management, reducing cardiovascular event risks, non-cirrhotic MASH), and Rybelsus (type 2 diabetes, reducing cardiovascular event risks).

## Warnings
Like all medications, Prozac carries some important warnings you should be aware of before and during treatment. Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following.
Boxed warning:
Fluoxetine carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious warning, regarding suicidal thoughts and behavior. Antidepressants, including fluoxetine, may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents, and young adult s, particularly in the first few months of treatment or when your dose is changed. This risk was not seen in adults over 24, and adults 65 and older actually showed a reduced risk.
Anyone starting this medicine should be closely monitored for worsening mood or new or worsening suicidal thoughts, and families and caregivers should stay in regular contact with the prescriber.
Other warnings:
- Serotonin syndrome: A potentially life-threatening condition that can occur when serotonin builds up to dangerous levels. This can occur when taken alone, but is more likely when taken with other serotonergic medications. Seek emergency care immediately if you experience agitation, hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, high fever, muscle rigidity, tremor, or seizures.
- Severe allergic reactions: Stop taking this medicine and seek emergency help if you develop trouble breathing, facial swelling, hives, or blistering rash.
- Abnormal bleeding: This medicine may increase the risk of bleeding or bruising, particularly if taken with blood thinners (such as warfarin), NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen), or aspirin.
- Eye problems (angle-closure glaucoma): This medicine can cause angle-closure glaucoma with symptoms of eye pain, vision changes, or swelling around the eye in some people. An eye exam before starting treatment may be recommended for some people to assess their risk.
- Seizures: Tell your doctor if you have a history of seizures before starting this medicine, or have conditions that potentially increase your risk of seizures
- Manic episodes Fluoxetine may trigger mania, including racing thoughts, reckless behavior, drastically reduced need for sleep, and unusual bursts of energy or irritability.
- Changes in appetite or weight: Weight and appetite changes can occur, with some patients having significant weight loss. Children and adolescents should have their height and weight monitored regularly during treatment.
- Low sodium (hyponatremia): Low blood sodium levels can occur, particularly in older adults. Symptoms include headache, weakness, confusion, and difficulty concentrating.
- Heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation): Fluoxetine can affect the heart's electrical activity, potentially causing a serious and life-threatening irregular heartbeat. Seek medical attention if you experience a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, or fainting.
- Sexual dysfunction: SSRIs, including fluoxetine, commonly affect sexual function. In men, this may include delayed or absent ejaculation or erectile problems. In women, it may include decreased libido or difficulty reaching orgasm. Talk to your doctor if this occurs, as treatment options are available.
- Drowsiness and impaired concentration: This medicine may affect your ability to think clearly, make decisions, or react quickly. Use caution when driving or operating machinery until you know how this medication affects you.
- Anxiety and Insomnia: May occur in some patients while taking this medicine.
- Blood sugar changes: People with diabetes may experience low blood sugar while taking this medicine, and high blood sugar when it is stopped. Your doctor may need to adjust your diabetes medications.

## Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) dosage information
Your doctor will choose the smallest dose that controls your condition, and may adjust it over time. Follow your prescription label and do not change your dose yourself.
HCTZ dose for high blood pressure (adults):
Tablets: The starting dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once a day, which may be increased to 50 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Doses above 50 mg a day are often associated with a marked drop in blood potassium. Most people do not need more than 50 mg a day when hydrochlorothiazide is taken alongside other blood pressure medicines
Capsules: The starting dose is a hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg capsule once a day, whether taken on its own or with other blood pressure medicines. Total daily doses above 50 mg are not recommended. Capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
HCTZ dose for fluid retention (adults):
Tablets: The usual dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg to 100 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Many people with fluid retention respond to intermittent treatment, such as taking it every other day or on 3 to 5 days each week. Excessive response and undesirable electrolyte imbalance are less likely to occur with intermittent dosing.
HCTZ dose for children for high blood pressure and fluid retention:
The usual HCTZ dose in children, for both high blood pressure and fluid retention, is 1 mg to 2 mg per kilogram of body weight (0.5 mg to 1 mg per pound) a day, given as a single dose or split into two doses.
- Infants under 6 months: may be need doses of up to 3 mg per kilogram (1.5 mg per pound) a day, given as two divided doses up to the same maximum 37.5 mg daily limit
- Infants and children under 2 years: do not exceed 37.5 mg a day
- Children 2 to 12 years: do not exceed 100 mg a day
The dose is based on your child's weight and must be worked out by their doctor.
Taking the oral suspension:
If your child has been prescribed the liquid form (oral suspension), the following applies:
- Shake the bottle well before every dose.
- Measure each dose with the oral dosing syringe. Ask your pharmacist for a syringe and a bottle adapter if you do not have them.
- Never measure a dose with a household teaspoon or tablespoon, because these do not give an accurate amount.
- Store the made-up suspension at room temperature and do not freeze it.
- Throw away any unused suspension 30 days after it was made up. The pharmacist will write this date on the bottle.
The oral suspension can be taken with or without food.
What happens if I miss a dose?:
Take the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take two doses at one time.
What happens if I overdose?:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
Overdose symptoms may include nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, thirst, and muscle pain or weakness.

## Sertraline FAQs
Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline has very little effect on norepinephrine and dopamine, and it has no meaningful effect on adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopamine, histamine, or benzodiazepine receptors, which is part of why it is described as selective.
How long does sertraline take to work?:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.
Should I take sertraline in the morning or at night?:
Either is fine. Sertraline is taken once a day, in the morning or the evening, and the label does not favor one over the other. What matters more is taking it at around the same time each day. Insomnia was reported by 20% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 13% on placebo, and sleepiness by 11% compared with 6%, so some people find one timing suits them better than the other. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does sertraline cause weight gain or weight loss?:
Reduced appetite is a common sertraline side effect, reported by 7% of adults in trials compared with 2% on placebo. Increased appetite was reported less often, in fewer than 2% of people. In children and teenagers taking sertraline for depression, there was a difference in weight change of roughly 1 kg compared with placebo over 10 weeks, representing slight weight loss on sertraline and slight gain on placebo. Around 7% of children lost more than 7% of their body weight, compared with none on placebo. In a longer 34 week extension study, weight gain was similar to what would be expected for their age. Height and weight should be monitored in younger patients. Tell your doctor about any weight change that concerns you.
Does sertraline make you tired or sleepy?:
It can. Sleepiness was reported by 11% of adults taking sertraline in trials, compared with 6% on placebo, and tiredness by 12% compared with 8%. Sertraline can also affect how clearly you think and how quickly you react, so do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.
Is sertraline a controlled substance?:
No. Sertraline is not a controlled substance. In a study comparing sertraline with alprazolam and d-amphetamine, sertraline did not produce the effects associated with a potential for misuse, such as euphoria or drug liking, that were seen with the other two medicines.
Can sertraline cause diarrhea or nausea?:
Yes, these are the two most common sertraline side effects. Nausea was reported by 26% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 12% on placebo, and diarrhea or loose stools by 20% compared with 10%. Nausea was also the most common reason people stopped treatment. Tell your doctor if these do not settle.
How do you stop taking sertraline safely?:
Lower the dose gradually rather than stopping all at once, and only under your doctor's guidance. Symptoms reported after stopping a serotonergic antidepressant, especially when it is stopped abruptly, include nausea, sweating, low or unstable mood, irritability, agitation, dizziness, unusual sensations such as electric shock feelings, tremor, anxiety, confusion, headache, lethargy, insomnia, hypomania, ringing in the ears, and seizures.
Can you drink alcohol while taking sertraline?:
Drinking alcohol is not recommended while you take sertraline. In healthy volunteers, sertraline did not increase the immediate effects of alcohol on thinking and coordination, but the advice for patients is still to avoid it. Separately, do not take sertraline oral solution with disulfiram, because the solution contains 12% alcohol.
Can you take sertraline while pregnant?:
That depends on your situation, and it is a decision to make with your doctor rather than on your own. Studies of first trimester use suggest no overall difference in the risk of major birth defects, but use late in pregnancy has been linked with newborn breathing problems and with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. At the same time, stopping an antidepressant during pregnancy raises the risk of depression coming back. The oral solution specifically is not recommended in pregnancy because it contains alcohol.
What are sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules for?:
Sertraline capsules come in 150 mg and 200 mg only, and they are not used to start treatment. They are for people who have already been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week and need a higher dose. The maximum is 200 mg a day, the same as for tablets. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not opened, crushed, or chewed. If you need to come off sertraline, the dose has to be lowered gradually using another sertraline product, because there is no capsule strength below 150 mg. Capsules are approved for depression in adults and OCD from age 6, not for panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, or PMDD.
Does sertraline interact with warfarin?:
Yes, in two ways. Sertraline can add to warfarin's effect on bleeding risk, and both medicines bind tightly to proteins in the blood, so taking them together can raise the free level of one or both. If you take warfarin with sertraline, your INR should be monitored carefully.

## What other drugs affect metoprolol?
The interactions that matter most are medicines that also slow the heart and medicines that block the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which raises metoprolol levels in your blood.
- Digoxin, clonidine, diltiazem, and verapamil. These all slow the heart's electrical signal and heart rate. Taking them with metoprolol raises the risk of a very slow heartbeat.
- Clonidine, when stopping either medicine. If you take both, the metoprolol is stopped several days before clonidine is slowly withdrawn, because beta blockers can worsen the blood pressure rebound that follows clonidine withdrawal.
- Quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, and propafenone. These strong CYP2D6 blockers double the amount of metoprolol in your blood. Quinidine tripled levels of one form of metoprolol and doubled how long it lasted. Weaker CYP2D6 blockers are likely to raise levels too.
- Reserpine and MAO inhibitors. These deplete adrenaline-type chemicals and can add to metoprolol's effect, causing low blood pressure or a marked slowing of the heart.
- Epinephrine. If you need epinephrine for a severe allergic reaction, the usual dose may not work as well while you are on a beta blocker.
- Other medicines that lower blood pressure or heart rate, including fingolimod, can add to metoprolol's effect.
Tell each of your healthcare providers about all medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here.

## Metformin side effects
Common side effects:
Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache. These side effects occurred in 5% or more of patients in the US clinical trial of using metformin for type 2 diabetic patients. In the same study, 6% of patients discontinued metformin due to diarrhea.
Less common side effects were abnormal stools, hypoglycemia, myalgia, lightheadedness, dyspnea, nail disorder, rash, increased sweating, taste disorder, chest discomfort, chills, flu syndrome, flushing, and palpitation, which occurred between 1% and less than 5% of patients.
Taking your medicine with meals can help reduce these side effects, and you may find the slow-release tablets reduce gastric side effects. Tell your doctor if the side effects bother you a lot, last for more than a few weeks, come back after they've gone away, or start later in therapy. You may need a lower dose or need to stop taking the medicine for a short period or for good.
Metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) by itself. However, hypoglycemia can happen if you do not eat enough, if you drink alcohol, or if you take other medicines to lower blood sugar.
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to metformin: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
This medicine can rarely cause patients to develop lactic acidosis, which can be fatal. See the “Warnings - Boxed Warning” for more details.
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of liver problems, such as upper stomach pain, loss of appetite, dark urine, clay-colored stools, or yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice).

## What is semaglutide used for?
Semaglutide FDA-approved uses for each brand are Ozempic (type 2 diabetes, reducing cardiovascular event risks, reducing risk of kidney function decline), Wegovy (weight management, reducing cardiovascular event risks, non-cirrhotic MASH), and Rybelsus (type 2 diabetes, reducing cardiovascular event risks).
Semaglutide should be used in addition to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
What is Ozempic used for?:
Ozempic tablets and injections are FDA-approved in adults for:
- type 2 diabetes to improve blood sugar control
- reducing the risk of a major cardiovascular event (such as heart attack, stroke, or death) in type 2 diabetic patients who are at high risk for these events
Ozempic injection is also FDA-approved in adults for:
- reducing the risk of kidney function decline, kidney failure, and cardiovascular death in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD)
What is Wegovy used for?:
Wegovy tablets and injections are FDA-approved in adults for:
- weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity or adults who are overweight and have a weight-related medical problem (e.g., blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, or high cholesterol)
- reducing major cardiovascular event risks (such as heart attack, stroke, or death) in adults with established CV disease and either obesity or overweight
Wegovy injection is also FDA-approved for:
- weight loss and weight management patients with obesity who are 12 years and older
- non-cirrhotic metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in adults with moderate to advanced liver fibrosis (consistent with stages F2 to F3 fibrosis), this is an accelerated approval.
What is Rybelsus used for?:
Rybelsus oral tablets are FDA-approved in adults for:
- type 2 diabetes in adults to help control blood sugar levels.
- reducing the risk of major cardiovascular events (such as heart attack, stroke, or death) in type 2 diabetic patients with known heart disease.

## How should I use Flonase Nasal Spray?
Use Flonase exactly as directed on the label, or as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Do not share this medicine with another person, even if they have the same symptoms you have. Sharing a bottle can spread germs.
Your dose will depend on the fluticasone brand or strength you use, and your dose may change once your symptoms improve. Follow all dosing instructions very carefully.
- A child using the nasal spray should be supervised by an adult.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Shake the bottle before each use. Flonase Allergy Relief should be shaken gently, and Flonase Sensimist should be shaken vigorously.
Use this product only once a day and do not use more than directed. Avoid getting the spray in your eyes or mouth.
If you switched to fluticasone from another steroid medicine, you should not stop using it suddenly. Follow your doctor's instructions about tapering your dose.
Storage differs between products. Store Flonase Allergy Relief and Children's Flonase Allergy Relief between 4°C and 30°C (39°F and 86°F). Store Flonase Sensimist between 15°C and 30°C (59°F and 86°F), and do not refrigerate or freeze it.
Throw the bottle away once you have used the number of sprays stated on the carton, even if there is still liquid in the bottle. The correct amount of medicine in each spray cannot be assured after the labeled number of sprays has been used. Bottle sizes vary between products and pack sizes, ranging from 30 to 144 metered sprays.
Dosing information:
Usual Adult Dose for Rhinitis (adults and children 12 years of age and older):
Flonase Allergy Relief Nasal Spray (fluticasone propionate 50 mcg per spray):
- Week 1: use 2 sprays in each nostril once daily
- Week 2 through 6 months: use 1 or 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, as needed to treat your symptoms
- After 6 months of daily use: ask your doctor if you can keep using this medicine
Flonase Sensimist Nasal Spray (fluticasone furoate 27.5 mcg per spray):
- Week 1: use 2 sprays in each nostril once daily
- Week 2 through 6 months: use 1 or 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, as needed to treat your symptoms
- After 6 months of daily use: ask your doctor if you can keep using this medicine
Usual Pediatric Dose for Rhinitis:
- 4 to 11 years: Flonase Allergy Relief or Children's Flonase Allergy Relief (fluticasone propionate 50 mcg per spray): 1 spray in each nostril once daily.
- 2 to 11 years: Flonase Sensimist or Children's Flonase Sensimist (fluticasone furoate 27.5 mcg per spray): 1 spray in each nostril once daily.
- Under 4 years: do not use fluticasone propionate nasal spray.
- Under 2 years: do not use fluticasone furoate nasal spray.
An adult should supervise a child using the spray. Children should use it for the shortest amount of time necessary to achieve symptom relief. Talk to your child's doctor if your child needs to use the spray for longer than two months a year.
What happens if I miss a dose?:
Use the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not use two doses at one time.
What happens if I overdose?:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
An overdose of Flonase is not expected to produce life-threatening symptoms. Using more than the recommended dose, or using it for longer than directed, may increase the chance of corticosteroid-related side effects such as cataracts or glaucoma, adrenal gland problems, an increased risk of infection, sores inside the nose, or slower growth in children.

Losartan is also used to decrease the risk of stroke in people who have high blood pressure and a heart condition called left ventricular hypertrophy (enlargement of the walls of the left side of the heart).
Losartan may not decrease the risk of stroke in African Americans who have these conditions.
Losartan is also used to treat kidney disease in people who have type 2 diabetes (condition in which the body does not use insulin normally and therefore cannot control the amount of sugar in the blood) and high blood pressure.
Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin II receptor antagonists. It works by blocking the action of certain natural substances that tighten the blood vessels, allowing the blood to flow more smoothly and the heart to pump more efficiently.

## Warnings
Like all medications, Prozac carries some important warnings you should be aware of before and during treatment. Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following.
Boxed warning:
Fluoxetine carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious warning, regarding suicidal thoughts and behavior. Antidepressants, including fluoxetine, may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents, and young adult s, particularly in the first few months of treatment or when your dose is changed. This risk was not seen in adults over 24, and adults 65 and older actually showed a reduced risk.
Anyone starting this medicine should be closely monitored for worsening mood or new or worsening suicidal thoughts, and families and caregivers should stay in regular contact with the prescriber.
Other warnings:
- Serotonin syndrome: A potentially life-threatening condition that can occur when serotonin builds up to dangerous levels. This can occur when taken alone, but is more likely when taken with other serotonergic medications. Seek emergency care immediately if you experience agitation, hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, high fever, muscle rigidity, tremor, or seizures.
- Severe allergic reactions: Stop taking this medicine and seek emergency help if you develop trouble breathing, facial swelling, hives, or blistering rash.
- Abnormal bleeding: This medicine may increase the risk of bleeding or bruising, particularly if taken with blood thinners (such as warfarin), NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen), or aspirin.
- Eye problems (angle-closure glaucoma): This medicine can cause angle-closure glaucoma with symptoms of eye pain, vision changes, or swelling around the eye in some people. An eye exam before starting treatment may be recommended for some people to assess their risk.
- Seizures: Tell your doctor if you have a history of seizures before starting this medicine, or have conditions that potentially increase your risk of seizures
- Manic episodes Fluoxetine may trigger mania, including racing thoughts, reckless behavior, drastically reduced need for sleep, and unusual bursts of energy or irritability.
- Changes in appetite or weight: Weight and appetite changes can occur, with some patients having significant weight loss. Children and adolescents should have their height and weight monitored regularly during treatment.
- Low sodium (hyponatremia): Low blood sodium levels can occur, particularly in older adults. Symptoms include headache, weakness, confusion, and difficulty concentrating.
- Heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation): Fluoxetine can affect the heart's electrical activity, potentially causing a serious and life-threatening irregular heartbeat. Seek medical attention if you experience a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, or fainting.
- Sexual dysfunction: SSRIs, including fluoxetine, commonly affect sexual function. In men, this may include delayed or absent ejaculation or erectile problems. In women, it may include decreased libido or difficulty reaching orgasm. Talk to your doctor if this occurs, as treatment options are available.
- Drowsiness and impaired concentration: This medicine may affect your ability to think clearly, make decisions, or react quickly. Use caution when driving or operating machinery until you know how this medication affects you.
- Anxiety and Insomnia: May occur in some patients while taking this medicine.
- Blood sugar changes: People with diabetes may experience low blood sugar while taking this medicine, and high blood sugar when it is stopped. Your doctor may need to adjust your diabetes medications.

## How should I use albuterol inhalation?
Use albuterol inhalation exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label. Do not use albuterol inhalation in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended.

Follow all medication instructions very carefully.

Use the dose counter on your albuterol inhaler device and get your prescription refilled before you run out of medicine completely. Always use the new inhaler device provided with your refill. Do not float a medicine canister in water to see if it is empty.

## Warnings
Boxed warning for lactic acidosis:
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).
Stop taking metformin and call your healthcare professional immediately if you have any symptoms of lactic acidosis, including if you feel:
- very weak and tired
- have unusual (not normal) muscle pain
- have trouble breathing
- have unusual sleepiness or sleep longer than usual
- have unexplained stomach or intestinal problems with nausea and vomiting, or diarrhea
- cold, especially in your arms and legs
- dizzy or lightheaded
- have a slow or irregular heartbeat
Other warnings:
Vitamin B12 deficiency: Metformin can lower your vitamin B12 levels over time. Your doctor may check your blood counts every year and your B12 levels every 2 to 3 years to catch any problems early.
Low blood sugar when taken with insulin or other diabetes medicines: Taking metformin along with insulin or certain other diabetes drugs (ones that boost insulin release) raises the risk of low blood sugar. If you're on one of these combinations, your doctor may lower the dose of the other medicine.
Macrovascular Outcomes: There have been no clinical studies that clearly show metformin reduces the risk of macrovascular disease, such as diseases or conditions that affect the coronary arteries, the aorta, and large arteries in the brain and limbs.

evidence:
## How does metformin help PCOS?
Metformin is prescribed to manage polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) because it improves how the body responds to insulin. PCOS affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age and is often marked by insulin resistance, in which the body doesn't respond well to insulin, prompting the pancreas to produce more. This excess insulin drives up androgen (male hormone) production, worsening symptoms like irregular periods, infertility, acne, and excess hair growth. Metformin helps by lowering insulin levels, decreasing the liver's glucose production, improving glucose uptake by muscles, and reducing circulating androgen levels as well, which can support more regular ovulation and menstrual cycles.
Although metformin is not FDA-approved to treat PCOS, it's widely prescribed as an off-label treatment, particularly for those with insulin resistance or fertility difficulties, and it's backed by extensive research and clinical guidelines. Beyond helping regulate cycles and support ovulation, metformin may also help reduce androgen-related symptoms such as acne and excess hair growth, and can aid with weight management for those affected by PCOS-related weight gain.

## What other drugs will affect tamsulosin?
Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood and increase the risk of side effects.
Do not take tamsulosin with:
- strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole
- other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin
Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take:
- moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin
- strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine
- cimetidine
- warfarin
- medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra). Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms.
Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg. Your doctor will decide what is right for you.
No dose change is needed if you take tamsulosin with nifedipine, atenolol, enalapril, digoxin, theophylline, or furosemide.

## What other drugs will affect metformin?
Many drugs can interact with metformin; this includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here. Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any medicine you start or stop using.
Medicines that have a carbonic anhydrase inhibiting effect like topiramate (often used for seizures or migraines), zonisamide (used for seizures), acetazolamide (used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, and other conditions), and dichlorphenamide (used for a muscle condition called periodic paralysis) can raise the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis when taken with metformin. These medicines commonly lower a substance in your blood called bicarbonate, which your body needs to keep its acid levels balanced. If you're taking metformin along with any of these medicines, your doctor may want to monitor you more closely.
Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.
Insulin or other diabetes medicines that raise insulin (like sulfonylureas): Combining these with metformin can lower your blood sugar too much. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you're taking more than one diabetes medicine.
Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis.
Contrast dye used in imaging tests (like CT scans): This type of dye can temporarily affect kidney function, which can let metformin build up in your body. Your doctor may have you stop taking metformin around the time of the test and restart it once your kidney function is confirmed to be back to normal.

## Warnings
Boxed warning for lactic acidosis:
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).
Stop taking metformin and call your healthcare professional immediately if you have any symptoms of lactic acidosis, including if you feel:
- very weak and tired
- have unusual (not normal) muscle pain
- have trouble breathing
- have unusual sleepiness or sleep longer than usual
- have unexplained stomach or intestinal problems with nausea and vomiting, or diarrhea
- cold, especially in your arms and legs
- dizzy or lightheaded
- have a slow or irregular heartbeat
Other warnings:
Vitamin B12 deficiency: Metformin can lower your vitamin B12 levels over time. Your doctor may check your blood counts every year and your B12 levels every 2 to 3 years to catch any problems early.
Low blood sugar when taken with insulin or other diabetes medicines: Taking metformin along with insulin or certain other diabetes drugs (ones that boost insulin release) raises the risk of low blood sugar. Common side effects:
Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache. These side effects occurred in 5% or more of patients in the US clinical trial of using metformin for type 2 diabetic patients. In the same study, 6% of patients discontinued metformin due to diarrhea.

## Gabapentin side effects
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema), and tiredness.
Other common gabapentin side effects may include:
- unsteadiness, poor coordination, or jerky movements
- nausea or vomiting
- headache
- trouble speaking
- blurred or double vision
- tremor
- signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to gabapentin: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Seek medical treatment if you have a serious drug reaction that can affect many parts of your body. Symptoms may include skin rash, fever, swollen glands, muscle aches, severe weakness, unusual bruising, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.
Tell your doctor right away if you have new or sudden changes in mood or behavior, including new or worse depression or anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, more active or talkative, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself, while taking this medicine and after stopping it.
Gabapentin can slow or stop your breathing, especially if you have recently used an opioid medicine or alcohol. A person caring for you should seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you are hard to wake up.
Some side effects are more likely in children taking gabapentin. Call your doctor if the child has behavior changes, memory problems, trouble concentrating, or is restless, hostile, or aggressive.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- drowsiness, dizziness, or weakness
- problems with balance or muscle movement
- increased seizures
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Spironolactone side effects
Reported spironolactone side effects:
Reported spironolactone side effects include breast and nipple pain in both men and women, a lower sex drive, trouble getting or keeping an erection, irregular or missed periods, bleeding after menopause, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, feeling sluggish, leg cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, indigestion, hair thinning, and itching.
The most common side effect of spironolactone is breast growth in men, known as gynecomastia. In the main heart failure study, about 9 in 100 men taking an average of 26 mg a day developed it. The chance goes up on higher doses. It can start anywhere from one or two months into treatment to more than a year later, and it usually goes away after the medicine is stopped.
Several of these effects are dose-related, so they are more likely on higher doses, and many settle after the dose is lowered or the medicine is stopped. How often most of them happen is not known, because they come from reports gathered after the medicine was approved rather than from counted numbers in trials.
Serious spironolactone side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to spironolactone: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of a high potassium level (hyperkalemia), such as muscle weakness or a heavy feeling in your legs, a slow or uneven heartbeat, numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or lips, nausea, or feeling restless and on edge;
- a light-headed feeling like you might pass out, which can be a sign you have low blood pressure (hypotension)
- little or no urination, or swelling in your ankles, hands, or feet, which can be signs your kidneys are struggling (worsening renal function);
- signs of a low sodium level, such as confusion, severe weakness, muscle pain or cramps, feeling unsteady, or slurred speech;
- severe or ongoing vomiting or diarrhea, since losing too much fluid and salt can send your blood pressure and kidney function the wrong way;
- a skin rash that spreads or blisters, peeling skin, sores in your mouth, or a rash with a fever and swollen glands, which can be signs of a rare but serious skin reaction;
- yellowing of your eyes or skin, dark urine, or pain in your upper stomach, which can be signs of a liver problem;
- a fever, sore throat, or unusual bruising or bleeding, which can be signs of a problem with your blood cells; or
- new confusion, unsteadiness, or extreme drowsiness if you have liver disease, since spironolactone can make brain function worse in people with cirrhosis.
Spironolactone side effects in men:
Men are most likely to notice effects linked to spironolactone blocking male hormones. These include breast growth and breast tenderness, a lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. Breast growth is dose related, so tell your doctor early rather than waiting, since a lower dose or a different medicine may be an option.
Spironolactone side effects in women:
Women may notice irregular periods, missed periods, breast tenderness, or bleeding after menopause. Some women also notice patchy darkening of the skin on the face. Report any unexpected bleeding after menopause to your doctor so it can be checked properly rather than assumed to be a side effect.
Long-term spironolactone side effects:
The main long-term concerns with spironolactone are chemical rather than something you would feel. Over time it can push your potassium too high, and it can also lower your sodium, magnesium, and calcium, raise your blood sugar, and raise your uric acid, which occasionally brings on gout. This is why you need regular blood tests for as long as you take it, not just at the start.
In animal studies, spironolactone given at high doses over long periods caused tumors in rats, mainly in hormone-producing glands and the liver. No increase in tumors was seen at the lower doses tested, which were still around five times the highest recommended human dose when adjusted for body size. Whether this happens in people is not known.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is levothyroxine?
Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.
Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
- treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
- lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.
Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly. This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression. When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although it may take several weeks before you notice a difference.
Levothyroxine is usually taken for life.
What levothyroxine is not used for:
Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet. It does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid. It is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland).
Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.

## What is hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) used for?
Hydrochlorothiazide is approved to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and fluid retention (edema) in certain patients.
High blood pressure:
HCTZ is used to manage high blood pressure (hypertension), either on its own or alongside other blood pressure medicines. Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events, mainly strokes and heart attacks.
All three forms of hydrochlorothiazide, tablets, capsules and the oral suspension, are approved for high blood pressure in adults, and the oral suspension is also approved for children.

- congestive heart failure
- cirrhosis of the liver
- kidney conditions, including nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney failure
- treatment with corticosteroid or estrogen medicines
The HCTZ oral suspension is approved for fluid retention associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and kidney disease including nephrotic syndrome, in both adults and children.
The capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
Not all forms of HCTZ are approved for all indications and age groups.

## What is spironolactone?
Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic (water pill) used for heart failure, high blood pressure, fluid build-up (edema) caused by liver or kidney disease, and a hormone condition called primary hyperaldosteronism. Spironolactone is sometimes prescribed off-label for women with acne or excessive facial hair growth (hirsutism).
Spironolactone works by blocking a hormone called aldosterone, which causes your body to pass more salt and water in your urine while keeping potassium in. This is why it is called potassium-sparing, and it is what makes spironolactone different from most other water pills, which flush potassium out.
Spironolactone also blocks androgens such as testosterone from binding to the androgen receptor, which explains several of its side effects, including breast tenderness and breast growth.
Spironolactone is FDA-approved to treat adults with:
- Heart failure (NYHA Class III-IV) with a reduced ejection fraction to help live longer, reduce swelling, and reduce the need for hospital stays. It is taken alongside other heart failure medicines rather than on its own.
- High blood pressure as an add-on treatment for people whose blood pressure is not controlled well enough by other medicines. Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of stroke and heart attack.
- Fluid build-up (edema) caused by cirrhosis of the liver when cutting back on fluid and salt has not been enough, and also for swelling caused by nephrotic syndrome (a kidney disorder) when treating the underlying disease and using other water pills have not worked well enough.
- Primary hyperaldosteronism, which is a condition where the adrenal glands make too much aldosterone. Spironolactone is used short-term to prepare for surgery, and long-term for people who are not suitable for surgery.
Spironolactone tablets come in 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg strengths. Spironolactone 25 mg is the strength most often used to start treatment. There is also a banana-flavored oral liquid for people who cannot swallow tablets. The liquid and the tablets are not interchangeable, so never switch between them without your doctor changing your dose.

You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:

## What is meloxicam?
Meloxicam is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). It works by reducing hormones that cause pain, fever, and inflammation in the body.
Meloxicam is used to relieve pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness caused by osteoarthritis (arthritis caused by a breakdown of the lining of the joints) and rheumatoid arthritis (arthritis caused by swelling of the lining of the joints).

Generic meloxicam is available.

## What other drugs will affect hydrochlorothiazide?
Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Medicines that need particular care:
- Lithium. Lithium and diuretics generally should not be taken together. Hydrochlorothiazide reduces how quickly the kidneys clear lithium, which carries a high risk of lithium toxicity.
- Cholestyramine and colestipol. These cholesterol-lowering resins bind hydrochlorothiazide in the gut and can reduce how much you absorb by up to 85 percent for cholestyramine and 43 percent for colestipol. The doses need to be separated. For the oral suspension, the label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide at least 4 hours before, or 4 to 6 hours after, the resin.
- NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), diclofenac, meloxicam, indomethacin, celecoxib and aspirin. These can reduce the fluid-clearing and blood-pressure-lowering effects of hydrochlorothiazide, and your doctor will check whether the medicine is still working as intended.
- Insulin and oral diabetes medicines. Your diabetes medicine dose may need adjusting.
- Corticosteroids and ACTH. Taken with hydrochlorothiazide, these increase the loss of salts from the body, particularly potassium.
- Digoxin and other digitalis medicines. Low potassium caused by hydrochlorothiazide can make the heart more sensitive to the toxic effects of digitalis, including irregular heart rhythms.
- Other blood pressure medicines. The effects add together, which may be intended, but can also lower blood pressure more than expected.
- Alcohol, barbiturates and opioid pain medicines. These can make the drop in blood pressure on standing worse, causing dizziness or fainting.
- Muscle relaxants used during surgery (nondepolarizing muscle relaxants such as tubocurarine). You may respond more strongly to them, so tell your surgeon and anesthetist that you take hydrochlorothiazide.
- Medicines that raise blood pressure (pressor amines such as norepinephrine). Your response to them may be reduced, although this does not usually prevent their use.
This list is not complete. Other medicines may affect hydrochlorothiazide, and hydrochlorothiazide may affect other medicines.

## Cyclobenzaprine side effects
The most common cyclobenzaprine side effects are drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, fatigue, and headache. Most side effects are mild and settle as your body adjusts, but cyclobenzaprine can occasionally cause serious heart rhythm effects and serotonin syndrome. 1
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects may include: 1
- drowsiness and tiredness;
- dry mouth;
- dizziness;
- fatigue;
- headache;
- nausea, indigestion, or constipation;
- blurred vision;
- unpleasant taste;
- nervousness or confusion.
In placebo-controlled trials of the immediate-release tablets, side effects were dose-related, occurring more often with 10 mg than with 5 mg: 1
Side effect | Cyclobenzaprine 5 mg | Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg | Placebo
Drowsiness | 29% | 38% | 10%
Dry mouth | 21% | 32% | 7%
Fatigue | 6% | 6% | 3%
Headache | 5% | 5% | 8%
With Amrix, the most common side effects are dry mouth (up to 14% at 30 mg), dizziness, fatigue, constipation, nausea, indigestion, and drowsiness. 2
With Tonmya, because it dissolves under the tongue, the most common side effects involve the mouth: reduced feeling or numbness in the mouth (23%), mouth discomfort, abnormal taste, tingling, mouth pain, and canker sores, along with sleepiness, fatigue, and dry mouth. Mouth-related effects usually begin within minutes of a dose and most resolve within an hour. Moistening your mouth with sips of water before dosing reduces the risk of numbness. Tell your healthcare provider if mouth effects are severe. 3
Serious cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to cyclobenzaprine: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; or itching. 2,3
Stop taking cyclobenzaprine and call your doctor at once if you have: 1,2,3
- fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeats;
- chest pain or pressure, or pain spreading to your jaw or shoulder;
- sudden numbness or weakness, slurred speech, or balance problems; or
- symptoms of serotonin syndrome: agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness or twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Serious side effects, including confusion, hallucinations, and heart problems leading to falls, are more likely in older adults. 1
Does cyclobenzaprine make you sleepy?:
Yes, drowsiness is the most common side effect of the tablets, affecting up to 38% of people taking the 10 mg dose in clinical trials. This is one reason 5 mg is the usual starting dose, since it causes less drowsiness with comparable effectiveness. Analysis of trial data shows cyclobenzaprine relieves muscle spasm whether or not sedation occurs, so drowsiness is not required for it to work. 1
Does cyclobenzaprine cause constipation?:
Constipation is a known side effect, reported in 1% to 3% of people taking the immediate-release tablets and up to 3% of people taking Amrix 30 mg in clinical trials. It results from the drug's anticholinergic (drying) effects, the same mechanism behind dry mouth and blurred vision. 1,2
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Prednisone FAQs
Is prednisone a steroid?:
Yes. Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid. Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally, and they work by lowering inflammation and immune activity. They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour, and many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day. Some conditions take several days or longer to respond. Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them, so the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours, which means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time. Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself. A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands for about one and a quarter to one and a half days, which is why prednisone is described as short-acting compared with steroids such as dexamethasone. This is also why a course of prednisone can affect your blood sugar, your sleep, and your energy for longer than the drug is measurable in your blood.
Why has my doctor prescribed prednisone every other day?:
Alternate day dosing means taking twice your usual daily dose every other morning instead of a dose every day. It is used for people who need steroid treatment for a long time. Giving your body a day off from the steroid lets your adrenal glands recover between doses, which reduces the risk of adrenal suppression, Cushing's syndrome, withdrawal symptoms, and slowed growth in children.
The trade-off is that your symptoms may flare a little late in the day you do not take it. Tell your doctor if this happens, since other treatment can often be added for that gap. Do not switch yourself to an every other day schedule, and do not double up on a day you were not meant to take a dose.
What is the difference between prednisone and prednisolone?:
Prednisone has to be converted by your liver into prednisolone before it can work, while prednisolone is already in the active form. For most people the two work in a very similar way at equivalent doses. Prednisolone is often chosen for people with significant liver disease, and for children, because it comes in liquid forms that are easier to dose.
Does prednisone cause weight gain?:
Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone. It happens for two reasons. Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water, which adds weight quickly in the first days or weeks, and it increases appetite, which adds body fat over longer courses. It also moves fat toward the face, neck, upper back and waist. Weight from fluid usually goes once you stop, but weight from extra eating takes longer to shift.
Can you drink alcohol while taking prednisone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and prednisone, but drinking is best kept to a minimum. Both irritate the stomach lining, so together they raise the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding. Alcohol also raises blood sugar and weakens bones, and prednisone does both of these too. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for you, especially if you are on a long course.
Can you take ibuprofen with prednisone?:
It is usually best to avoid ibuprofen while you are taking prednisone. Ibuprofen is an NSAID, and taking an NSAID with a steroid raises the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding. The same applies to naproxen, diclofenac, and regular doses of aspirin. If you need a painkiller, ask your doctor or pharmacist first.
Can you take Tylenol with prednisone?:
Acetaminophen (Tylenol) does not interact with prednisone and does not irritate the stomach, so it is generally the preferred choice for pain or fever while you are taking prednisone. Stay within the recommended daily limit on the packet and check whether any other product you take already contains acetaminophen.
Why does prednisone keep me awake?:
Prednisone acts like your body's stress hormone, which naturally peaks in the morning to help you wake up. Taking it, especially later in the day, can leave you feeling wired, restless or unable to sleep. Taking your dose in the morning often helps. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does prednisone raise blood pressure?:
It can. Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water, which raises blood pressure in some people, particularly at higher doses or on longer courses. Your blood pressure should be checked during treatment, and your doctor may ask you to reduce salt in your diet.
What is considered a high dose of prednisone?:
There is no official cutoff, but doctors generally treat doses under 7.5 mg a day as low, 7.5 mg to 40 mg a day as moderate, and more than 40 mg a day as high. A dose of 20 mg a day sits in the moderate range. What matters as much as the number is how long you take it, because side effects build up over time.
Can prednisone make you tired?:
Yes. Some people feel energized on prednisone while others feel drained. Poor sleep, mood changes and muscle weakness all contribute. Tiredness that starts as your dose is being lowered, or after you stop, can be a sign that your adrenal glands have not caught up yet, so tell your doctor if it is severe or comes with dizziness, nausea, or body aches.

## Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) dosage information
Your doctor will choose the smallest dose that controls your condition, and may adjust it over time. Follow your prescription label and do not change your dose yourself.
HCTZ dose for high blood pressure (adults):
Tablets: The starting dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once a day, which may be increased to 50 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Doses above 50 mg a day are often associated with a marked drop in blood potassium. Most people do not need more than 50 mg a day when hydrochlorothiazide is taken alongside other blood pressure medicines
Capsules: The starting dose is a hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg capsule once a day, whether taken on its own or with other blood pressure medicines. Total daily doses above 50 mg are not recommended. Capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
HCTZ dose for fluid retention (adults):
Tablets: The usual dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg to 100 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Many people with fluid retention respond to intermittent treatment, such as taking it every other day or on 3 to 5 days each week. Excessive response and undesirable electrolyte imbalance are less likely to occur with intermittent dosing.
HCTZ dose for children for high blood pressure and fluid retention:
The usual HCTZ dose in children, for both high blood pressure and fluid retention, is 1 mg to 2 mg per kilogram of body weight (0.5 mg to 1 mg per pound) a day, given as a single dose or split into two doses.
- Infants under 6 months: may be need doses of up to 3 mg per kilogram (1.5 mg per pound) a day, given as two divided doses up to the same maximum 37.5 mg daily limit
- Infants and children under 2 years: do not exceed 37.5 mg a day
- Children 2 to 12 years: do not exceed 100 mg a day
The dose is based on your child's weight and must be worked out by their doctor.
Taking the oral suspension:
If your child has been prescribed the liquid form (oral suspension), the following applies:
- Shake the bottle well before every dose.
- Measure each dose with the oral dosing syringe. Ask your pharmacist for a syringe and a bottle adapter if you do not have them.
- Never measure a dose with a household teaspoon or tablespoon, because these do not give an accurate amount.
- Store the made-up suspension at room temperature and do not freeze it.
- Throw away any unused suspension 30 days after it was made up. The pharmacist will write this date on the bottle.
The oral suspension can be taken with or without food.
What happens if I miss a dose?:
Take the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take two doses at one time.
What happens if I overdose?:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
Overdose symptoms may include nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, thirst, and muscle pain or weakness.

## What other drugs will affect hydrochlorothiazide?
Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Medicines that need particular care:
- Lithium. Lithium and diuretics generally should not be taken together. Hydrochlorothiazide reduces how quickly the kidneys clear lithium, which carries a high risk of lithium toxicity.
- Cholestyramine and colestipol. These cholesterol-lowering resins bind hydrochlorothiazide in the gut and can reduce how much you absorb by up to 85 percent for cholestyramine and 43 percent for colestipol. The doses need to be separated. For the oral suspension, the label advises taking hydrochlorothiazide at least 4 hours before, or 4 to 6 hours after, the resin.
- NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), diclofenac, meloxicam, indomethacin, celecoxib and aspirin. These can reduce the fluid-clearing and blood-pressure-lowering effects of hydrochlorothiazide, and your doctor will check whether the medicine is still working as intended.
- Insulin and oral diabetes medicines. Your diabetes medicine dose may need adjusting.
- Corticosteroids and ACTH. Taken with hydrochlorothiazide, these increase the loss of salts from the body, particularly potassium.
- Digoxin and other digitalis medicines. Low potassium caused by hydrochlorothiazide can make the heart more sensitive to the toxic effects of digitalis, including irregular heart rhythms.
- Other blood pressure medicines. The effects add together, which may be intended, but can also lower blood pressure more than expected.
- Alcohol, barbiturates and opioid pain medicines. These can make the drop in blood pressure on standing worse, causing dizziness or fainting.
- Muscle relaxants used during surgery (nondepolarizing muscle relaxants such as tubocurarine). You may respond more strongly to them, so tell your surgeon and anesthetist that you take hydrochlorothiazide.
- Medicines that raise blood pressure (pressor amines such as norepinephrine). Your response to them may be reduced, although this does not usually prevent their use.
This list is not complete. Other medicines may affect hydrochlorothiazide, and hydrochlorothiazide may affect other medicines.

## What other drugs will affect tamsulosin?
Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood and increase the risk of side effects.
Do not take tamsulosin with:
- strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole
- other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin
Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take:
- moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin
- strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine
- cimetidine
- warfarin
- medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra). Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms.
Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg. Your doctor will decide what is right for you.
No dose change is needed if you take tamsulosin with nifedipine, atenolol, enalapril, digoxin, theophylline, or furosemide.

Common side effects:
Common furosemide side effects may include:
- diarrhea, constipation, loss of appetite
- numbness or tingling
- headache, dizziness
- blurred vision
- redness, bruising, swelling, or pain where a subcutaneous dose is given.

- ringing in your ears, hearing loss
