## Hydrochlorothiazide side effects
The most noticeable effect of hydrochlorothiazide is passing urine more often, particularly in the first few weeks. This is how the medicine works rather than a side effect, and it usually settles as your body adjusts.
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat.
Get emergency medical help if you have a severe skin reaction, such as a spreading red or purple rash with blistering and peeling, or skin that is painful to touch.
Stop taking hydrochlorothiazide and get medical help immediately if you have a sudden change in your vision or pain in your eye.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- severe pain in your upper stomach that spreads to your back, with nausea and vomiting, which can be a sign of inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)
- yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice)
- fever, chills, sore throat, mouth sores or other signs of infection
- unusual bruising or bleeding, or pale skin and unusual tiredness, which can be signs of a blood problem
- shortness of breath, wheezing, or a cough with frothy mucus
- passing much less urine than usual, or swelling in your legs and ankles
- light-headedness or fainting, especially when standing up
- signs of dehydration or a salt imbalance, such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, confusion, muscle cramps, irregular heartbeat or unusual weakness
Other side effects:
Other hydrochlorothiazide side effects include:
- dizziness, a spinning sensation (vertigo), headache, restlessness, or tingling and numbness (paresthesia)
- weakness
- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, stomach cramping, stomach irritation, or loss of appetite
- muscle spasm
- increased sensitivity to sunlight, causing sunburn more easily
- hair loss or thinning
- difficulty getting or keeping an erection
- temporary blurred vision, or objects looking yellow-tinged (xanthopsia)
- swelling and tenderness of the salivary glands
- raised blood sugar, sugar in the urine, or raised uric acid
If a side effect is moderate or severe, your doctor may lower your dose or stop the medicine. Do not stop taking HCTZ on your own without speaking to your doctor first.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Like all medications, Prozac can cause side effects. Not everyone experiences them, and many improve after the first few weeks as your body adjusts to the medication. Tell your doctor if any side effects bother you or do not go away.

## What is metoprolol?
Metoprolol is a beta-blocker medication used to treat high blood pressure, chest pain (angina), and heart failure, and to improve survival after a heart attack. It works mainly on the heart, so it is called a cardioselective beta-blocker.
Metoprolol works by blocking the effect of adrenaline and noradrenaline on beta-1 receptors in your heart. This slows your heart rate, reduces how hard your heart squeezes, and lowers your blood pressure. Because the heart is doing less work, it needs less oxygen, which is why metoprolol also helps with angina. Exactly how metoprolol works for high blood pressure, heart failure, and after a heart attack is not fully understood.
At higher blood levels, metoprolol also blocks beta-2 receptors in the airways and blood vessels, which is why it still needs care in people with breathing problems.
Metoprolol comes as two different salts, metoprolol tartrate and metoprolol succinate. They are not interchangeable dose for dose:
- Metoprolol tartrate, an immediate-release tablet usually taken once or twice a day (brand name Lopressor)
- Metoprolol succinate, an extended-release tablet or capsule taken once a day (brand names Toprol-XL and Kapspargo Sprinkle)
Metoprolol tartrate is also given as an injection into a vein in a hospital during a heart attack.

Atorvastatin is a prescription medicine used to treat high cholesterol and to reduce the risk of heart attack, stroke, angina, and to decrease the chance that heart surgery will be needed in people who have heart disease or who are at risk of developing heart disease.

## Sertraline side effects
Common sertraline side effects:
The most common sertraline side effects are nausea, diarrhea or loose stools, trouble sleeping, dry mouth, tiredness, dizziness, sleepiness, tremor, indigestion, agitation, reduced appetite, increased sweating, and sexual problems.
The table below shows how often each side effect was reported in pooled placebo-controlled trials in 3,066 adults, compared with 2,293 people taking placebo.
Side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Nausea | 26% | 12%
Diarrhea or loose stools | 20% | 10%
Insomnia (trouble sleeping) | 20% | 13%
Dry mouth | 14% | 9%
Fatigue (tiredness) | 12% | 8%
Dizziness | 12% | 8%
Somnolence (sleepiness) | 11% | 6%
Tremor (shaking) | 9% | 2%
Dyspepsia (indigestion) | 8% | 4%
Agitation | 8% | 5%
Decreased appetite | 7% | 2%
Hyperhidrosis (heavy sweating) | 7% | 3%
Constipation | 6% | 4%
Decreased libido (lower sex drive) | 6% | 2%
Palpitations | 4% | 2%
Visual impairment | 4% | 2%
Vomiting | 4% | 1%
Some side effects were more common with particular conditions. Sleepiness was more common in depression trials, insomnia and agitation in OCD trials, constipation and agitation in panic disorder trials, tiredness in PTSD trials, and insomnia, dizziness, tiredness, dry mouth, and a general feeling of being unwell in social anxiety disorder trials. In PMDD trials, sleepiness, dry mouth, dizziness, tiredness, and stomach pain were more common.
In these trials, 12% of people taking sertraline stopped treatment because of a side effect, compared with 4% of people taking placebo. The most common reasons for stopping were nausea (3%), diarrhea (2%), agitation (2%), and insomnia (2%).
Sexual side effects of sertraline:
SSRIs including sertraline can cause sexual problems. In men, this can mean delayed ejaculation or being unable to ejaculate, lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. In women, it can mean lower sex drive and delayed orgasm or being unable to have an orgasm.
Sexual side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Ejaculation failure (men) | 8% | 1%
Decreased libido (men) | 7% | 2%
Erectile dysfunction (men) | 4% | 1%
Ejaculation disorder (men) | 3% | 0%
Male sexual dysfunction | 2% | 0%
Decreased libido (women) | 4% | 2%
Changes in sex drive and sexual function can also be part of depression and anxiety themselves, so the timing of when symptoms started matters. These numbers may underestimate how often sexual side effects happen, because people and their providers do not always raise the subject. Tell your provider about any change in sexual function, since there may be ways to manage it.
Serious sertraline side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to sertraline: rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of serotonin syndrome, which can be life threatening: agitation, hallucinations, confusion, coma or other changes in mental state, a racing heartbeat, high or low blood pressure, dizziness, heavy sweating, fever, muscle stiffness, twitching or overactive reflexes, loss of coordination, seizures, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea;
- unusual bleeding or bruising, including nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in vomit or stools, or black tarry stools;
- signs of a manic episode: greatly increased energy, severe trouble sleeping, racing thoughts, reckless behavior, unusually grand ideas, excessive happiness or irritability, or talking more or faster than usual;
- seizures or convulsions;
- eye pain, changes in vision, or swelling or redness in or around the eye, which can be signs of angle-closure glaucoma (a sudden rise in pressure inside the eye);
- signs of low sodium in the blood (hyponatremia): headache, trouble concentrating or thinking, memory problems, confusion, weakness, or feeling unsteady, which can lead to falls. Severe cases have caused hallucinations, fainting, seizures, coma, and death;
- fainting, chest discomfort, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation.
Sertraline side effects in children and teenagers:
The overall pattern of side effects in 281 children and teenagers treated with sertraline was generally similar to that seen in adults. Side effects reported in at least 2% of children and teenagers, and at least twice as often as with placebo, that were not common in adults were fever, hyperkinesia (abnormally increased movement), urinary incontinence, aggression, nosebleeds, purpura (purple spots under the skin), joint pain, weight loss, muscle twitching, and anxiety.
Reduced appetite and weight loss have been seen with SSRIs, so height and weight should be monitored during treatment.
Other reported side effects:
Less common side effects reported during studies include tachycardia (fast heartbeat), tinnitus (ringing in the ears), underactive thyroid, enlarged pupils, blurred vision, blood in the stools, swelling, unsteady walking, irritability, fever, raised liver enzymes, anaphylaxis, diabetes, high cholesterol, low blood sugar, increased appetite, joint pain, muscle spasms, poor coordination, coma, convulsions, reduced alertness, numbness, lethargy, restlessness, fainting, aggression, teeth grinding, confusion, euphoric mood, hallucination, blood in the urine, milk production from the breasts, priapism (a long-lasting erection), vaginal bleeding, wheezing, yawning, hair loss, cold sweats, skin inflammation, blistering, itching, rash, hives, bleeding, high blood pressure, and flushing.
Side effects reported after sertraline came onto the market include increased clotting times, AV block, slow heartbeat, atrial arrhythmias, QTc prolongation, ventricular tachycardia including Torsade de Pointes, breast enlargement in men, raised prolactin, irregular periods, SIADH, blindness, optic neuritis, cataract, severe liver problems including hepatitis, jaundice, and liver failure with some fatal outcomes, pancreatitis, several blood disorders, angioedema, low sodium, high blood sugar, rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), lockjaw, serotonin syndrome, movement disorders including akathisia and dystonia, psychosis, bedwetting, nightmares, sudden kidney failure, pulmonary hypertension, eosinophilic pneumonia, loss of smell, photosensitivity, severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, spasm of blood vessels in the brain, and vasculitis.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is Flonase?
Flonase is a nasal spray containing fluticasone propionate. Fluticasone propionate is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation in the lining of the nose.
Flonase Nasal Spray is used to treat nasal congestion, sneezing, runny nose, and itchy or watery eyes caused by seasonal or year-round allergies.

The brand-name prescription version of Flonase nasal spray has been discontinued in the United States. Generic fluticasone propionate nasal spray is still available by prescription, and over-the-counter Flonase products and store brands remain on the market.

## What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
Taking gabapentin with other medicines that make you drowsy or slow your breathing can cause dangerous side effects, including life-threatening breathing problems. Ask your doctor before using gabapentin with:
- opioid pain medicines such as hydrocodone, oxycodone, morphine, or buprenorphine
- sleeping pills such as zolpidem
- anxiety medicines such as lorazepam and other benzodiazepines
- muscle relaxers, sedatives, or other seizure medicines that cause drowsiness
Avoid drinking alcohol while taking gabapentin, because it can add to these effects.
Some medicines change the amount of gabapentin in your body:
- Antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium (such as Maalox) can reduce gabapentin absorption. Take gabapentin at least 2 hours after an antacid.
- Morphine can increase gabapentin levels, which may increase drowsiness and the risk of breathing problems. Your doctor may adjust your dose.
Gabapentin does not usually interact with other seizure medicines, such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproic acid, or phenobarbital, because it is not broken down by the liver. Your doctor can still check for interactions with your specific medicines.
Tell your doctor about all your current medicines, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. This list does not include all possible drug interactions.

## Metoprolol warnings
The most important warning with metoprolol is not to stop it suddenly. Stopping a beta blocker abruptly can bring on worse chest pain and, in some cases, a heart attack. If your treatment needs to stop, your prescriber will lower the dose gradually over 1 to 2 weeks and watch how you respond. This applies even if you only take metoprolol for blood pressure, because heart disease is common and is not always known about.
Talk to your care team before starting metoprolol if any of these apply to you.
- Asthma or other breathing problems. Beta blockers can tighten the airways. Metoprolol is used in people with these conditions only when other treatments are not suitable, at the lowest possible dose, with a reliever inhaler on hand.
- Heart failure. Heart failure can get worse while the dose is being increased. Tell your doctor about weight gain or increasing breathlessness.
- A slow heart rate or a conduction problem in the heart. This includes first-degree heart block, sinus node problems, and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Your heart rate should be monitored.
- Diabetes or long gaps without food. Metoprolol can hide the early warning signs of low blood sugar, such as a fast heartbeat, and can make low blood sugar more severe or last longer. The risk is higher if you are fasting, not eating regularly, or vomiting.
- An overactive thyroid. Metoprolol can mask signs of an overactive thyroid. Stopping it suddenly can trigger a thyroid crisis.
- Circulation problems in your arms or legs. Beta blockers can make symptoms of poor circulation worse.
- A history of severe allergic reactions. If you have anaphylaxis while taking a beta blocker, the usual dose of injectable epinephrine may not work as well.
- Pheochromocytoma (a tumor of the adrenal gland). Metoprolol must only be started after an alpha blocker has been started, or blood pressure can rise sharply.
- Liver disease. Metoprolol is broken down by the liver, so levels can build up. Treatment is usually started at a lower dose.
Surgery. Tell your surgeon and dentist that you take metoprolol. Long-term beta blocker treatment is not usually stopped before surgery. Starting a high dose of extended-release metoprolol shortly before non-cardiac surgery is avoided, because in one large trial this was linked to more slow heartbeats, low blood pressure, strokes, and deaths.

## What is the difference between hydroxyzine hydrochloride and hydroxyzine pamoate?
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) and hydroxyzine pamoate are two salt forms of the same active medicine. Taken by mouth, FDA-approved labeling gives them the same approved uses, the same doses, the same warnings, and the same side effects.
The injection is the exception. It is a hydroxyzine HCl product; there is no pamoate injection, and it has its own approved uses, doses, and warnings.
The practical differences are:
- Form. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride comes as tablets and as an oral solution. Hydroxyzine pamoate comes as capsules.
- How they dissolve. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride is very soluble in water. Hydroxyzine pamoate is practically insoluble in water.
- How the strength is measured. Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules are labeled by the amount of hydroxyzine HCl they are equivalent to. A 25 mg pamoate capsule delivers the same amount of active medicine as a hydroxyzine hydrochloride 25 mg tablet.
The two salts also had different brand names. Vistaril was the brand name for hydroxyzine pamoate, and Atarax was the brand name for hydroxyzine hydrochloride. Both brands have been discontinued in the United States, and hydroxyzine is now available as a generic medicine.
Is hydroxyzine pamoate stronger or longer lasting than hydroxyzine hydrochloride?:
No. You may read that hydroxyzine pamoate works better for anxiety, lasts longer, or reaches the brain more effectively than hydroxyzine hydrochloride. FDA-approved labeling does not support this.

Treatment of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg orally once a day for up to 8 weeks; however an additional 8 weeks may be considered for patients who have not healed after the initial treatment. 40 mg orally once a day. Data have revealed that monotherapy with daily doses of 40 mg have been associated with complete gastric ulcer healing in up to 87% and 97% of patients after 4 weeks and 8 weeks respectively.

## Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) dosage information
Your doctor will choose the smallest dose that controls your condition, and may adjust it over time. Follow your prescription label and do not change your dose yourself.
HCTZ dose for high blood pressure (adults):
Tablets: The starting dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once a day, which may be increased to 50 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Doses above 50 mg a day are often associated with a marked drop in blood potassium. Most people do not need more than 50 mg a day when hydrochlorothiazide is taken alongside other blood pressure medicines
Capsules: The starting dose is a hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg capsule once a day, whether taken on its own or with other blood pressure medicines. Total daily doses above 50 mg are not recommended. Capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
HCTZ dose for fluid retention (adults):
Tablets: The usual dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg to 100 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Many people with fluid retention respond to intermittent treatment, such as taking it every other day or on 3 to 5 days each week. Excessive response and undesirable electrolyte imbalance are less likely to occur with intermittent dosing.
HCTZ dose for children for high blood pressure and fluid retention:
The usual HCTZ dose in children, for both high blood pressure and fluid retention, is 1 mg to 2 mg per kilogram of body weight (0.5 mg to 1 mg per pound) a day, given as a single dose or split into two doses.
- Infants under 6 months: may be need doses of up to 3 mg per kilogram (1.5 mg per pound) a day, given as two divided doses up to the same maximum 37.5 mg daily limit
- Infants and children under 2 years: do not exceed 37.5 mg a day
- Children 2 to 12 years: do not exceed 100 mg a day
The dose is based on your child's weight and must be worked out by their doctor.
Taking the oral suspension:
If your child has been prescribed the liquid form (oral suspension), the following applies:
- Shake the bottle well before every dose.
- Measure each dose with the oral dosing syringe. Ask your pharmacist for a syringe and a bottle adapter if you do not have them.
- Never measure a dose with a household teaspoon or tablespoon, because these do not give an accurate amount.
- Store the made-up suspension at room temperature and do not freeze it.
- Throw away any unused suspension 30 days after it was made up. The pharmacist will write this date on the bottle.
The oral suspension can be taken with or without food.
What happens if I miss a dose?:
Take the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take two doses at one time.
What happens if I overdose?:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
Overdose symptoms may include nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, thirst, and muscle pain or weakness.

## What is levothyroxine?
Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.
Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
- treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
- lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.
Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly. This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression. When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although it may take several weeks before you notice a difference.
Levothyroxine is usually taken for life.
What levothyroxine is not used for:
Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet. It does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid. It is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland).
Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.

Your blood pressure will need to be checked often, and you may need other medical tests.

The most common sertraline side effects are nausea, diarrhea or loose stools, trouble sleeping, dry mouth, tiredness, dizziness, sleepiness, tremor, indigestion, agitation, reduced appetite, increased sweating, and sexual problems.

SSRIs including sertraline can cause sexual problems. In men, this can mean delayed ejaculation or being unable to ejaculate, lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. In women, it can mean lower sex drive and delayed orgasm or being unable to have an orgasm.

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to sertraline: rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of serotonin syndrome, which can be life threatening: agitation, hallucinations, confusion, coma or other changes in mental state, a racing heartbeat, high or low blood pressure, dizziness, heavy sweating, fever, muscle stiffness, twitching or overactive reflexes, loss of coordination, seizures, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea;
- unusual bleeding or bruising, including nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in vomit or stools, or black tarry stools;

- seizures or convulsions;

evidence:
## What is levothyroxine?
Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.
Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
- treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
- lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.
Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly. This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression. When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although it may take several weeks before you notice a difference.
Levothyroxine is usually taken for life.
What levothyroxine is not used for:
Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet. It does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid. It is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland).
Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.

## Hydrochlorothiazide side effects
The most noticeable effect of hydrochlorothiazide is passing urine more often, particularly in the first few weeks. This is how the medicine works rather than a side effect, and it usually settles as your body adjusts.
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat.
Get emergency medical help if you have a severe skin reaction, such as a spreading red or purple rash with blistering and peeling, or skin that is painful to touch.
Stop taking hydrochlorothiazide and get medical help immediately if you have a sudden change in your vision or pain in your eye.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- severe pain in your upper stomach that spreads to your back, with nausea and vomiting, which can be a sign of inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis)
- yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice)
- fever, chills, sore throat, mouth sores or other signs of infection
- unusual bruising or bleeding, or pale skin and unusual tiredness, which can be signs of a blood problem
- shortness of breath, wheezing, or a cough with frothy mucus
- passing much less urine than usual, or swelling in your legs and ankles
- light-headedness or fainting, especially when standing up
- signs of dehydration or a salt imbalance, such as extreme thirst, dry mouth, confusion, muscle cramps, irregular heartbeat or unusual weakness
Other side effects:
Other hydrochlorothiazide side effects include:
- dizziness, a spinning sensation (vertigo), headache, restlessness, or tingling and numbness (paresthesia)
- weakness
- nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, stomach cramping, stomach irritation, or loss of appetite
- muscle spasm
- increased sensitivity to sunlight, causing sunburn more easily
- hair loss or thinning
- difficulty getting or keeping an erection
- temporary blurred vision, or objects looking yellow-tinged (xanthopsia)
- swelling and tenderness of the salivary glands
- raised blood sugar, sugar in the urine, or raised uric acid
If a side effect is moderate or severe, your doctor may lower your dose or stop the medicine. Do not stop taking HCTZ on your own without speaking to your doctor first.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Warnings and precautions
Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole. These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up, which may make you feel dizzy or faint. This is most likely when you first start taking it, when your dose changes, or when you start it again after a break. Get up slowly from sitting or lying down. Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases (probably fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients), tamsulosin can cause priapism, a painful erection that lasts a long time and is not related to sexual activity. Get medical help straight away if this happens, because without prompt treatment it can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction.
An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together. Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.
Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery. Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken it in the past, even if you stopped months ago. Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to. If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again. You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose.
Many other medicines can interact with tamsulosin. Tell your doctor about everything you take, including prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

## How should I take apixaban?
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose. Use the medicine exactly as directed.
Apixaban is usually taken twice per day.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine. If you cannot swallow a tablet whole, you may crush it and mix the medicine with a small amount of applesauce, apple juice, or water.
If your child is prescribed the tablets for oral suspension, it should be mixed with water, infant formula, apple juice, or apple sauce. Do not swallow the tablet.
If your child is taking capsules for oral suspension, the capsule should be opened and mixed with water or infant formula only. Do not swallow the capsule.
Mixed medicine should be used right away. Apixaban may also be given through a feeding tube.
apixaban can also make it easier for you to bleed, even from a minor injury such as a fall or a bump on the head. Tell your doctor or seek emergency medical attention if you fall or hit your head, or have any bleeding that will not stop.
If you have a planned surgery or dental procedure, your doctor may tell you to stop taking apixaban for a short time.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
If your child vomits within 30 minutes after taking apixaban, take another dose. If the child vomits after more than 30 minutes of taking apixaban, do not take another dose and give the next dose as scheduled.
Do not change your dose or stop taking apixaban unless your doctor tells you to. If you stop taking apixaban for any reason, your doctor may prescribe another medicine to prevent blood clots. Keep all follow-up visits with your healthcare provider.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat.

An adult should supervise a child using the spray. Children should use it for the shortest amount of time necessary to achieve symptom relief. Talk to your child's doctor if your child needs to use the spray for longer than two months a year.

Use the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not use two doses at one time.

## Metoprolol side effects
The most common side effects of metoprolol are tiredness, dizziness, low mood (depression), diarrhea, shortness of breath, a slow heartbeat (bradycardia), and itching or rash. Most side effects reported in studies were mild and did not last.
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to metoprolol: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Common side effects of metoprolol:
In studies of people taking metoprolol for high blood pressure or angina:
- Tiredness and dizziness occurred in about 10% of people
- Low mood or depression was reported in about 5 out of 100 people
- Diarrhea occurred in about 5% of people
- Itching or rash occurred in about 5% of people
- Shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat occurred in about 3% of people
- Cold hands and feet, palpitations, swelling of the ankles, and low blood pressure were each reported in about 1% of people
- Nausea, dry mouth, stomach pain, constipation, gas, and heartburn were each reported in about 1% of people
Headache, nightmares, trouble sleeping, confusion, and short-term memory loss have also been reported.
In the heart failure study of extended-release metoprolol, dizziness or vertigo was reported by 1.8% of people taking metoprolol compared with 1.0% taking placebo, and a slow heartbeat by 1.5% compared with 0.4%.
Other reported side effects:
These have been reported since metoprolol came on the market. Their frequency is not known:
- Hair thinning or hair loss, which reversed after stopping
- Reduced sex drive and difficulty getting an erection
- Dry eyes, blurred vision, and ringing in the ears
- Sweating, sensitivity to sunlight, and worsening of psoriasis
- Change in taste, joint and muscle pain, and fainting
- Liver inflammation (hepatitis)
- A severe drop in white blood cells (agranulocytosis), which can show up as fever, chills, or a sore throat
Serious side effects of metoprolol:
Some of these, such as shortness of breath and a slow heartbeat, are also listed as common side effects above. They need urgent attention when they are severe, new, or getting worse.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- A very slow heartbeat, pauses in your heartbeat, or a feeling that you might faint. Sinus pause, heart block, and cardiac arrest have all been reported.
- Signs that heart failure is getting worse, such as weight gain over a few days, more shortness of breath, or swelling of your feet or lower legs
- Wheezing or trouble breathing
- Chest pain that is worse or more frequent than usual, especially if you have recently stopped or missed doses
- Cold, pale, or blue fingers and toes, or pain in your legs when you walk
- Confusion, hallucinations, or memory problems
- Yellowing of your skin or eyes, which can be a sign of liver inflammation
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Warnings
Meloxicam can increase your risk of a fatal heart attack or stroke, especially if you use it long term or take high doses, or if you have heart disease. Even people without heart disease or risk factors could have a stroke or heart attack while taking this medicine.
Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG).
Avoid taking meloxicam after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to. You may have an increased risk of another heart attack if you take this medicine after a recent heart attack.
Get emergency medical help if you have chest pain, weakness, shortness of breath, slurred speech, or problems with vision or balance.
Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding, which can be fatal. These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
Call your doctor at once if you have symptoms of stomach bleeding, such as black, bloody, or tarry stools, or coughing up blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Avoid smoking and drinking alcohol, as they also increase your risk of stomach bleeding.

You should not use furosemide if you are allergic to it or are unable to urinate.

Usual Adult Bupropion Dose for Depression:
Immediate-release tablets:
- Initial dose: 100 mg orally twice a day, increase if necessary after 3 days to 100 mg orally three times a day.
- Maintenance dose: 100 mg orally three times a day
- Maximum dose: 450 mg/day in up to 4 divided doses; single doses should not exceed 150 mg
- Immediate-release tablets should be given at least 6 hours apart.
- Dose increases of the immediate-release tablet should not exceed 100 mg per day in a 3-day period.
Sustained-release tablets:
- Initial dose: 150 mg orally once a day in the morning, increase if necessary after 3 days to 150 mg orally twice a day.
- Maintenance dose: 150 mg orally twice a day
- Maximum dose: 400 mg/day; maximum single dose should not exceed 200 mg
- Sustained-release oral tablets should be given at least 8 hours apart
Extended-release tablets:
- Initial dose: 150 mg orally once a day in the morning, increase if necessary after 4 days to 300 mg orally once a day.
- Maintenance dose: 300 mg orally once a day
- Maximum dose: 450 mg/day
- Extended-release oral tablets should be given at least 24 hours apart
Comments:
So as not to exceed the maximum single dose of 150 mg for immediate-release tablets, a dose of 100 mg orally four times a day (using the 100 mg tablet) may be administered. Patients who are taking 300 mg/day for at least 2 weeks (OR are currently taking 450 mg/day) of any formulation may be switched to the extended-release 450 mg dose. Bupropion hydrobromide 174 mg oral tablet is equivalent to bupropion hydrochloride 150 mg. Patients should be periodically reviewed to determine the need for maintenance treatment and the appropriate dose for such treatment.

Extended-release tablets:
- Initial dose: 150 mg orally once a day in the morning, increased if necessary after 7 days to 300 mg orally once a day
- Maintenance dose: 150 to 300 mg orally once a day
- Maximum dose: 300 mg/day
Comments:
Treatment should be initiated in the autumn prior to the onset of depressive symptoms, continued through the winter season, and discontinued in early spring. Patients taking bupropion hydrochloride 300 mg orally per day during the autumn-winter season should have their dose tapered to 150 mg once a day for 2 weeks prior to discontinuation. The timing of initiation and treatment duration for seasonal affective disorder should be individualized according to the patient's historical pattern of seasonal major depressive episodes.

- Maintenance dose: 150 mg orally twice a day

## What is amlodipine?
Amlodipine besylate is a prescription medicine used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to prevent certain types of angina (chest pain). It belongs to a class of medications called calcium channel blockers.
Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.
Amlodipine besylate controls angina chest pain by increasing the supply of blood to the heart. If taken regularly, this medicine controls chest pain, but it does not stop chest pain once it starts. Your doctor may prescribe a different medication to take when you have chest pain.
Amlodipine is also used alone or in combination with other medicines to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) in adults and children at least 6 years old. Lowering blood pressure may lower your risk of a stroke or heart attack.
Amlodipine besylate is available as:
- Amlodipine 5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 10 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 2.5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL solution (Norliqva)

## Metoprolol dosage
The usual starting dose is 25 mg to 100 mg once a day for extended-release metoprolol, and 100 mg a day for immediate-release metoprolol. Your dose is then adjusted at intervals of a week or longer until your blood pressure or symptoms are controlled.
Metoprolol tartrate (immediate-release tablets) dosage for adults:
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range
High blood pressure | 100 mg a day, as one dose or split into two | 100 mg to 450 mg a day. Doses above 450 mg a day have not been studied.
Angina | 100 mg a day, split into two doses | 100 mg to 400 mg a day. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
After a heart attack | 50 mg every 6 hours for 48 hours, starting 15 minutes after the last dose given into a vein. If the full intravenous dose was not tolerated, 25 mg is used. | Maintenance is 100 mg twice a day, continued for at least 3 months.
With immediate-release tablets, a once-daily dose may not keep blood pressure controlled for the full 24 hours, especially at 100 mg. Splitting the dose or taking a larger daily dose may be needed.
Metoprolol succinate (extended-release tablets and capsules) dosage for adults:
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range
High blood pressure | 25 mg to 100 mg once a day | Adjust weekly or less often. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
Angina | 100 mg once a day | Increase weekly until symptoms are controlled or your heart rate slows noticeably. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
Heart failure | 25 mg once a day for two weeks, or 12.5 mg once a day in more severe heart failure | Double the dose every two weeks to the highest dose you tolerate, up to 200 mg once a day.
Kapspargo Sprinkle capsules are not suitable to start heart failure treatment if a dose below 25 mg is needed.
Metoprolol dosage for children:
Extended-release metoprolol is the only form approved for children, and only for high blood pressure in children aged 6 years and older. The starting dose is 1 mg for each kilogram of body weight once a day, up to a maximum first dose of 50 mg. Doses above 2 mg/kg, or above 200 mg a day, have not been studied. Extended-release metoprolol has not been studied in children under 6 years.
Dose adjustments:
- Liver problems. Start at a lower dose than usual and increase slowly.
- Kidney problems. No dose reduction is needed.
- Older adults. A low starting dose is generally used, because liver, kidney, and heart function are more often reduced and other medicines are more often involved.
- Switching between forms. When changing from immediate-release to extended-release metoprolol, the same total daily dose is used.

## Warnings and precautions
Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole. These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up, which may make you feel dizzy or faint. This is most likely when you first start taking it, when your dose changes, or when you start it again after a break. Get up slowly from sitting or lying down. Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases (probably fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients), tamsulosin can cause priapism, a painful erection that lasts a long time and is not related to sexual activity. Get medical help straight away if this happens, because without prompt treatment it can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction.
An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together. Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.
Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery. Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken it in the past, even if you stopped months ago. Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to. If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again. You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose.
Many other medicines can interact with tamsulosin. Tell your doctor about everything you take, including prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

Does metformin work for weight loss?:
Yes. Metformin can lead to a modest weight loss, though results vary, and it's generally smaller amount of weight loss than what's seen with medications specifically approved for weight loss.
In the landmark Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), a randomized controlled trial in people at high risk for diabetes, participants taking metformin lost more weight than those on placebo. Metformin patients lost 2.7% of body weight after one year, compared to 0.43% for placebo, and 2.1% after two years compared to essentially no change (0.02%) for placebo. Looking at it another way, 29% of people on metformin lost at least 5% of their starting body weight after one year, versus just 13% on placebo, a gap that held up at the two-year mark (26% vs. 14%).
Metformin is not FDA-approved for weight loss.

## Warnings
Do not take spironolactone if you have a high potassium level in your blood, if you have Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder), or if you are taking eplerenone (Inspra), another medicine of the same type.
Spironolactone can raise your potassium to a dangerous level. A high potassium level can cause a life-threatening change in your heart rhythm, and it often causes no symptoms until it is already high. Your doctor should check your potassium with a blood test within a week of you starting spironolactone or having your dose changed, and regularly after that.
Your risk of high potassium is greater if your kidneys do not work well, if you take potassium supplements or a salt substitute containing potassium, or if you take an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, an NSAID, heparin, or trimethoprim.
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless your doctor has specifically told you to.
Passing too much fluid can drop your blood pressure and make your kidney function worse, especially if you are also taking an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. Tell your doctor if you feel faint, or if you become unwell with vomiting or diarrhea.
If you have cirrhosis with fluid in your abdomen, spironolactone is usually started in hospital, because sudden shifts in fluid and salt can affect how your brain works.
Spironolactone should be avoided in pregnancy where possible, because it blocks male hormones and may affect how a male baby develops.

## What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
Taking gabapentin with other medicines that make you drowsy or slow your breathing can cause dangerous side effects, including life-threatening breathing problems. Ask your doctor before using gabapentin with:
- opioid pain medicines such as hydrocodone, oxycodone, morphine, or buprenorphine

## What is prednisone?
Prednisone is a prescription corticosteroid (steroid) used to reduce inflammation, suppress an overactive immune system, and treat endocrine and metabolic disorders. Prednisone is used for a wide range of conditions, including severe allergies, asthma and COPD flare-ups, rheumatoid arthritis and other forms of arthritis, lupus, psoriasis and other skin conditions, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, eye inflammation, some blood disorders, and low adrenal hormone levels.
Prednisone works by mimicking the effects of glucocorticoid hormones secreted naturally by our adrenal glands. Prednisone is a man-made (synthetic) version of these hormones. Prednisone is different from steroids taken to build muscle (anabolic steroids).
Prednisone belongs to the drug class called glucocorticoids, which are a type of corticosteroid.
Prednisone tablets come in 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, and 50 mg strengths. Prednisone 20 mg and prednisone 10 mg tablets are the strengths most often used for short courses in adults. Prednisone also comes as a delayed-release tablet (Rayos), as an oral liquid, and as a concentrated oral solution (Prednisone Intensol) that is measured with a special dropper.
Many of the original brands are discontinued; however, generic prednisone is available.

## Spironolactone FAQs
Is spironolactone a diuretic?:
Yes. Spironolactone is a diuretic, or water pill, and it belongs to the group called potassium-sparing diuretics. It works by blocking aldosterone, a hormone that makes your kidneys hold onto salt and water. Unlike most water pills, which make you lose potassium, spironolactone makes your body keep potassium in. It is a weaker diuretic than medicines such as furosemide, which is one reason it is often given alongside another water pill rather than instead of one.
Is spironolactone used for acne?:
Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating acne, but doctors sometimes prescribe it off-label for hormonal acne in women. Off-label means a doctor is prescribing a medicine for something other than its approved uses, which is legal and common, but it means the FDA has not reviewed the medicine for that purpose.
The reason it is used this way relates to how spironolactone works. As well as blocking aldosterone, spironolactone attaches to the androgen receptor, the docking point for male hormones such as testosterone. Male hormones increase how much oil the skin produces, and oil production is one factor in acne.
Because acne is not an approved use, there is no FDA-approved dose for it. Any dose is chosen by the prescriber. Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy because it may affect how a male baby develops, which is an important consideration for anyone taking it for a skin condition rather than a heart or kidney condition.
If you are considering spironolactone for acne, this is a conversation to have with a doctor or dermatologist who can review your full medical history, since spironolactone still carries the same risk of raising your potassium level, whatever it is prescribed for.
Does spironolactone cause weight gain?:
Weight gain is not a recognized side effect of spironolactone, and it is not listed in the medicine's official prescribing information. Spironolactone is a diuretic, so it usually causes a small drop in weight in the first week or two as your body sheds extra fluid.
If you are gaining weight while taking it, it is worth telling your doctor rather than assuming the medicine is to blame. Rapid weight gain with swelling in your ankles or legs or shortness of breath can be a sign of fluid building up, which may mean the condition being treated needs a closer look. Slower weight gain is more often down to appetite, activity, or another medicine.
Does spironolactone cause hair loss?:
Hair thinning, known as alopecia, is listed as a possible side effect of spironolactone, though how often it happens is not known. It is reported far less often than breast tenderness or breast growth.
The picture is complicated because spironolactone is also prescribed off label for hair loss in women, on the basis that blocking male hormones may help with hormone-related thinning. Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating hair loss. If your hair is thinning while you take it, speak to your doctor, since there are several possible causes worth ruling out.
How long does it take for spironolactone to work?:
It depends what you are taking it for. Spironolactone reaches its highest level in your blood in about 2 to 3 hours, and its active breakdown product peaks at around 4 hours, so it starts having an effect on your kidneys the same day.
The results you notice take longer. For fluid build-up, spironolactone is given for at least five days before the dose is increased, because that is how long the full effect takes to show. For high blood pressure, the dose is adjusted at two-week intervals, so give it a couple of weeks before judging it. For heart failure, the benefit is a lower risk of being admitted to hospital and living longer, which is not something you feel week to week.
How long does spironolactone stay in your system?:
Spironolactone itself leaves your blood very quickly, with a half-life of about 1.4 hours, meaning half of it is gone in that time. Its active breakdown products last much longer, with half-lives of roughly 14 to 17 hours. Because of those, the effect of a dose carries on well after the spironolactone itself has gone, and it takes a few days for the medicine to clear fully after you stop. Clearance is slower if you have cirrhosis.
Is spironolactone a blood thinner?:
No. Spironolactone is not a blood thinner. It does not affect blood clotting and it is not used to prevent clots or strokes in the way that warfarin, apixaban, or aspirin are. It is a diuretic that lowers blood pressure and reduces fluid build-up.
Spironolactone does interact with some blood thinners indirectly. Heparin and low molecular weight heparin can raise potassium, so taking them with spironolactone increases the risk of a high potassium level.
Can I stop taking spironolactone suddenly?:
Spironolactone does not cause withdrawal symptoms and does not need to be tapered the way a steroid does. Even so, do not stop it without speaking to your doctor. Stopping it can allow fluid to build up again, your blood pressure to rise, or your heart failure to worsen, and if you are taking it for heart failure it is one of the medicines shown to help people live longer. If side effects are the reason you want to stop, a dose change or a different medicine may be an option.
Can you take spironolactone at night?:
There is no fixed time of day for spironolactone. What matters more is that you take it at the same time each day and always the same way with regard to food, since food changes how much you absorb. Many people prefer the morning because spironolactone makes you pass more urine, and a late dose can mean getting up in the night. If a nighttime dose suits you better, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.
Can you drink alcohol while taking spironolactone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and spironolactone, but drinking is best kept modest. Both can lower your blood pressure and make you light-headed, so together they raise the chance of feeling dizzy or faint, particularly when you stand up. Alcohol is also a problem in its own right if you are taking spironolactone for liver disease. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for your situation.
Can you take spironolactone while pregnant?:
Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy. It blocks the action of male hormones, and in animal studies male offspring exposed before birth developed abnormally. Human data are limited and have not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern is enough that the manufacturer advises avoiding it or discussing the potential risk to a male baby.
Do not stop spironolactone on your own if you find out you are pregnant. Tell your doctor straight away, because untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry serious risks in pregnancy and your treatment will need to be changed carefully.
Does spironolactone cause constipation?:
Constipation is not a listed side effect of spironolactone. The digestive side effects that have been reported are the opposite, including diarrhea and stomach cramping, along with nausea, vomiting, and indigestion. If you are constipated while taking spironolactone, another cause is more likely, and it is worth mentioning to your pharmacist, who can check the rest of your medicines.
Is 200 mg of spironolactone too much?:
It depends on the reason you are taking it. For fluid build-up, the approved dose range goes up to 200 mg a day, and for primary hyperaldosteronism it goes up to 400 mg a day, so 200 mg is within the licensed range for both.
For high blood pressure it would be above the usual range, since doses over 100 mg a day do not lower blood pressure any further. For heart failure the usual dose is 25 mg to 50 mg a day, so 200 mg would be well above what is normally used. Higher doses also carry a greater risk of high potassium and of breast growth in men. If your dose seems high for your condition, ask your prescriber rather than adjusting it yourself.
Why is spironolactone described as a high-risk medicine?:
The main reason is the risk of a high potassium level, which can cause a dangerous change in your heart rhythm and often gives no warning symptoms. The risk rises if your kidneys do not work well or if you take other medicines that raise potassium, and several very common medicines do, including ibuprofen and some blood pressure tablets.
This risk is manageable, which is why blood tests are built into treatment. Your potassium should be checked within a week of starting spironolactone or changing your dose, and regularly after that. Spironolactone also needs care in pregnancy and in people with liver disease.

## Warnings
Ibuprofen can increase your risk of fatal heart attack, heart failure, or stroke. Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG). Avoid taking ibuprofen after a recent heart attack, unless your doctor tells you to.

## Before taking this medicine
Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions and medications before starting fluoxetine (Prozac), as some may interact with it or affect whether it is safe for you.
Tell your doctor if you take any of the following medications or supplements:
- Triptans (for migraine)
- Antidepressants or mood stabilizers, including SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, MAOIs, lithium, buspirone, or antipsychotics
- Amphetamines
- Opioid pain medications, including tramadol, fentanyl, meperidine, or methadone
- Over-the-counter supplements such as St. John's Wort or tryptophan
- Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
Many of these combinations can increase the risk of serotonin syndrome, a potentially serious condition.

- Liver, kidney, or heart problems
- Seizures or epilepsy
- Bipolar disorder or mania
- Low sodium levels in the blood
- A stroke or high blood pressure
- Bleeding problems
Pregnancy
Tell your healthcare provider if you are pregnant, become pregnant, or plan to become pregnant while taking fluoxetine tablets. Using fluoxetine later in pregnancy may increase the risk of complications in the newborn, including problems that need a longer hospital stay, breathing support, or tube feeding, and a serious lung condition called persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Untreated depression also carries risks in pregnancy, so discuss the benefits and risks of treatment with your healthcare provider rather than stopping on your own.
If you become pregnant while taking fluoxetine tablets, ask your healthcare provider about joining the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants, which tracks pregnancy outcomes in women who take these medicines. You can enroll by calling 1-866-961-2388 or visiting womensmentalhealth.org.
Breastfeeding:
Fluoxetine passes into breast milk. Tell your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed, and discuss the best way to feed your baby while you are taking fluoxetine tablets. If you do breastfeed, watch your baby for agitation, irritability, poor feeding, or poor weight gain, and seek medical advice if you notice any of these.

## What is gabapentin?
Gabapentin is a prescription medicine used to treat partial seizures, nerve pain from shingles (postherpetic neuralgia), and restless legs syndrome (Horizant brand only). It may also be prescribed off-label for other conditions including diabetic nerve pain, anxiety, and fibromyalgia. Gabapentin is thought to work by calming overactive nerve signals in the brain and nervous system. It is an anticonvulsant and nerve pain medication from the drug class gabapentinoids
Gabapentin brand names are Neurontin, Gralise, Horizant, and Relgaabi, which may not be interchangeable.
Gabapentin is not a federally controlled substance, but some states classify it as Schedule V and others require gabapentin prescriptions to be reported to their prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP). Rules on refills and quantity limits vary by state.
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), and swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema). These often improve as your body adjusts, but do not drive until you know how gabapentin affects you.

## How should I take amoxicillin?
Take amoxicillin exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Take amoxicillin at the same time each day.
Some forms of amoxicillin may be taken with or without food. Check your medicine label to see if you should take your medicine with food or not.
Shake the oral suspension (liquid) before you measure a dose.
Measure liquid medicine with the dosing syringe provided, or use a medicine dose-measuring device (not a kitchen spoon). You may mix the liquid with water, milk, baby formula, fruit juice, or ginger ale. Drink all of the mixture right away. Do not save for later use.
You must chew the chewable tablet before you swallow it.
Swallow the regular tablet whole and do not crush, chew, or break it.
If you are taking amoxicillin with clarithromycin and/or lansoprazole to treat stomach ulcer, use all of your medications as directed. Read the medication guide or patient instructions provided with each medication. Do not change your doses or medication schedule without your doctor's advice.
Use this medicine for the full prescribed length of time, even if your symptoms quickly improve. Skipping doses can increase your risk of infection, that is resistant to medication. Amoxicillin will not treat a viral infection such as the flu or a common cold.
Do not share this medicine with another person, even if they have the same symptoms you have.
This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests. Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using this medicine.
Store tablets and capsules at room temperature, away from moisture, heat, and light.
Liquid amoxicillin may need to be stored in a refrigerator or at room temperature, depending on the brand. Check your label for storage instructions. If stored in the refrigerator, do not allow it to freeze. Throw away any liquid medicine that is not used within 14 days after it was mixed at the pharmacy.

Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline has very little effect on norepinephrine and dopamine, and it has no meaningful effect on adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopamine, histamine, or benzodiazepine receptors, which is part of why it is described as selective.
How long does sertraline take to work?:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.
Should I take sertraline in the morning or at night?:
Either is fine. Sertraline is taken once a day, in the morning or the evening, and the label does not favor one over the other. What matters more is taking it at around the same time each day. Insomnia was reported by 20% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 13% on placebo, and sleepiness by 11% compared with 6%, so some people find one timing suits them better than the other. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does sertraline cause weight gain or weight loss?:
Reduced appetite is a common sertraline side effect, reported by 7% of adults in trials compared with 2% on placebo. Increased appetite was reported less often, in fewer than 2% of people. In children and teenagers taking sertraline for depression, there was a difference in weight change of roughly 1 kg compared with placebo over 10 weeks, representing slight weight loss on sertraline and slight gain on placebo. Around 7% of children lost more than 7% of their body weight, compared with none on placebo. In a longer 34 week extension study, weight gain was similar to what would be expected for their age. Height and weight should be monitored in younger patients. Tell your doctor about any weight change that concerns you.
Does sertraline make you tired or sleepy?:
It can. Sleepiness was reported by 11% of adults taking sertraline in trials, compared with 6% on placebo, and tiredness by 12% compared with 8%. Sertraline can also affect how clearly you think and how quickly you react, so do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.
Is sertraline a controlled substance?:
No. Sertraline is not a controlled substance. In a study comparing sertraline with alprazolam and d-amphetamine, sertraline did not produce the effects associated with a potential for misuse, such as euphoria or drug liking, that were seen with the other two medicines.
Can sertraline cause diarrhea or nausea?:
Yes, these are the two most common sertraline side effects. Nausea was reported by 26% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 12% on placebo, and diarrhea or loose stools by 20% compared with 10%. Nausea was also the most common reason people stopped treatment. Tell your doctor if these do not settle.
How do you stop taking sertraline safely?:
Lower the dose gradually rather than stopping all at once, and only under your doctor's guidance. Symptoms reported after stopping a serotonergic antidepressant, especially when it is stopped abruptly, include nausea, sweating, low or unstable mood, irritability, agitation, dizziness, unusual sensations such as electric shock feelings, tremor, anxiety, confusion, headache, lethargy, insomnia, hypomania, ringing in the ears, and seizures.
Can you drink alcohol while taking sertraline?:
Drinking alcohol is not recommended while you take sertraline. In healthy volunteers, sertraline did not increase the immediate effects of alcohol on thinking and coordination, but the advice for patients is still to avoid it. Separately, do not take sertraline oral solution with disulfiram, because the solution contains 12% alcohol.
Can you take sertraline while pregnant?:
That depends on your situation, and it is a decision to make with your doctor rather than on your own. Studies of first trimester use suggest no overall difference in the risk of major birth defects, but use late in pregnancy has been linked with newborn breathing problems and with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. At the same time, stopping an antidepressant during pregnancy raises the risk of depression coming back. The oral solution specifically is not recommended in pregnancy because it contains alcohol.
What are sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules for?:
Sertraline capsules come in 150 mg and 200 mg only, and they are not used to start treatment. They are for people who have already been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week and need a higher dose. The maximum is 200 mg a day, the same as for tablets. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not opened, crushed, or chewed. If you need to come off sertraline, the dose has to be lowered gradually using another sertraline product, because there is no capsule strength below 150 mg. Capsules are approved for depression in adults and OCD from age 6, not for panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, or PMDD.
Does sertraline interact with warfarin?:
Yes, in two ways. Sertraline can add to warfarin's effect on bleeding risk, and both medicines bind tightly to proteins in the blood, so taking them together can raise the free level of one or both. If you take warfarin with sertraline, your INR should be monitored carefully.

## What is levothyroxine?
Levothyroxine is a man-made form of thyroxine (T4), one of the hormones your thyroid gland normally produces. It belongs to a class of medications called hormones, and it works by replacing thyroid hormone that your body is not making enough of.
Levothyroxine is used in adults and children, including newborn babies, to:
- treat hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid - a condition where the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone). It replaces the missing hormone whether the condition was present from birth or developed later, and whether the problem starts in the thyroid gland itself or in the pituitary gland or hypothalamus; and
- lower the level of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the blood in people being treated for a certain type of thyroid cancer, alongside surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.
Levothyroxine injection is used in adults to treat myxedema coma, a rare and life-threatening complication of a severely underactive thyroid.
Without thyroid hormone, your body cannot function properly. This may result in poor growth, slow speech, lack of energy, excessive tiredness, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, dry, thick skin, increased sensitivity to cold, joint and muscle pain, heavy or irregular menstrual periods, and depression. When taken correctly, levothyroxine reverses these symptoms, although it may take several weeks before you notice a difference.
Levothyroxine is usually taken for life.
What levothyroxine is not used for:
Levothyroxine is not used to shrink benign (noncancerous) thyroid nodules or a nontoxic diffuse goiter in people who get enough iodine in their diet. It does not help in these situations, and taking more thyroid hormone than your body needs can cause an overactive thyroid. It is also not used to treat hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis (inflammation of the thyroid gland).
Levothyroxine is not used to treat obesity or for weight loss.

## Before taking this medicine
You should not take ergocalciferol if you have had an allergic reaction to vitamin D, or if you have:
- high levels of vitamin D in your body (hypervitaminosis D);
- high levels of calcium in your blood (hypercalcemia); or

- kidney disease; or
- an electrolyte imbalance.

## What other drugs will affect sertraline?
Several medicines interact with sertraline. Give a full list of everything you take to any provider who treats you. The most important interactions are:
- MAOIs. Taking sertraline with an MAOI raises the risk of serotonin syndrome, and the combination is contraindicated. Examples include selegiline, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid, phenelzine, linezolid, and methylene blue.
- Pimozide. Sertraline raises pimozide levels, which can lead to QTc prolongation and irregular heartbeats. The combination is contraindicated.
- Other medicines that raise serotonin. These add to the risk of serotonin syndrome. Examples include other SSRIs and SNRIs, triptans for migraine, tricyclic antidepressants, opioids, lithium, tryptophan, buspirone, amphetamines, and St. John's wort.
- Blood thinners and antiplatelet medicines. Aspirin, clopidogrel, heparin, and warfarin can add to the bleeding risk. If you take warfarin, your INR should be monitored carefully.
- Medicines broken down by CYP2D6. Sertraline blocks this liver enzyme, so levels of these drugs can rise and doses may need to be lowered. Examples include propafenone, flecainide, atomoxetine, desipramine, dextromethorphan, metoprolol, nebivolol, perphenazine, thioridazine, tolterodine, and venlafaxine.
- Phenytoin and fosphenytoin. Sertraline can raise phenytoin levels, so levels should be checked when sertraline is started or the dose is changed.
- Medicines that prolong the QTc interval. These should generally be avoided. Examples include certain antipsychotics (ziprasidone, iloperidone, chlorpromazine, mesoridazine, droperidol), certain antibiotics (erythromycin, gatifloxacin, moxifloxacin, sparfloxacin), Class 1A antiarrhythmics (quinidine, procainamide), Class III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol), and others including pentamidine, methadone, halofantrine, mefloquine, dolasetron, probucol, and tacrolimus.
- Disulfiram, with the oral solution only, because of its alcohol content.
No dose adjustment is needed when sertraline is taken with cimetidine, diazepam, lithium, atenolol, tolbutamide, digoxin, or medicines broken down by CYP3A4.
This list is not complete. Many other prescription medicines, over-the-counter products, vitamins, and herbal products can interact with sertraline.

## Fluoxetine Side Effects
Like all medications, Prozac can cause side effects. Not everyone experiences them, and many improve after the first few weeks as your body adjusts to the medication. Tell your doctor if any side effects bother you or do not go away.
Common Fluoxetine Side Effects:
The most commonly reported side effects of fluoxetine (Prozac) include:
- Nausea
- Trouble sleeping (insomnia)
- Drowsiness or sleepiness
- Anxiety or feeling nervous or on edge
- Trembling or shaking (tremor)
- Excessive sweating
- Loss of appetite
- Diarrhea
- Dry mouth
- Indigestion or upset stomach
- Weakness or fatigue
- Sore throat
- Sinus congestion or infection
- Flu-like symptoms
- Skin rash
- Flushing or feeling of warmth
- Yawning
- Unusual or vivid dreams
- Decreased sex drive
- Difficulty getting or keeping an erection
- Delayed or abnormal ejaculation
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to this medicine (hives, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).
Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor, such as mood or behavior changes, anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, hyperactive (mentally or physically), more depressed, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself.
This medicine may cause serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- blurred vision, tunnel vision, eye pain or swelling, or seeing halos around lights;
- fast or pounding heartbeats, fluttering in your chest, shortness of breath, and sudden dizziness (like you might pass out);
- low levels of sodium in the body - headache, confusion, slurred speech, severe weakness, vomiting, loss of coordination, feeling unsteady; or
- severe nervous system reaction - very stiff (rigid) muscles, high fever, sweating, confusion, fast or uneven heartbeats, tremors, feeling like you might pass out.
Seek medical attention right away if you have symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as: agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is gabapentin?
Gabapentin is a prescription medicine used to treat partial seizures, nerve pain from shingles (postherpetic neuralgia), and restless legs syndrome (Horizant brand only). It may also be prescribed off-label for other conditions including diabetic nerve pain, anxiety, and fibromyalgia. Gabapentin is thought to work by calming overactive nerve signals in the brain and nervous system. It is an anticonvulsant and nerve pain medication from the drug class gabapentinoids
Gabapentin brand names are Neurontin, Gralise, Horizant, and Relgaabi, which may not be interchangeable.
Gabapentin is not a federally controlled substance, but some states classify it as Schedule V and others require gabapentin prescriptions to be reported to their prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP). Rules on refills and quantity limits vary by state.
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), and swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema). These often improve as your body adjusts, but do not drive until you know how gabapentin affects you.

## Before taking this medicine
Tell your doctor about all your medical conditions and medications before starting fluoxetine (Prozac), as some may interact with it or affect whether it is safe for you.
Tell your doctor if you take any of the following medications or supplements:
- Triptans (for migraine)
- Antidepressants or mood stabilizers, including SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, MAOIs, lithium, buspirone, or antipsychotics
- Amphetamines
- Opioid pain medications, including tramadol, fentanyl, meperidine, or methadone
- Over-the-counter supplements such as St. John's Wort or tryptophan
- Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
Many of these combinations can increase the risk of serotonin syndrome, a potentially serious condition.
Tell your doctor if you have or have had any of the following:
- Liver, kidney, or heart problems
- Seizures or epilepsy
- Bipolar disorder or mania
- Low sodium levels in the blood
- A stroke or high blood pressure
- Bleeding problems
Pregnancy
Tell your healthcare provider if you are pregnant, become pregnant, or plan to become pregnant while taking fluoxetine tablets. Using fluoxetine later in pregnancy may increase the risk of complications in the newborn, including problems that need a longer hospital stay, breathing support, or tube feeding, and a serious lung condition called persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Untreated depression also carries risks in pregnancy, so discuss the benefits and risks of treatment with your healthcare provider rather than stopping on your own.
If you become pregnant while taking fluoxetine tablets, ask your healthcare provider about joining the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants, which tracks pregnancy outcomes in women who take these medicines. You can enroll by calling 1-866-961-2388 or visiting womensmentalhealth.org.
Breastfeeding:
Fluoxetine passes into breast milk. Tell your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed, and discuss the best way to feed your baby while you are taking fluoxetine tablets. If you do breastfeed, watch your baby for agitation, irritability, poor feeding, or poor weight gain, and seek medical advice if you notice any of these.
