## Dosing information
Usual adult dose for edema associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and chronic renal disease (including nephrotic syndrome):
Oral: initial dose 20 to 80 mg orally once. This may be repeated at the same dose or increased by 20 or 40 mg no sooner than 6 to 8 hours after the previous dose, until the desired diuretic effect has been obtained.
Maintenance dose: administer the dose that provided the desired diuretic effect once or twice a day (for example, at 8 am and 2 pm).
Comments: edema may be most efficiently and safely mobilized by giving this drug on 2 to 4 consecutive days each week. When doses greater than 80 mg/day are given for prolonged periods, careful clinical observation and laboratory monitoring are particularly advisable.
Usual Furoscix adult and pediatric 43 kg and above dose (ReadyFlow autoinjector):
- 80 mg of furosemide given subcutaneously in about 10 seconds.
Usual Furoscix adult and pediatric 43 kg and above dose (On-Body Infusor):
- 30 mg of furosemide over the first hour, then 12.5 mg per hour for the subsequent 4 hours. This dose is delivered automatically by the On-Body Infusor.
- In children weighing at least 43 kg, the device must be applied by a healthcare provider or adult caregiver.
Furoscix is not for chronic use and should be replaced with oral diuretics as soon as practical. People with significantly reduced kidney function may need additional diuretic therapy, because both Furoscix devices deliver a fixed 80 mg dose.
Usual adult furosemide dose for pulmonary edema:
IV: 40 mg IV slowly over 1 to 2 minutes. If a satisfactory response does not occur within one hour, this may be increased to 80 mg IV slowly over 1 to 2 minutes.
Use: adjunctive therapy in acute pulmonary edema. IV administration is indicated when a rapid onset of diuresis is desired.
Usual adult furosemide dose for hypertension:
Oral: initial dose 80 mg/day, usually divided into 40 mg orally twice a day.
Use: treatment of hypertension alone or in combination with other antihypertensive agents.
Usual pediatric furosemide oral dose for edema:
Initial dose: 2 mg/kg orally once. If the diuretic response to the initial dose is not satisfactory, this may be increased by 1 or 2 mg/kg, given no sooner than 6 to 8 hours after the previous dose. Doses greater than 6 mg/kg body weight are not recommended.
Maintenance dose: adjust to the minimum effective dose.
Use: treatment of edema associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver and renal disease, including the nephrotic syndrome, especially when an agent with greater diuretic potential is desired.

## Cyclobenzaprine dosage
The usual cyclobenzaprine dose for muscle spasm is 5 mg three times a day, which may be increased to 10 mg three times a day if needed. The maximum dose is 30 mg per day. Cyclobenzaprine is taken for a maximum of 2 to 3 weeks. 1
Cyclobenzaprine dosage chart:
Immediate-release tablets: the usual starting dose is 5 mg three times a day, increased to 10 mg three times a day based on your response. In adults 65 and older and in people with mild liver problems, treatment should start at 5 mg and be increased slowly, if at all. The tablets are not recommended with moderate to severe liver impairment. 1
Amrix extended-release capsules: the recommended dose is 15 mg once daily for most adults; some people may need 30 mg once daily (one 30 mg capsule or two 15 mg capsules). Amrix is not recommended in adults 65 and older, or in anyone with liver impairment of any severity. 2
Tonmya sublingual tablets (fibromyalgia): The recommended starting dose of Tonmya is 2.8 mg (1 sublingual tablet) once daily at bedtime for the first 14 days, then increases to the target dose of 5.6 mg (2 sublingual tablets) once daily at bedtime from day 15 onward. The maximum is 5.6 mg once daily. In adults 65 and older and in people with mild liver impairment, the maximum is 2.8 mg once daily at bedtime, and Tonmya is not recommended with moderate or severe liver impairment. 3
Product | Usual adult dose | Maximum dose | How long
Immediate-release tablets, formerly sold as Flexeril (adults and children 15 and older) | 5 mg three times a day, increased to 10 mg three times a day if needed | 30 mg per day (10 mg three times a day) | Up to 2 to 3 weeks
Amrix extended-release capsules | 15 mg once daily | 30 mg once daily | Up to 2 to 3 weeks
Tonmya sublingual tablets (fibromyalgia) | 2.8 mg once daily at bedtime for 14 days, then 5.6 mg once daily at bedtime | 5.6 mg once daily | Ongoing, as directed
1,2,3
Can I take 2 cyclobenzaprine 10 mg at the same time?:
No. Do not take two cyclobenzaprine 10 mg tablets at once. The maximum recommended single dose of the immediate-release tablet is 10 mg, taken up to three times a day. Taking 20 mg at one time increases the risk of side effects such as severe drowsiness and fast heart rate, and in overdose cyclobenzaprine can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems, without providing better muscle spasm relief. If your dose is not controlling your symptoms, talk with your doctor rather than doubling up. 1
How often can you take cyclobenzaprine?:
Immediate-release tablets are taken three times a day. Amrix extended-release capsules and Tonmya sublingual tablets are taken once a day. Do not take extra doses between scheduled doses. 1,2,3
How long does cyclobenzaprine take to work, and how long does it last?:
In clinical trials of the immediate-release tablets, the muscle relaxant effect was measurable within the first several days, with significant improvement in muscle spasm and pain by day 3 or 4 of treatment. 1
With Amrix extended-release capsules, the drug is first detectable in the blood about 1.5 hours after a dose, with peak levels at 7 to 8 hours, and one daily dose provides day-long coverage. 2
How long does cyclobenzaprine stay in your system?:
Cyclobenzaprine stays in your system for about 3 to 7 days after your last dose. It has a half-life of around 18 hours for the immediate-release tablets, and a drug takes 4 to 5 half-lives to clear from the body. 1
The once-daily forms last longer: the half-life is about 32 hours for Amrix extended-release capsules and about 36 hours for Tonmya sublingual tablets, so these can take a week or more to fully clear. Cyclobenzaprine also stays in the body longer in older adults and in people with liver problems, in whom blood levels run higher. 1,2,3
Does cyclobenzaprine show up on a drug test?:
No, cyclobenzaprine does not usually show up on a drug test, as it is not a controlled substance and it is not one of the five substances (amphetamines, cannabinoids, cocaine, opiates, and phencyclidine) required on standard federal workplace drug tests. 3,5
However, cyclobenzaprine has a similar structure to tricyclic antidepressants, and it is a recognized cause of false positive results on tricyclic antidepressant immunoassays, including urine immunoassays. Tests for tricyclic antidepressants are not part of routine drugs-of-abuse screening. 5
If you take cyclobenzaprine and need a drug test, tell the testing provider what medicines you take. A screening result is only presumptive, and a confirmatory laboratory test such as gas chromatography-mass spectrometry can tell cyclobenzaprine apart from a tricyclic antidepressant. 5

Patients 12 years and older Dose: starting dose gabapentin 300 mg 3 times a day, which may be titrated up to a maximum dose of 600 mg 3 times a day if needed.

Rosuvastatin is used:

## What are the side effects of hydroxyzine?
The most common side effects of hydroxyzine are drowsiness, dry mouth, and headache. These are usually mild and do not last long.
A skin rash is different. If you develop a rash while taking hydroxyzine, stop taking it and call your doctor, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction.
Common side effects:
Common hydroxyzine side effects include dry mouth, headache, and drowsiness. The drowsiness is usually temporary and may go away after a few days of treatment or when the dose is lowered.
Serious side effects:
Stop taking hydroxyzine and call your doctor right away if you develop a skin rash, if a skin condition you are treating gets worse, or if you have any other sign of an allergic reaction.
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.
If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given. In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may happen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is allopurinol?
Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors. It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body. High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur. Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid that builds up in the blood as tumors break down in people with certain types of cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy medications. It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

## What is metoprolol used for?
Metoprolol is FDA-approved to treat high blood pressure, angina, heart failure, and heart attack, but the two forms are not approved for the same conditions.
Condition | Metoprolol tartrate (immediate release) | Metoprolol succinate (extended release)
High blood pressure (hypertension) in adults | Yes | Yes
High blood pressure in children 6 years and older | No | Yes
Angina (chest pain) | Yes | Yes
Heart failure | No | Yes
Heart attack (myocardial infarction) | Yes | No
High blood pressure (hypertension). Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal heart and blood vessel events, mainly strokes and heart attacks. Metoprolol can be used on its own or with other blood pressure medicines. Many people need more than one medicine to reach their blood pressure goal.
Angina. Metoprolol is used for long-term treatment of angina, to reduce how often attacks happen and to help you do more before chest pain starts. It is not used to stop an attack that has already begun.
Heart failure. Only the extended-release form is approved for heart failure. It is used to reduce the risk of dying from heart and blood vessel causes and to reduce hospital admissions for heart failure.
Heart attack (myocardial infarction). Metoprolol tartrate is used in people whose blood pressure and circulation are stable after a definite or suspected heart attack, to reduce the risk of dying from heart and blood vessel causes. In hospital, it may be started as an injection into a vein and then continued as tablets.

## Warnings
Cetirizine can cause side effects that may impair your thinking or reactions. Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be awake and alert. Avoid drinking alcohol. It can increase some of the side effects of cetirizine.
Tell your doctor if you regularly use other medicines that make you sleepy (such as other cold or allergy medicine, narcotic pain medicine, sleeping pills, muscle relaxers, and medicine for seizures, depression, or anxiety). They can add to sleepiness caused by cetirizine.
Call your doctor if your symptoms do not improve, if they get worse, or if you also have a fever.

Rarely, some people have reported severe itching when stopping cetirizine after daily, long-term use of at least a few months or several years. If you experience widespread, severe itching on stopping this medication, contact your healthcare provider.

## How should I use furosemide?
Take or administer furosemide exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Furosemide oral tablets and liquid are taken by mouth. Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device, not a kitchen spoon.
Furosemide injection is given in a muscle, under the skin, or in a vein. A healthcare provider will give you this injection if you are unable to take the medicine by mouth.
Using subcutaneous furosemide at home:
You or your caregiver should be trained before your first dose, and you should read the Instructions for Use that comes with your prescription. Wash your hands first, and check that the liquid is clear and colorless to slightly yellow. Do not use it if you see particles or if it is cloudy or discolored.
Subcutaneous furosemide is given into the abdomen only, and you should use a different spot on the abdomen each time.
Furoscix ReadyFlow autoinjector
- Choose a site at least two inches from your belly button, avoiding skin that is broken or irritated and any scars or stretch marks. Clean it and let it dry.
- Pull the blue cap straight off, then press the device firmly against your skin and hold it there for about 10 seconds, until the yellow plunger rod stops moving and fills the viewing window.
- If you lift the device away before the window is completely yellow, you may not get the full dose. Call your healthcare provider if this happens, and do not use a second device unless you are told to.
Furoscix On-Body Infusor and Lasix ONYU Infusor
- The infusion takes about 5 hours, so plan to stay somewhere you can relax and reach a bathroom.
- Apply the device to a flat, clean, hairless area of the abdomen below the rib cage and above the belt line, and press it firmly into place. Do not remove and reapply it.
- Limit your activity while wearing it and avoid bending as much as you can. Do not exercise or do anything that might knock it off.
- Do not get the infusor wet. Do not bathe, shower, or swim while wearing it, and do not apply lotions or creams to the area where it is placed.
- Traveling by car or airplane while wearing the infusor is not recommended, and the Furoscix On-Body Infusor cannot be used in an MRI setting.
- Do not use the infusor within 12 inches of mobile phones, tablets, computers, or wireless accessories such as a remote control or Bluetooth device.
- Your healthcare provider will show you what the indicator light and alarms mean. You must use the infusor in a setting where you can detect and respond to these alarms to ensure you receive the full dose. If the device falls off, or the light blinks red, call your healthcare provider and do not reuse it.
Dispose of used autoinjectors, infusors, and cartridges in a sharps container. Do not put them in household trash and do not recycle them.
General furosemide dosing information:
Do not use more than your recommended dose. High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
This medicine will make you urinate more often, and you may get dehydrated easily. Follow your doctor's instructions about using potassium supplements or getting enough salt and potassium in your diet.
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often, and you may need other medical tests.
If you have high blood pressure, keep using furosemide even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
If you need surgery, tell the surgeon ahead of time that you are using furosemide.

Data have revealed that monotherapy with daily doses of 40 mg have been associated with complete duodenal ulcer healing in up to 87% and 94% of patients after 4 weeks and 8 weeks respectively.

Common insulin glargine side effects may include low blood sugar, swelling, weight gain, allergic reaction, itching, rash, or thickening or hollowing of the skin where you injected the medicine (lipodystrophy).
Serious insulin glargine side effects
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of insulin allergy: redness or swelling where an injection was given, itchy skin rash over the entire body, trouble breathing, fast heartbeats, feeling like you might pass out, or swelling in your tongue or throat.
Insulin glargine may cause other serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- rapid weight gain, swelling in your feet or ankles;
- shortness of breath; or

## How should I take empagliflozin?
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose. Use the medicine exactly as directed.
Take empagliflozin once a day in the morning, with or without food.
Your blood sugar will need to be checked often, and you may also need to test the level of ketones in your urine. Empagliflozin can cause life-threatening ketoacidosis (too much acid in the blood). Even if your blood sugar is normal, contact your doctor if a urine test shows that you have high ketones in the urine.
Blood sugar can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can make you feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, or shaky. To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink hard candy, crackers, raisins, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. Your doctor may prescribe glucagon injection in case of severe hypoglycemia.
You may get dehydrated during prolonged illness. Call your doctor if you are sick with vomiting or diarrhea.
This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests. Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using empagliflozin.
Your treatment may also include diet, exercise, weight control, and special medical care.
Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat.

## Warnings
Respiratory depression. Gabapentin can cause life-threatening breathing problems (respiratory depression), especially if you already have a breathing disorder (such as COPD), are elderly, or if you use other medicines that can make you drowsy or slow your breathing, such as opioids or CNS depressants. Seek emergency medical attention if you have very slow breathing.
Suicidal thoughts or behaviors. Some people have thoughts about suicide while taking and after discontinuing this medicine. Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms. Tell your doctor right away if you have any sudden changes in mood or behavior, or thoughts about suicide.
Abrupt or rapid discontinuation. Seizures may occur if you stop using gabapentin suddenly. Ask your doctor before stopping the medicine. Stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms such as anxiety, trouble sleeping, nausea, pain, and sweating.
Sleepiness, sedation, and dizziness. Avoid driving or participating in hazardous activities until you know how gabapentin will affect you. Dizziness or drowsiness can cause falls, accidents, or severe injuries.
Brand substitution. Brands of gabapentin may not be interchangeable.

## Warnings and precautions
Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole. These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up, which may make you feel dizzy or faint. This is most likely when you first start taking it, when your dose changes, or when you start it again after a break. Get up slowly from sitting or lying down. Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases (probably fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients), tamsulosin can cause priapism, a painful erection that lasts a long time and is not related to sexual activity. Get medical help straight away if this happens, because without prompt treatment it can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction.
An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together. Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.
Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery. Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken it in the past, even if you stopped months ago. Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to. If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again. You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose.
Many other medicines can interact with tamsulosin. Tell your doctor about everything you take, including prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

## Warnings
You should not take bupropion if you have seizures, an eating disorder, or suddenly stopped using alcohol, seizure medication, or sedatives. You should not take two medicines together that contain bupropion for example, if you take Wellbutrin for depression, you should not also take Contrave for weight control or Aplenzin for depression.
Do not use bupropion within 14 days before or 14 days after you have used a MAO inhibitors, such as isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, or tranylcypromine.
Some young people (up to 24 years of age) have thoughts about suicide when first taking this medicine. Stay alert to changes in your mood or symptoms. Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor.
You should know that your mental health may change in unexpected ways when you take bupropion or other antidepressants even if you are an adult over age 24 or if you do not have a mental illness and you are taking bupropion to treat a different type of condition. You may become suicidal, especially at the beginning of your treatment and any time that your dose is increased or decreased. You, your family, or your caregiver should call your doctor right away if you experience any of the following symptoms: new or worsening depression; thinking about harming or killing yourself, or planning or trying to do so; extreme worry; agitation; panic attacks; difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep; aggressive behavior; irritability; acting without thinking; severe restlessness; and frenzied abnormal excitement. Be sure that your family or caregiver knows which symptoms may be serious so they can call the doctor if you are unable to seek treatment on your own.
This medicine may cause seizures, especially in people with certain medical conditions or when using certain drugs. Tell your doctor about all of your medical conditions and the drugs you use.
Bupropion can cause mild pupillary dilation, which can lead to an episode of angle-closure glaucoma in susceptible individuals. Angle-closure glaucoma has occurred in patients with untreated anatomically narrow angles treated with antidepressants.

## How should I use Flonase Nasal Spray?
Use Flonase exactly as directed on the label, or as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Do not share this medicine with another person, even if they have the same symptoms you have. Sharing a bottle can spread germs.
Your dose will depend on the fluticasone brand or strength you use, and your dose may change once your symptoms improve. Follow all dosing instructions very carefully.
- A child using the nasal spray should be supervised by an adult.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Shake the bottle before each use. Flonase Allergy Relief should be shaken gently, and Flonase Sensimist should be shaken vigorously.
Use this product only once a day and do not use more than directed. Avoid getting the spray in your eyes or mouth.
If you switched to fluticasone from another steroid medicine, you should not stop using it suddenly. Follow your doctor's instructions about tapering your dose.
Storage differs between products. Store Flonase Allergy Relief and Children's Flonase Allergy Relief between 4°C and 30°C (39°F and 86°F). Store Flonase Sensimist between 15°C and 30°C (59°F and 86°F), and do not refrigerate or freeze it.
Throw the bottle away once you have used the number of sprays stated on the carton, even if there is still liquid in the bottle. The correct amount of medicine in each spray cannot be assured after the labeled number of sprays has been used. Bottle sizes vary between products and pack sizes, ranging from 30 to 144 metered sprays.
Dosing information:
Usual Adult Dose for Rhinitis (adults and children 12 years of age and older):
Flonase Allergy Relief Nasal Spray (fluticasone propionate 50 mcg per spray):
- Week 1: use 2 sprays in each nostril once daily
- Week 2 through 6 months: use 1 or 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, as needed to treat your symptoms
- After 6 months of daily use: ask your doctor if you can keep using this medicine
Flonase Sensimist Nasal Spray (fluticasone furoate 27.5 mcg per spray):
- Week 1: use 2 sprays in each nostril once daily
- Week 2 through 6 months: use 1 or 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, as needed to treat your symptoms
- After 6 months of daily use: ask your doctor if you can keep using this medicine
Usual Pediatric Dose for Rhinitis:
- 4 to 11 years: Flonase Allergy Relief or Children's Flonase Allergy Relief (fluticasone propionate 50 mcg per spray): 1 spray in each nostril once daily.
- 2 to 11 years: Flonase Sensimist or Children's Flonase Sensimist (fluticasone furoate 27.5 mcg per spray): 1 spray in each nostril once daily.
- Under 4 years: do not use fluticasone propionate nasal spray.
- Under 2 years: do not use fluticasone furoate nasal spray.
An adult should supervise a child using the spray. Children should use it for the shortest amount of time necessary to achieve symptom relief. Talk to your child's doctor if your child needs to use the spray for longer than two months a year.
What happens if I miss a dose?:
Use the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not use two doses at one time.
What happens if I overdose?:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
An overdose of Flonase is not expected to produce life-threatening symptoms. Using more than the recommended dose, or using it for longer than directed, may increase the chance of corticosteroid-related side effects such as cataracts or glaucoma, adrenal gland problems, an increased risk of infection, sores inside the nose, or slower growth in children.

## Metoprolol dosage
The usual starting dose is 25 mg to 100 mg once a day for extended-release metoprolol, and 100 mg a day for immediate-release metoprolol. Your dose is then adjusted at intervals of a week or longer until your blood pressure or symptoms are controlled.
Metoprolol tartrate (immediate-release tablets) dosage for adults:
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range
High blood pressure | 100 mg a day, as one dose or split into two | 100 mg to 450 mg a day. Doses above 450 mg a day have not been studied.
Angina | 100 mg a day, split into two doses | 100 mg to 400 mg a day. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
After a heart attack | 50 mg every 6 hours for 48 hours, starting 15 minutes after the last dose given into a vein. If the full intravenous dose was not tolerated, 25 mg is used. | Maintenance is 100 mg twice a day, continued for at least 3 months.
With immediate-release tablets, a once-daily dose may not keep blood pressure controlled for the full 24 hours, especially at 100 mg. Splitting the dose or taking a larger daily dose may be needed.
Metoprolol succinate (extended-release tablets and capsules) dosage for adults:
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range
High blood pressure | 25 mg to 100 mg once a day | Adjust weekly or less often. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
Angina | 100 mg once a day | Increase weekly until symptoms are controlled or your heart rate slows noticeably. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
Heart failure | 25 mg once a day for two weeks, or 12.5 mg once a day in more severe heart failure | Double the dose every two weeks to the highest dose you tolerate, up to 200 mg once a day.
Kapspargo Sprinkle capsules are not suitable to start heart failure treatment if a dose below 25 mg is needed.
Metoprolol dosage for children:
Extended-release metoprolol is the only form approved for children, and only for high blood pressure in children aged 6 years and older. The starting dose is 1 mg for each kilogram of body weight once a day, up to a maximum first dose of 50 mg. Doses above 2 mg/kg, or above 200 mg a day, have not been studied. Extended-release metoprolol has not been studied in children under 6 years.
Dose adjustments:
- Liver problems. Start at a lower dose than usual and increase slowly.
- Kidney problems. No dose reduction is needed.
- Older adults. A low starting dose is generally used, because liver, kidney, and heart function are more often reduced and other medicines are more often involved.
- Switching between forms. When changing from immediate-release to extended-release metoprolol, the same total daily dose is used.

Boxed warning for lactic acidosis:
Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
This is an extremely rare side effect but certain things can raise your risk of lactic acidosis, including kidney problems, taking certain other medicines, being over 65, having an imaging test that uses contrast dye, having surgery or other medical procedures, conditions that lower oxygen levels in the body, drinking too much alcohol, liver problems, and certain rare inherited metabolic disorders (mitochondrial diseases).

- have unusual (not normal) muscle pain
- have trouble breathing
- have unusual sleepiness or sleep longer than usual
- have unexplained stomach or intestinal problems with nausea and vomiting, or diarrhea
- cold, especially in your arms and legs

## What are the side effects of hydroxyzine?
The most common side effects of hydroxyzine are drowsiness, dry mouth, and headache. These are usually mild and do not last long.
A skin rash is different. If you develop a rash while taking hydroxyzine, stop taking it and call your doctor, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction.
Common side effects:
Common hydroxyzine side effects include dry mouth, headache, and drowsiness. The drowsiness is usually temporary and may go away after a few days of treatment or when the dose is lowered.
Serious side effects:
Stop taking hydroxyzine and call your doctor right away if you develop a skin rash, if a skin condition you are treating gets worse, or if you have any other sign of an allergic reaction.

## Warning and precautions
Fluid and salt imbalance:
Hydrochlorothiazide can lower the levels of potassium, sodium, magnesium and chloride in your blood. Low potassium (hypokalemia) is the most common of these and is more likely at higher doses, during rapid fluid loss, if you have severe cirrhosis, or after long-term use.. Your doctor will check your blood before you start and at intervals during treatment.
Contact your doctor if you have any of the following, which can be signs of a fluid or salt imbalance:
- dry mouth, thirst, or unusual weakness or tiredness
- drowsiness, restlessness or confusion
- muscle pain, cramps or muscle fatigue
- fast heartbeat
- passing much less urine than usual
- nausea or vomiting
- seizures
Kidney and liver problems:
HCTZ reduces the fluid volume in your body, which can lead to sudden kidney injury. The risk is higher if you have chronic kidney disease, heart failure, or are already low on fluid. If you have liver disease, small changes in fluid and salt balance can trigger a serious complication called hepatic coma. Your doctor will monitor your kidney function and watch for changes in alertness.
Sudden vision changes need urgent care:
Rarely, hydrochlorothiazide causes sudden short-sightedness (acute myopia) and a sharp rise in pressure inside the eye (acute angle-closure glaucoma), usually within hours to weeks of starting the medicine. Stop taking it and get medical help immediately if your vision drops suddenly or your eye hurts. Left untreated, this can cause permanent loss of vision. A history of allergy to sulfa medicines or penicillin may increase the risk.
Blood sugar, cholesterol, uric acid and calcium:
Hydrochlorothiazide can raise blood sugar, cholesterol, triglycerides, uric acid and calcium. Your diabetes medicine or insulin dose may need adjusting, and diabetes that was previously unnoticed can become apparent during treatment. The rise in uric acid is related to the dose and can cause gout or make existing gout worse. Because the medicine also affects calcium, it is stopped before parathyroid function tests, so tell any doctor arranging tests that you take it. Your doctor will check these levels from time to time.
Skin cancer risk:
Long-term use of hydrochlorothiazide is linked to a small increase in the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer, mainly squamous cell carcinoma. In a large safety study the increase was about 1 extra case per 16,000 people per year, rising to about 1 extra case per 6,700 people per year among white patients who had taken a total of 50,000 mg or more.
Protect your skin from the sun, wear protective clothing and use sunscreen, avoid sunlamps and tanning beds, and have regular skin checks. Tell your doctor about any new or changing skin growth, or a sore that does not heal.
Lupus and allergic reactions:
Thiazide diuretics have been reported to worsen lupus or bring it on. Sensitivity reactions can happen whether or not you have a history of allergies or asthma.

## What other drugs will affect metformin?
Many drugs can interact with metformin; this includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here. Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any medicine you start or stop using.
Medicines that have a carbonic anhydrase inhibiting effect like topiramate (often used for seizures or migraines), zonisamide (used for seizures), acetazolamide (used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, and other conditions), and dichlorphenamide (used for a muscle condition called periodic paralysis) can raise the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis when taken with metformin. These medicines commonly lower a substance in your blood called bicarbonate, which your body needs to keep its acid levels balanced. If you're taking metformin along with any of these medicines, your doctor may want to monitor you more closely.
Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.
Insulin or other diabetes medicines that raise insulin (like sulfonylureas): Combining these with metformin can lower your blood sugar too much. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you're taking more than one diabetes medicine.
Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis.
Contrast dye used in imaging tests (like CT scans): This type of dye can temporarily affect kidney function, which can let metformin build up in your body. Your doctor may have you stop taking metformin around the time of the test and restart it once your kidney function is confirmed to be back to normal.

## Sertraline FAQs
Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline has very little effect on norepinephrine and dopamine, and it has no meaningful effect on adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopamine, histamine, or benzodiazepine receptors, which is part of why it is described as selective.
How long does sertraline take to work?:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.
Should I take sertraline in the morning or at night?:
Either is fine. Sertraline is taken once a day, in the morning or the evening, and the label does not favor one over the other. What matters more is taking it at around the same time each day. Insomnia was reported by 20% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 13% on placebo, and sleepiness by 11% compared with 6%, so some people find one timing suits them better than the other. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does sertraline cause weight gain or weight loss?:
Reduced appetite is a common sertraline side effect, reported by 7% of adults in trials compared with 2% on placebo. Increased appetite was reported less often, in fewer than 2% of people. In children and teenagers taking sertraline for depression, there was a difference in weight change of roughly 1 kg compared with placebo over 10 weeks, representing slight weight loss on sertraline and slight gain on placebo. Around 7% of children lost more than 7% of their body weight, compared with none on placebo. In a longer 34 week extension study, weight gain was similar to what would be expected for their age. Height and weight should be monitored in younger patients. Tell your doctor about any weight change that concerns you.
Does sertraline make you tired or sleepy?:
It can. Sleepiness was reported by 11% of adults taking sertraline in trials, compared with 6% on placebo, and tiredness by 12% compared with 8%. Sertraline can also affect how clearly you think and how quickly you react, so do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.
Is sertraline a controlled substance?:
No. Sertraline is not a controlled substance. In a study comparing sertraline with alprazolam and d-amphetamine, sertraline did not produce the effects associated with a potential for misuse, such as euphoria or drug liking, that were seen with the other two medicines.
Can sertraline cause diarrhea or nausea?:
Yes, these are the two most common sertraline side effects. Nausea was reported by 26% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 12% on placebo, and diarrhea or loose stools by 20% compared with 10%. Nausea was also the most common reason people stopped treatment. Tell your doctor if these do not settle.
How do you stop taking sertraline safely?:
Lower the dose gradually rather than stopping all at once, and only under your doctor's guidance. Symptoms reported after stopping a serotonergic antidepressant, especially when it is stopped abruptly, include nausea, sweating, low or unstable mood, irritability, agitation, dizziness, unusual sensations such as electric shock feelings, tremor, anxiety, confusion, headache, lethargy, insomnia, hypomania, ringing in the ears, and seizures.
Can you drink alcohol while taking sertraline?:
Drinking alcohol is not recommended while you take sertraline. In healthy volunteers, sertraline did not increase the immediate effects of alcohol on thinking and coordination, but the advice for patients is still to avoid it. Separately, do not take sertraline oral solution with disulfiram, because the solution contains 12% alcohol.
Can you take sertraline while pregnant?:
That depends on your situation, and it is a decision to make with your doctor rather than on your own. Studies of first trimester use suggest no overall difference in the risk of major birth defects, but use late in pregnancy has been linked with newborn breathing problems and with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. At the same time, stopping an antidepressant during pregnancy raises the risk of depression coming back. The oral solution specifically is not recommended in pregnancy because it contains alcohol.
What are sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules for?:
Sertraline capsules come in 150 mg and 200 mg only, and they are not used to start treatment. They are for people who have already been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week and need a higher dose. The maximum is 200 mg a day, the same as for tablets. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not opened, crushed, or chewed. If you need to come off sertraline, the dose has to be lowered gradually using another sertraline product, because there is no capsule strength below 150 mg. Capsules are approved for depression in adults and OCD from age 6, not for panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, or PMDD.
Does sertraline interact with warfarin?:
Yes, in two ways. Sertraline can add to warfarin's effect on bleeding risk, and both medicines bind tightly to proteins in the blood, so taking them together can raise the free level of one or both. If you take warfarin with sertraline, your INR should be monitored carefully.

## Sertraline side effects
Common sertraline side effects:
The most common sertraline side effects are nausea, diarrhea or loose stools, trouble sleeping, dry mouth, tiredness, dizziness, sleepiness, tremor, indigestion, agitation, reduced appetite, increased sweating, and sexual problems.
The table below shows how often each side effect was reported in pooled placebo-controlled trials in 3,066 adults, compared with 2,293 people taking placebo.
Side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Nausea | 26% | 12%
Diarrhea or loose stools | 20% | 10%
Insomnia (trouble sleeping) | 20% | 13%
Dry mouth | 14% | 9%
Fatigue (tiredness) | 12% | 8%
Dizziness | 12% | 8%
Somnolence (sleepiness) | 11% | 6%
Tremor (shaking) | 9% | 2%
Dyspepsia (indigestion) | 8% | 4%
Agitation | 8% | 5%
Decreased appetite | 7% | 2%
Hyperhidrosis (heavy sweating) | 7% | 3%
Constipation | 6% | 4%
Decreased libido (lower sex drive) | 6% | 2%
Palpitations | 4% | 2%
Visual impairment | 4% | 2%
Vomiting | 4% | 1%
Some side effects were more common with particular conditions. Sleepiness was more common in depression trials, insomnia and agitation in OCD trials, constipation and agitation in panic disorder trials, tiredness in PTSD trials, and insomnia, dizziness, tiredness, dry mouth, and a general feeling of being unwell in social anxiety disorder trials. In PMDD trials, sleepiness, dry mouth, dizziness, tiredness, and stomach pain were more common.
In these trials, 12% of people taking sertraline stopped treatment because of a side effect, compared with 4% of people taking placebo. The most common reasons for stopping were nausea (3%), diarrhea (2%), agitation (2%), and insomnia (2%).
Sexual side effects of sertraline:
SSRIs including sertraline can cause sexual problems. In men, this can mean delayed ejaculation or being unable to ejaculate, lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. In women, it can mean lower sex drive and delayed orgasm or being unable to have an orgasm.
Sexual side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Ejaculation failure (men) | 8% | 1%
Decreased libido (men) | 7% | 2%
Erectile dysfunction (men) | 4% | 1%
Ejaculation disorder (men) | 3% | 0%
Male sexual dysfunction | 2% | 0%
Decreased libido (women) | 4% | 2%
Changes in sex drive and sexual function can also be part of depression and anxiety themselves, so the timing of when symptoms started matters. These numbers may underestimate how often sexual side effects happen, because people and their providers do not always raise the subject. Tell your provider about any change in sexual function, since there may be ways to manage it.
Serious sertraline side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to sertraline: rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of serotonin syndrome, which can be life threatening: agitation, hallucinations, confusion, coma or other changes in mental state, a racing heartbeat, high or low blood pressure, dizziness, heavy sweating, fever, muscle stiffness, twitching or overactive reflexes, loss of coordination, seizures, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea;
- unusual bleeding or bruising, including nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in vomit or stools, or black tarry stools;
- signs of a manic episode: greatly increased energy, severe trouble sleeping, racing thoughts, reckless behavior, unusually grand ideas, excessive happiness or irritability, or talking more or faster than usual;
- seizures or convulsions;
- eye pain, changes in vision, or swelling or redness in or around the eye, which can be signs of angle-closure glaucoma (a sudden rise in pressure inside the eye);
- signs of low sodium in the blood (hyponatremia): headache, trouble concentrating or thinking, memory problems, confusion, weakness, or feeling unsteady, which can lead to falls. Severe cases have caused hallucinations, fainting, seizures, coma, and death;
- fainting, chest discomfort, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation.
Sertraline side effects in children and teenagers:
The overall pattern of side effects in 281 children and teenagers treated with sertraline was generally similar to that seen in adults. Side effects reported in at least 2% of children and teenagers, and at least twice as often as with placebo, that were not common in adults were fever, hyperkinesia (abnormally increased movement), urinary incontinence, aggression, nosebleeds, purpura (purple spots under the skin), joint pain, weight loss, muscle twitching, and anxiety.
Reduced appetite and weight loss have been seen with SSRIs, so height and weight should be monitored during treatment.
Other reported side effects:
Less common side effects reported during studies include tachycardia (fast heartbeat), tinnitus (ringing in the ears), underactive thyroid, enlarged pupils, blurred vision, blood in the stools, swelling, unsteady walking, irritability, fever, raised liver enzymes, anaphylaxis, diabetes, high cholesterol, low blood sugar, increased appetite, joint pain, muscle spasms, poor coordination, coma, convulsions, reduced alertness, numbness, lethargy, restlessness, fainting, aggression, teeth grinding, confusion, euphoric mood, hallucination, blood in the urine, milk production from the breasts, priapism (a long-lasting erection), vaginal bleeding, wheezing, yawning, hair loss, cold sweats, skin inflammation, blistering, itching, rash, hives, bleeding, high blood pressure, and flushing.
Side effects reported after sertraline came onto the market include increased clotting times, AV block, slow heartbeat, atrial arrhythmias, QTc prolongation, ventricular tachycardia including Torsade de Pointes, breast enlargement in men, raised prolactin, irregular periods, SIADH, blindness, optic neuritis, cataract, severe liver problems including hepatitis, jaundice, and liver failure with some fatal outcomes, pancreatitis, several blood disorders, angioedema, low sodium, high blood sugar, rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), lockjaw, serotonin syndrome, movement disorders including akathisia and dystonia, psychosis, bedwetting, nightmares, sudden kidney failure, pulmonary hypertension, eosinophilic pneumonia, loss of smell, photosensitivity, severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, spasm of blood vessels in the brain, and vasculitis.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is lisinopril?
Lisinopril is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children 6 years of age and older.
Lisinopril is also used in adults to treat congestive heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack.
Lisinopril belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. It works by decreasing certain chemicals that tighten the blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart can pump blood more efficiently.
High blood pressure is a common condition and when not treated, can cause damage to the brain, heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and other parts of the body. ## What is the usual prednisone dosage?
The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
- There is no single standard dose. Your doctor will decide on a starting dose, then lower it in small steps to the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
- Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight, and must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days. A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days. Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes. Some people take it for a few days or weeks for a problem that will settle, such as an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction. Others take it every day for months or years for an ongoing condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or ulcerative colitis.
If you take prednisone long term, your doctor will settle you on a maintenance dose. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. It may need to go up for a time if your condition flares, or if you have surgery, a fever, an infection, or another serious illness, and it may come down again afterwards. Do not adjust it yourself.
How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Call your doctor if you feel unwell while your dose is being lowered or after you finish.

## How does hydroxyzine work?
Hydroxyzine is thought to work by quieting activity in certain deeper regions of the brain, below the outer layer known as the cortex. It is not a cortical depressant, meaning it does not work by slowing down the outer layer of the brain the way some other sedatives do.
Hydroxyzine also blocks histamine, a chemical your body releases during an allergic reaction. This is what relieves itching.
Laboratory and clinical studies have also shown that hydroxyzine relaxes skeletal muscle, widens the airways (bronchodilation), and reduces pain. These are effects that have been observed rather than uses the medicine is approved for.
Hydroxyzine has also been shown to reduce nausea and vomiting. This is an approved use for the injection, but not for the forms taken by mouth.

## How should I take buspirone?
Take buspirone exactly as it was prescribed for you. Follow all directions on your prescription label. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose to make sure you get the best results. Do not take this medicine in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended.

## Spironolactone side effects
Reported spironolactone side effects:
Reported spironolactone side effects include breast and nipple pain in both men and women, a lower sex drive, trouble getting or keeping an erection, irregular or missed periods, bleeding after menopause, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, feeling sluggish, leg cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, indigestion, hair thinning, and itching.
The most common side effect of spironolactone is breast growth in men, known as gynecomastia. In the main heart failure study, about 9 in 100 men taking an average of 26 mg a day developed it. The chance goes up on higher doses. It can start anywhere from one or two months into treatment to more than a year later, and it usually goes away after the medicine is stopped.
Several of these effects are dose-related, so they are more likely on higher doses, and many settle after the dose is lowered or the medicine is stopped. How often most of them happen is not known, because they come from reports gathered after the medicine was approved rather than from counted numbers in trials.
Serious spironolactone side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to spironolactone: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of a high potassium level (hyperkalemia), such as muscle weakness or a heavy feeling in your legs, a slow or uneven heartbeat, numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or lips, nausea, or feeling restless and on edge;
- a light-headed feeling like you might pass out, which can be a sign you have low blood pressure (hypotension)
- little or no urination, or swelling in your ankles, hands, or feet, which can be signs your kidneys are struggling (worsening renal function);
- signs of a low sodium level, such as confusion, severe weakness, muscle pain or cramps, feeling unsteady, or slurred speech;
- severe or ongoing vomiting or diarrhea, since losing too much fluid and salt can send your blood pressure and kidney function the wrong way;
- a skin rash that spreads or blisters, peeling skin, sores in your mouth, or a rash with a fever and swollen glands, which can be signs of a rare but serious skin reaction;
- yellowing of your eyes or skin, dark urine, or pain in your upper stomach, which can be signs of a liver problem;
- a fever, sore throat, or unusual bruising or bleeding, which can be signs of a problem with your blood cells; or
- new confusion, unsteadiness, or extreme drowsiness if you have liver disease, since spironolactone can make brain function worse in people with cirrhosis.
Spironolactone side effects in men:
Men are most likely to notice effects linked to spironolactone blocking male hormones. These include breast growth and breast tenderness, a lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. Breast growth is dose related, so tell your doctor early rather than waiting, since a lower dose or a different medicine may be an option.
Spironolactone side effects in women:
Women may notice irregular periods, missed periods, breast tenderness, or bleeding after menopause. Some women also notice patchy darkening of the skin on the face. Report any unexpected bleeding after menopause to your doctor so it can be checked properly rather than assumed to be a side effect.
Long-term spironolactone side effects:
The main long-term concerns with spironolactone are chemical rather than something you would feel. Over time it can push your potassium too high, and it can also lower your sodium, magnesium, and calcium, raise your blood sugar, and raise your uric acid, which occasionally brings on gout. This is why you need regular blood tests for as long as you take it, not just at the start.
In animal studies, spironolactone given at high doses over long periods caused tumors in rats, mainly in hormone-producing glands and the liver. No increase in tumors was seen at the lower doses tested, which were still around five times the highest recommended human dose when adjusted for body size. Whether this happens in people is not known.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## How should I use furosemide?
Take or administer furosemide exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Furosemide oral tablets and liquid are taken by mouth. Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device, not a kitchen spoon.
Furosemide injection is given in a muscle, under the skin, or in a vein. A healthcare provider will give you this injection if you are unable to take the medicine by mouth.
Using subcutaneous furosemide at home:
You or your caregiver should be trained before your first dose, and you should read the Instructions for Use that comes with your prescription. Wash your hands first, and check that the liquid is clear and colorless to slightly yellow. Do not use it if you see particles or if it is cloudy or discolored.
Subcutaneous furosemide is given into the abdomen only, and you should use a different spot on the abdomen each time.
Furoscix ReadyFlow autoinjector
- Choose a site at least two inches from your belly button, avoiding skin that is broken or irritated and any scars or stretch marks. Clean it and let it dry.
- Pull the blue cap straight off, then press the device firmly against your skin and hold it there for about 10 seconds, until the yellow plunger rod stops moving and fills the viewing window.
- If you lift the device away before the window is completely yellow, you may not get the full dose. Call your healthcare provider if this happens, and do not use a second device unless you are told to.
Furoscix On-Body Infusor and Lasix ONYU Infusor
- The infusion takes about 5 hours, so plan to stay somewhere you can relax and reach a bathroom.
- Apply the device to a flat, clean, hairless area of the abdomen below the rib cage and above the belt line, and press it firmly into place. Do not remove and reapply it.
- Limit your activity while wearing it and avoid bending as much as you can. Do not exercise or do anything that might knock it off.
- Do not get the infusor wet. Do not bathe, shower, or swim while wearing it, and do not apply lotions or creams to the area where it is placed.
- Traveling by car or airplane while wearing the infusor is not recommended, and the Furoscix On-Body Infusor cannot be used in an MRI setting.
- Do not use the infusor within 12 inches of mobile phones, tablets, computers, or wireless accessories such as a remote control or Bluetooth device.
- Your healthcare provider will show you what the indicator light and alarms mean. You must use the infusor in a setting where you can detect and respond to these alarms to ensure you receive the full dose. If the device falls off, or the light blinks red, call your healthcare provider and do not reuse it.
Dispose of used autoinjectors, infusors, and cartridges in a sharps container. Do not put them in household trash and do not recycle them.
General furosemide dosing information:
Do not use more than your recommended dose. High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
This medicine will make you urinate more often, and you may get dehydrated easily. Follow your doctor's instructions about using potassium supplements or getting enough salt and potassium in your diet.
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often, and you may need other medical tests.
If you have high blood pressure, keep using furosemide even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
If you need surgery, tell the surgeon ahead of time that you are using furosemide.

## Dosing Information
Adult Tramadol Dosage for Pain:
Immediate-release formulations (tablets and oral solution)
- Treatment usually starts at 25 mg a day, increasing by 25 mg every 3 days to reach 100 mg a day (25 mg four times a day). Doses of 25 mg are measured using the oral solution, as immediate-release tramadol tablets are only available as 50 mg.
- For the immediate-release tablets, a common starting dose is one 50 mg tablet a day to see how well you tolerate it, or the dose prescribed by your doctor.
- If needed, the total daily dose can then be increased by 50 mg every 3 days as tolerated, to reach 200 mg a day (one 50 mg tablet four times a day).
- After this titration, 50 mg to 100 mg (one or two 50 mg tablets) can be taken every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain.
- The maximum is 400 mg a day: eight 50 mg tablets in divided doses, or 80 mL of the 5 mg/mL oral solution.
Extended-release capsules and tablets
- Tramadol ER 100 mg once a day (one 100 mg tablet or capsule) at approximately the same time each day.
- Can be increased by 100 mg every 5 days if needed, to a maximum of 300 mg a day, taken as one dose once a day.
- Extended-release tramadol is not intended for as-needed pain relief, and should not be taken with any other tramadol product.
Dosage in kidney or liver impairment
- Severe kidney impairment: for immediate-release tramadol, doses are spaced 12 hours apart, and the maximum is 200 mg a day (four 50 mg tablets, given as two 100 mg doses 12 hours apart).
- Severe liver impairment: for immediate-release tramadol, the recommended dose is 50 mg (one 50 mg tablet) every 12 hours, which is 100 mg a day.
- Extended-release tramadol is not recommended for people with severe kidney or severe liver impairment.
Dosage in older adults
- No separate maximum dose applies on the basis of age, but tramadol should be started at the low end of the dosing range and increased slowly, with frequent review for drowsiness and breathing problems.
- Side effects that led people to stop treatment were more common over the age of 75, mostly stomach and bowel effects, such as constipation. Kidney function also tends to decline with age, which affects how tramadol is cleared, so your doctor may take this into account when choosing your dose.

## How should I take potassium chloride?
Take potassium chloride exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Take potassium chloride with a full glass of water. Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.
Measure liquid medicine with the dosing syringe provided, or with a special dose-measuring spoon or medicine cup. If you do not have a dose-measuring device, ask your pharmacist for one.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on a tablet or capsule. Sucking on the pill could irritate your mouth or throat.
Call your doctor if you have trouble swallowing a potassium chloride capsule or tablet. You may be able to dissolve the tablet in water, or mix the medicine from a capsule with soft food. Carefully follow your doctor's instructions.
Mix the powder form of this medicine with at least 4 ounces (one-half cup) of cold water or fruit juice before taking. Drink the mixture slowly, over 5 to 10 minutes in all. To make sure you get the entire dose, add a little more water to the same glass, swirl gently and drink right away.
To be sure this medicine is helping your condition, you may need frequent blood tests. You may not notice any change in your symptoms, but your blood work will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium chloride. Your heart function may need to be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG). Even if you have no symptoms, tests can help your doctor determine if this medicine is effective.
Your treatment may include a special diet. Follow the diet plan created for you by your doctor or nutrition counselor. Get familiar with the list of foods you should eat or avoid to help control your condition.
Potassium-rich foods include: squash, baked potatoes (skin on), spinach, lentils, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, zucchini, kidney or navy beans, raisins, watermelon, orange juice, bananas, cantaloupe, and low-fat milk or yogurt. Consume only the daily amounts recommended by your doctor or nutrition counselor.
Some tablets are made with a shell that is not absorbed or melted in the body. Part of this shell may appear in your stool. This is normal and will not make the medicine less effective.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat. Keep the medication in a closed container.

## What is the usual prednisone dosage?
The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
- There is no single standard dose. Your doctor will decide on a starting dose, then lower it in small steps to the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
- Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight, and must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days. A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days. Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes. Some people take it for a few days or weeks for a problem that will settle, such as an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction. Others take it every day for months or years for an ongoing condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or ulcerative colitis.
If you take prednisone long term, your doctor will settle you on a maintenance dose. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. It may need to go up for a time if your condition flares, or if you have surgery, a fever, an infection, or another serious illness, and it may come down again afterwards. Do not adjust it yourself.
How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Call your doctor if you feel unwell while your dose is being lowered or after you finish.
Prednisone formulations:
- Prednisone 1 mg tablets
- Prednisone 2.5 mg tablets
- Prednisone 5 mg tablets

- Prednisone 50 mg tablets
- Prednisone Oral Solution 5 mg per 5 mL
- Prednisone Intensol™ Oral Solution (Concentrate) 5 mg per mL
- Prednisone delayed-release tablets (Rayos) 1 mg, 2 mg, and 5 mg

Take gabapentin exactly as prescribed. Your dose may differ from the ranges shown here.
Usual Gabapentin Dose for Epilepsy (immediate-release):
Patients 12 years and older Dose: starting dose gabapentin 300 mg 3 times a day, which may be titrated up to a maximum dose of 600 mg 3 times a day if needed.

## Empagliflozin side effects
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction: hives, difficult breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Seek medical attention right away if you have signs of a serious genital infection (penis or vagina): burning, itching, odor, discharge, pain, tenderness, redness or swelling of the genital or rectal area, fever, not feeling well. These symptoms may get worse quickly.
Empagliflozin may cause serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out;
- low blood sugar -- headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery;
- dehydration --dizziness, confusion, feeling very thirsty, less urination;
- ketoacidosis (too much acid in the blood) --nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, confusion, unusual drowsiness, or trouble breathing; or
- signs of a bladder infection --pain or burning when you urinate, blood in your urine, pain in pelvis or back.
Common side effects of empagliflozin may include:
- a bladder infection; or
- yeast infection in women (vaginal itching or discharge).
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What other drugs will affect tamsulosin?
Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood and increase the risk of side effects.
Do not take tamsulosin with:
- strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole
- other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin
Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take:
- moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin
- strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine
- cimetidine
- warfarin
- medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra). Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms.
Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg. Your doctor will decide what is right for you.
No dose change is needed if you take tamsulosin with nifedipine, atenolol, enalapril, digoxin, theophylline, or furosemide.
This list is not complete, and many other medicines may interact with tamsulosin. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

## How does fluoxetine (Prozac) work?
Fluoxetine works by blocking the reabsorption (reuptake) of serotonin in the brain, leaving more of it active between nerve cells. Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that helps regulate mood, emotions, and sleep. By increasing the availability of serotonin, fluoxetine can relieve symptoms of depression, anxiety, and OCD.
Fluoxetine belongs to a class of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). SSRIs are one of the most commonly prescribed antidepressant classes because they are generally well-tolerated and effective across a range of conditions.
Most people need to take fluoxetine for 4 to 6 weeks before feeling the full effects.

## What other drugs will affect tramadol?
You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines. Tramadol is broken down by two liver enzymes called CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, and medicines that block or speed up these enzymes change how much tramadol and how much of its active form are in your body. Because starting one of these medicines and stopping one both shift the balance, tell your doctor whenever you begin or finish a course of an antibiotic, antifungal medication, heart or blood pressure medication, seizure medication, or medicine to treat HIV or hepatitis C.
Many other drugs can be dangerous when used with tramadol. Tell your doctor if you also use:
- medicine for allergies, asthma, blood pressure, motion sickness, irritable bowel, or overactive bladder
- other opioid medicines
- buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, or pentazocine. These opioids work differently and can block tramadol's pain-relieving effect or bring on sudden withdrawal symptoms, so they are generally not taken with tramadol
- a benzodiazepine sedative like Valium, Klonopin, or Xanax
- sleep medicine, muscle relaxers, or other drugs that make you drowsy
- drugs that affect serotonin, such as antidepressants, stimulants, or medicine for migraines or Parkinson's disease
- carbamazepine, which is not recommended with tramadol because it can significantly reduce tramadol's pain-relieving effect and add to the risk of seizures
- digoxin or warfarin, which need extra monitoring when taken with tramadol.
This list is not complete. Other drugs may interact with tramadol, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here.

Amlodipine besylate is a prescription medicine used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to prevent certain types of angina (chest pain). It belongs to a class of medications called calcium channel blockers.

## What is Tirzepatide?
Tirzepatide is a once-weekly injection available as two brands: Zepbound (for weight loss, weight management, and obstructive sleep apnea) and Mounjaro (for type 2 diabetes and to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in those with type 2 diabetes at high risk).
Zepbound (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity, or in overweight adults with at least one weight-related medical condition. Zepbound is also approved to treat moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity.
Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar (glucose) levels, used alongside diet and exercise. It is also approved to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events.
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist, meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar. It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes. It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.
